blocks.x: I. Wrong Ways of Looking at Christ's Sufferings

s: 1. First, some people think about Christ's sufferings in a way that makes them angry at the Jews. They sing and grieve over poor Judas, and then they are satisfied. It is just like the way they are used to complaining about other people. They condemn them and spend their time with their enemies.
This kind of exercise could truly be called thinking about the wickedness of Judas and the Jews, not about the sufferings of Christ.
2. Second, others have pointed out the different benefits and fruits that come from thinking about Christ's Passion.

Here people are misled by a saying credited to Albertus. It says that thinking just once, on the surface, about Christ's sufferings is better than fasting for a whole year or praying through the Psalms every day, and so on.
So people blindly follow him and act against the true fruits of Christ's Passion. For they are looking for their own selfish gain in it.

That is why they decorate themselves with pictures and little books, with letters and crucifixes. Some even go so far as to imagine that these things protect them from the dangers of water, fire, and the sword, and from every other danger.
In this way they expect Christ's suffering to keep them from suffering. But that goes against its nature and character.

3. A third group feels so sorry for Christ that they weep and grieve for him because he was so innocent. They are like the women who followed Christ out of Jerusalem. He rebuked them and told them they should rather weep for themselves and for their children.

These are the people who run far away in the middle of the Passion season. They get great benefit from Christ's leaving Bethany and from the pain and sorrow of the Virgin Mary. But they never get any further.
So they put off the Passion for many hours. And only God knows whether this is planned more for sleeping than for staying awake.
Among these fanatics are also those who taught what great blessings come from the holy mass. In their simple way, they think it is enough just to attend mass.

Some teachers have led us to this with their sayings. They say that the mass works opere operati, non opere operantis, and is acceptable in itself, even without our merit and worthiness. They act as if that were enough.
But the mass was not set up for the sake of its own worthiness. It was given to test us, and especially so that we would think deeply about Christ's sufferings.
Where this does not happen, we turn the mass into a passing work that bears no fruit, however good it may be in itself.
What good is it to you that God is God, if he is not God to you?

What good is it that eating and drinking are healthy and good in themselves, if they are not healthy for you? And we should fear that our many masses never make us any better, if we do not look for the true fruit in them.

blocks.x: II. The Right Way of Looking at Christ's Sufferings

s: 4. Fourth, the people who think about Christ's Passion in the right way are those who look at Christ so that their hearts are filled with terror at the sight. Their conscience sinks at once into despair.

This terror should rise up in you so that you see God's severe anger and his unchanging seriousness about sin and sinners. He was not willing for his only, dearly loved Son to set sinners free unless the Son paid the costly ransom for them. As Isaiah 53:8 says: "He was struck for the wrongdoing of my people."
What happens to the sinner, then, when the dear child is struck like this?

There must be a seriousness here that words cannot express and no one can bear. For a person so great beyond measure goes out to meet it, suffers, and dies for it. If you think very deeply about this, that God's Son, the eternal wisdom of the Father, suffers himself, you will be filled with terror. And the more you think about it, the deeper the impression will be.
5. Fifth, you must believe deeply and never doubt in the least that you are the one who put Christ through this torment.
For it was surely your sins that did it.

This is how St. Peter struck the Jews with terror, like a bolt of lightning, in Acts 2:36-37. He spoke to all of them together: "You crucified him." So three thousand people were filled with terror that same day. Trembling, they cried out to the apostles: "Dear brothers, what are we to do?"
So when you see the nails piercing his hands, firmly believe that this is your doing.
When you see his crown of thorns, believe that the thorns are your wicked thoughts, and so on.
6. Sixth, now see this: where one thorn pierces Christ, more than a thousand thorns should pierce you. Yes, they should pierce you like this forever, and even more painfully.

Where one nail is driven through his hands and feet, you should suffer nails like these forever, and even more painful ones. And this will indeed happen to those who let Christ's sufferings be lost and wasted on them.
For Christ, this serious mirror, will not lie or mock. Whatever he says must surely come true.

7. Seventh, St. Bernard was so terrified by Christ's sufferings that he said: I thought I was safe. I knew nothing of the eternal sentence passed on me in heaven. Then I saw that the eternal Son of God took pity on me. He stepped forward and offered himself for me in that same judgment.
Oh, it is not right for me to keep on playing and feeling safe when there is such seriousness behind those sufferings.
So he commanded the women: "Do not weep for me. Weep for yourselves and for your children."
Luke 23:28. And in verse 31 he gives the reason: "For if they do these things to the green tree, what will be done to the dry one?"
It is as if he were saying: Learn from my torment what you have deserved and how you should be repaid.
For here the saying is true: a little dog was killed to frighten a big one.
In the same way the prophet also said: "All generations will mourn and weep over themselves more than over him." It does not say they will mourn for him, but for themselves rather than for him.
In the same way, the apostles were also filled with terror in Acts 2:27, as mentioned before, so that they said to the apostles: "Oh, brothers, what are we to do?"
So the church also sings: I will think about it carefully, and so my soul within me will wear itself out.

8. Eighth, a person must practice this point with skill. For the benefit of Christ's sufferings depends almost completely on this: that a person comes to truly know himself, and is terrified and slain before himself.
Where a person does not come to this point, Christ's sufferings have been of no true benefit to him.

For the natural work that is typical of Christ's sufferings is to make all people equal and alike. Christ was horribly tortured in body and soul in our sins. So we too, like him, must be tortured in our consciences by our sins.
This does not happen through many words. It happens through deep thoughts and a deep awareness of our sins.

Here is an example. Suppose a criminal were sentenced because he had killed the child of a prince or king. And suppose you were safe, singing and playing as if you were completely innocent. Then someone seized you in a terrifying way and proved to you that you had made it possible for that wicked man to do the deed. You would be in the greatest distress, especially if your own conscience also turned against you.
You should be much more anxious than that when you think about Christ's sufferings.

For the evildoers, the Jews, have now judged and banished God. Even so, they were the servants of your sins. You are truly the one who strangled and crucified the Son of God through your sins, as has been said.
9. Ninth, a person may find that he is so hard and barren that Christ's sufferings do not terrify him or lead him to a knowledge of him. That person should fear and tremble.

It cannot be any other way. You must become like the picture and the sufferings of Christ, whether that happens in life or in hell. At the time of death, if not sooner, you must fall into terror. You must tremble and shake and go through everything Christ suffered on the cross.
It is truly terrible to have to deal with this on your deathbed. So you should pray that God will soften your heart and let you think about Christ's Passion in a way that bears fruit.
For we cannot think deeply about Christ's sufferings on our own, unless God sinks them into our hearts.

Also, neither this meditation nor any other teaching is given to you so that you would rush at it on your own to get it done. First you are to seek and long for God's grace, so that you may do it through God's grace and not by your own strength.

That is why the people mentioned above never deal with Christ's sufferings in the right way. They never call on God for this. Instead, they come up with their own way, based on their own ability. And they treat those sufferings in a purely human way that bears no fruit.

10. Tenth, suppose someone thinks about God's sufferings in this way for a day, an hour, or even a quarter of an hour. We want to say freely and openly that this is better than fasting a whole year and praying through the Psalms every day. Yes, it is better than hearing a hundred masses.
For this kind of meditation changes a person's character. He is born again, made new, almost as in baptism.

Then Christ's suffering does its true, natural, and noble work. It kills the old Adam. It drives out all the lust, pleasure, and security that a person may get from God's creatures, just as Christ was abandoned by everyone, even by God.
11. Eleventh, this work is not in our hands. So it sometimes happens that we pray for it and do not receive it at that time. Even so, we should not despair or stop praying.

Sometimes it comes when we are not praying for it, as God knows and wills. For it wants to be free and unbound. Then a person is troubled in his conscience and deeply unhappy with his own life. It may easily happen that he does not know that Christ's Passion is doing this very thing in him. Perhaps he was not aware of it. In the same way, the others thought about Christ's Passion so exclusively that, in their knowledge of themselves, they could not get free from that state of meditation.

With the first group, Christ's sufferings are quiet and true. With the others, they are a show and false. And by its nature, God often turns the page. So those who do not meditate on the Passion really do meditate on it. Those who hear mass do not hear it. And those who do not hear it do hear it.

blocks.x: III. The Comfort of Christ's Sufferings

s: 12. Up to now we have been in Passion Week and have kept Good Friday in the right way. Now we come to Easter and Christ's resurrection.

When a person sees his sins in this light and is completely terrified in his conscience, he must be careful. His sins must not stay in his conscience like this, or nothing but pure doubt will come of it. Just as the sins flowed out of Christ and we became aware of them, so we should pour them back onto him and set our conscience free.

So be careful not to act like twisted people. They bite and eat themselves up in their hearts with their sins. They run here and there with their good works or with their own ways of making up for sin. Or they even work their way out of this condition with indulgences and get rid of their sins. But that is impossible. And sadly, this false refuge of making amends and going on pilgrimages has spread far and wide.

13. Thirteenth. Then throw your sins off yourself and onto Christ. Believe with a joyful spirit that your sins are his wounds and sufferings, that he carries them and pays for them. As Isaiah 53:6 says: "Jehovah has laid on him the wrongdoing of us all." And St. Peter says in his first letter, 2:24: "He himself carried our sins in his body on the tree" of the cross. And St. Paul says in 2 Corinthians 5:21: "He who knew no sin was made to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him."
You must lean on these passages and others like them with all your weight. And the harder your conscience torments you, the more you must do so.
If you do not do this, and you miss the chance to quiet your heart, you will never find peace. In the end you will still despair in doubt.
For suppose we deal with our sins in our own conscience. We let them stay inside us and nurse them in our hearts. Then they become much too strong for us to handle. And they will live forever.
But when we see that they are laid on Christ and that he has conquered them by his resurrection, and we believe this without fear, then they are dead. They have become nothing.
For they cannot stay on Christ. There they are swallowed up by his resurrection. And now you see no wound and no pain in him, that is, no sign of sin.

This is what St. Paul says in Romans 4:25: he was given up because of our wrongs and raised so that we would be declared righteous. That is, in his sufferings he made our sins known and also crucified them. But by his resurrection he makes us righteous and free from all sin, even if we believe this in different ways.
14. Fourteenth. Now if you cannot believe, then, as I said before, you should pray to God for faith.
For this is something that is entirely free and in God's hands. It is also given in the same way, sometimes knowingly and sometimes secretly, as was just said about suffering.

15. But now stir yourself toward this goal. First, stop looking at Christ's sufferings. They have already done their work and terrified you. Instead, push through every difficulty and look at his friendly heart. See how full of love it is toward you. That love moved him to carry the heavy load of your conscience and your sin.
Then your heart will become loving and sweet toward him, and the certainty of your faith will grow stronger.

Then climb higher, through the heart of Christ to the heart of God. See that Christ could not have loved you if God had not willed it in eternal love. Christ obeys that love in his love for you. There you will find the good, divine heart of a Father. And, as Christ says, you will be drawn to the Father through Christ in this way.
Then you will understand what Christ says in John 3:16: "God loved the world so much that he gave his only Son," and so on.

That is what it means to know God rightly: when we grasp him not by his power and wisdom, which terrify us, but by his goodness and love. Then our faith and trust can stand firm and unshaken. And in this way a person is truly born again in God.

16. Sixteenth. Your heart may now be established in Christ like this. You may be an enemy of sin out of love, and not out of fear of punishment. Then Christ's sufferings should also be an example for your whole life. You should think about them in a different way.

Up to now we have looked at Christ's Passion as a sacrament that works in us while we undergo it. Now we look at it so that we also do the work. It goes like this: if a day of sorrow or sickness weighs you down, think how small that is compared with the thorns and nails of Christ.
If you have to do something, or not do something, that you find unpleasant, think how Christ was led here and there, tied up and a prisoner.
Does pride attack you? Look at how your Lord was mocked and disgraced along with murderers.
Do sexual impurity and lust push against you? Think how bitter it was for Christ to have his tender flesh torn, pierced, and beaten again and again.
Do hatred and envy fight against you, or do you want revenge? Remember how Christ, with many tears and cries, prayed for you and for all his enemies. And he surely had more reason to want revenge.
If trouble or any hardship of body or soul hits you, strengthen your heart and say: Oh, why shouldn't I also suffer a little? My Lord sweat blood in the garden because of fear and grief.
A servant would be lazy and shameful if he wanted to lie in bed while his master had to fight the agony of death.
17. See, this is how we can find strength and comfort in Christ against every vice and bad habit.
That is the right way to keep Christ's Passion, and that is the fruit of his suffering. Whoever practices it in this way does better than by hearing the whole Passion or reading all the masses.

And the people who are called true Christians are those who build the life and name of Christ into their own lives. As St. Paul says in Galatians 5:24: "And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts."
For Christ's Passion must not be handled with words and outward show, but in our lives and in truth.

So St. Paul urges us in Hebrews 12:3: "Think about him who put up with such opposition from sinners against himself, so that you do not grow tired and lose heart in your souls." And St. Peter says in his first letter, 4:1: "As Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves too with the same mind."
But this kind of meditation has now fallen out of use and is very rare, even though the letters of St. Paul and St. Peter are full of it.
We have turned the real thing into a mere show. We have painted the meditation on Christ's sufferings only in letters and on walls.
1. The holy sacrament of the altar is also called the sacrament of the holy and true body of Christ. Like the sacrament of holy baptism, it has three parts. We need to know all three.

The first part is the sacrament itself, which is the sign. The second is what the sacrament means. The third is the faith that both of these call for. These three parts must be found in every sacrament.
The sacrament must be outward and visible, with some physical form. Its meaning must be inward and spiritual, inside a person's spirit. And faith must take hold of both and put them to use.

2. The sacrament, or outward sign, comes in the form of bread and wine, just as the sign of baptism is water. But the sign is not just the bread and wine themselves. It is the use of them, when we eat and drink. In the same way, the water of baptism is used when a person is dipped into it or has it poured over them.
The sacrament, or sign, has to be received, or at least longed for, if it is going to bring a blessing.

These days the people are not given both kinds, the bread and the wine, every day, as they were long ago. That is not necessary anyway. The priests take it every day in front of the people. It is enough for the people to long for it every day and to receive one of the two kinds at the proper time, as the Christian Church orders and offers.
3. Still, I think it would be good for the Church, meeting in a general council, to decide once again that everyone, not just the priests, should be given both kinds.
This is not because one kind is not enough. In fact, the simple longing of faith is enough, as St. Augustine says: "Why are you getting your stomach and teeth ready?

Just believe, and you have already received the sacrament." No, the reason is that it would be fitting and right to give the form, or sign, of the sacrament completely, not just part of it. I said the same about baptism: it would be better to dip people fully into the water than to pour it on them, so that the sign is whole and perfect.
This sacrament stands for the complete union and undivided fellowship of the saints, as we will see. Using only one part of the sacrament shows this poorly and in a way that does not fit.

Also, using the cup is not as dangerous as people think. After all, people seldom go to this sacrament. And Christ knew very well about every danger that would come. Even so, He chose to set up both kinds for all His Christians to use.

4. The meaning, or purpose, of this sacrament is the fellowship of all saints. That is where its common name comes from: synaxis or communio, which means "fellowship." And communicare means to take part in this fellowship, or, as we say, to go to the sacrament. This is because Christ and all saints are one spiritual body. It is like the people of a city, who form one community and one body. Each citizen is a member of the others and a member of the whole city.

So all the saints are members of Christ and of the Church. The Church is God's spiritual and eternal city. Anyone who is taken into this city is said to be welcomed into the community of saints. That person is made part of Christ's spiritual body and becomes a member of Him.

On the other hand, excommunicare means to put someone out of the community and cut a member off from this body. In our language we call that "putting someone under the ban." Yet there is a difference, as I will show in the next treatise, which is about the ban.

So receiving the bread and wine of this sacrament means nothing other than receiving a sure sign. It is a sign that you share in this fellowship and are joined into one body with Christ and all saints.
It is as if a citizen were given a sign, a document, or some other token. It would prove that he is a citizen of the city and a member of the community.
That is just what St. Paul says: "We are all one bread and one body, because we all share in one bread and one cup."
[1 Corinthians 10:17]

5. This fellowship works like this. All the spiritual riches of Christ and His saints are given to and shared with the person who receives this sacrament. And in return, all that person's sufferings and sins are shared with them. In this way love produces love and unites everyone.

To take our everyday picture further: it is like a city where every citizen shares everything with all the others. They share the city's name, honor, freedom, trade, customs, ways of doing things, help, support, protection, and so on. On the other hand, they also share every danger: fire and flood, enemies and death, losses, taxes, and so on.
Whoever wants a share in the common gains must also share in the losses. And he must always answer love with love.
Here we see that whoever harms one citizen harms the whole city and all its citizens. And whoever does good to one citizen earns favor and thanks from all the others.

It is the same with our physical body. St. Paul says so in 1 Corinthians 12, where he explains this sacrament in a spiritual way. The parts of the body care for each other. If one part suffers, all the parts suffer with it. If one part is honored, all the parts are glad with it.
[1 Corinthians 12:25–26]

We can see this plainly. If someone's foot hurts, even just the smallest toe, the eye looks at it right away. The fingers take hold of it, the face frowns, and the whole body bends down to it. Every part is concerned about this one small part. And when it is taken care of, all the other parts are glad.
Anyone who wants to understand this sacrament must think this picture through carefully. The Scriptures use it for the sake of people who have not had much schooling.

6. So in this sacrament God Himself, through the priest, gives a person a sure sign. It shows that, in the same way, he will be united with Christ and His saints and will share everything with them. Christ's sufferings and life will be his own, along with the lives and sufferings of all the saints. So whoever hurts him hurts Christ and all the saints. As God says through the prophet, "Whoever touches you touches the apple of My eye" [Zechariah 2:8]. On the other hand, whoever is kind to him is kind to Christ and all His saints. As He says, "What you have done for one of the least of My brothers, you have done for Me."
[Matthew 25:40] In return, he must be willing to share all the burdens and troubles of Christ and His saints, both their sorrow and their joy.
We will look more closely at these two sides of the fellowship.
7. Now, trouble attacks us in more than one way.
First, there is the sin that stays in our flesh even after baptism. It is the pull toward anger, hatred, pride, sexual impurity, and so on. It attacks us as long as we live.

Against this sin we need the help of the church family and of Christ, so that they can fight it together with us. But we also need Christ and His saints to pray for us before God. Then our sin will not be counted against us by God's strict judgment.

So God gives us this sacrament to give us strength and courage against these sins. It is as if He were saying: "Look, many kinds of sin are attacking you. Take this sign. With it I give you My promise that sin is attacking not only you, but also My Son Christ and all His saints in heaven and on earth.
So be brave and confident. You are not fighting alone. Great help and support are all around you."
King David also says about this bread: "Bread makes a person's heart strong" [Psalm 104:15]. And in other places the Scriptures describe this sacrament as something that gives strength.
So in Acts 9 we read that St. Paul was baptized, and when he had eaten some food, he grew strong again.
[Acts 9:19] Second, the evil spirit attacks us without stopping, with many sins and troubles.
Third, the world is full of wickedness. It tempts us and persecutes us, and it is completely bad.
Finally, our own guilty conscience attacks us. It brings up our past sins, and it fills us with fear of death and of the pains of hell.
All these troubles wear us out and make us weak, unless we look for strength in this fellowship and find it there.

8. Maybe someone is in despair. Maybe his sinful conscience troubles him, or he is terrified of death, or some other burden weighs on his heart, and he wants to be free of all of it. Then let him go joyfully to the sacrament of the altar. There he can lay down his grief in the middle of the church family and ask the whole company of the spiritual body for help. It is just like a citizen whose property has been damaged or ruined by his enemies. He brings his complaint to the town council and his fellow citizens and asks them for help.

That is why God gives us His endless grace and mercy in this sacrament. There we can lay down all our misery and trouble and place it on the church family, and above all on Christ. Then we can joyfully strengthen and comfort ourselves and say: "I am a sinner and I have fallen. This or that trouble has come upon me. Even so, I will go to the sacrament to receive a sign from God. It shows that Christ's righteousness, life, and sufferings are on my side. So are all the holy angels, all the blessed in heaven, and all godly people on earth.
If I die, I am not alone in death. If I suffer, they suffer with me.
I have shared all my trouble with Christ and the saints, because I have a sure sign that they love me."
You see, this is the good that comes from this sacrament. This is how we should use it. Then the heart cannot help being glad and comforted.
9. So when you have received this sacrament, or want to receive it, you must in turn share the troubles of the church family too, as was said.
But what are these troubles?

Christ in heaven, the angels, and all the saints have no troubles of their own, except when harm is done to the truth and to God's Word. In fact, as we said, every harm and every blessing that comes to any of the saints on earth touches them.

That is where your heart must reach out in love and devotion. You must learn that this sacrament is a sacrament of love. Love and service are given to you, and in return you must give love and service to Christ and to His people in need.

You must feel sorrow over all the dishonor done to Christ in His holy Word. You must feel sorrow over all the misery of Christians everywhere and all the unfair suffering of innocent people. The whole world is overflowing with these things. You must fight, work, and pray. And if you cannot do more, you must feel deep sympathy from your heart.
That is how you carry, in your turn, the troubles and hardships of Christ and His saints.
This is where Paul's saying fits:
"Carry each other's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ."
[Galatians 6:2] You see, in this way you hold them all up, and they all hold you up in return. Everything is shared, both good and bad.
Then everything becomes easy, and the evil spirit cannot win against a community like that.
When Christ set up the sacrament, He said: "This is My body, which is given for you. This is My blood, which is poured out for you. Whenever you do this, remember Me."

[Luke 22:19–20] It is as if He were saying: "I am the Head. I will be the first to give Myself for you. I will make your suffering and trouble My own and carry it for you. Then you, in your turn, can do the same for Me and for one another. You can share everything in Me and with Me. Let this sacrament be a sure token of all this for you, so that you do not forget Me. Every day, remember and encourage one another by what I have done for you and am still doing. Then you will be made strong by it, and you will also be patient with one another."
10. This is also a reason, in fact the main reason, why we receive this sacrament many times, while baptism is given only once.
Baptism is the beginning of a new life and the door into it. Along the way, endless troubles attack us through sins and suffering, both our own and other people's.
As was said, the devil, the world, and our own flesh and conscience never stop chasing us and pressing us down.

So we need the strength, support, and help of Christ and His saints. These are promised to us in this sacrament, as if by a sure token. Through it we are made one with them and joined into one body with them. And all our suffering is laid down in the middle of the church family.
That is why this holy sacrament does little or no good for people who have no troubles or worries, or who do not feel their hardships.
It is given only to those who need strength and comfort. It is for people with fearful hearts and terrified consciences, who are attacked by sin or have even fallen into sin.
What could it do for people who are untroubled and feel falsely safe? They do not need it, and they do not want it.
As the Mother of God says, "He fills only the hungry, and He comforts those who are in distress." [Luke 1:53]

11. So Christ wanted His disciples to be truly worthy and well prepared for this sacrament. That is why He first made them sad. He told them about His going away and His death, and this troubled them deeply.
Then He frightened them badly when He said that one of them would betray Him.

[Matthew 25:21 and following] Now they were full of sorrow and worry, and they were troubled by the sorrow and sin of betrayal. That is when they were worthy, and He gave them His holy body to make them strong.

In this way He teaches us that this sacrament gives strength and comfort to those who are troubled and distressed by sin and evil. St. Augustine says the same: "This food wants only hungry souls. No one avoids it more than a soul that is already full and does not need it."
In the same way, the Jews had to eat the Passover with bitter herbs, standing up and in a hurry. This also shows that this sacrament calls for souls that are longing, needy, and sad.

Now suppose someone makes the troubles of Christ and of all Christians his own. Suppose he defends the truth, stands against wrongdoing, and helps carry the needs of innocent people and the sufferings of all Christians. He will find plenty of trouble and hardship. And that is on top of what his own evil nature, the world, the devil, and sin put on him every day.

And God wants and plans to set so many hunting dogs on us, to chase us and to give us bitter herbs everywhere. He does this so that we will long for this strength and delight in the holy sacrament. That is how we become worthy of it, which means that we long for it.
12. So He wants us to receive it often. Then we will remember Him and practice this fellowship by following His example.
If His example were no longer kept in front of us, the fellowship would soon be forgotten too.

Sadly, that is what we see today. Many masses are held, yet the Christian fellowship has completely died out. This fellowship should be preached, practiced, and kept in front of us by Christ's example. Now we hardly know what this sacrament is for or how it should be used. In fact, with our masses we often destroy this fellowship and twist everything.
This is the fault of the preachers. They do not preach the Gospel or the sacraments. Instead they preach made-up human stories about all the works people should do and how to live the right way.

But long ago this sacrament was used properly. People were taught to understand this fellowship so well that they even gathered food and goods in the church. There they shared them out among those in need, as St. Paul writes [1 Corinthians 11:21].
A trace of this still remains in the word "collect," which is still used in the mass. It means a general collection, like when a common fund is gathered to give to the poor.
That was the time when so many people became martyrs and saints.

There were fewer masses, but those masses brought much strength and blessing. Christians took care of each other, helped each other, felt for each other, and carried each other's burdens and troubles.
All of this has disappeared. What is left is just the many masses, and the many people who receive this sacrament without understanding or living out what it means at all.

13. Some people, of course, want to share the benefits but not the cost. They are glad to hear that in this sacrament the help, fellowship, and support of all the saints are promised and given to them. But they are afraid of the world. So they are not willing to do their part for this fellowship in return. They will not help the poor, put up with sins, care for the sick, suffer with those who suffer, or pray for others. They will not defend the truth or work for the reform of the Church and of all Christians, if it puts their life, property, or honor at risk.
They do not want to suffer disfavor, harm, shame, or death. Yet God wants them to be driven, for the sake of the truth and their neighbors, to long for the great grace and strength of this sacrament.
They are selfish people, and this sacrament does them no good.
It is just like a citizen who wants the community to help him, protect him, and give him freedom, but who will do nothing for it in return and will not serve it. We could not stand such a person.
No, if we want Christ and His saints to make our troubles their own, we must make other people's troubles our own. Then the fellowship will be complete, and the sacrament will be given its due.
The sacrament brings no blessing and has no meaning unless love grows every day. That love must change a person so much that he becomes one with all others.
14. To picture this fellowship, God chose signs for the sacrament that fit this purpose in every way. Their very form urges us and moves us toward this fellowship.

Think of how bread is made from many grains that are ground and mixed together. Out of many separate grains comes one loaf of bread. Each grain loses its own shape and body and takes on the shared body of the bread. In the same way, drops of wine lose their own form and become one wine. That is how it should be with us. And that is how it really is, if we use this sacrament the right way.

Christ, together with all saints, takes on our form out of love. He fights alongside us against sin, death, and every evil [Philippians 2:7]. This lights such a love in us that we take on His form. We rely on His righteousness, His life, and His blessed joy. Through this exchange of His blessings and our troubles, we become one loaf, one bread, one body, one drink, and we share everything.
Paul says this is a great sacrament [Ephesians 5:32]: that Christ and the Church are one flesh and bone [Ephesians 5:31].

In the same way, this same love should change us. We should make the weaknesses of all other Christians our own. We should take on their form and their needs, and give them all the good we are able to give, so that they can enjoy it [Judges 9:2].
That is real fellowship, and that is the true meaning of this sacrament.
In this way love changes us into one another and brings us into fellowship with one another. Without love, no such change can happen.
15. He chose this double form, bread and wine, instead of anything else, to show even more clearly the union and fellowship in this sacrament.
There is no union closer, deeper, or harder to break than the union between food and the person who eats it. The food goes into him, becomes part of his very nature, and becomes one with his being.
Other ways of joining things, with nails, glue, ropes, and so on, do not turn the joined things into one substance that cannot be divided.

In the sacrament we become united with Christ and are made one body with all the saints. So He cares about us and acts for us as if He were what we are. What matters to us matters to Him as much as it does to us, and even more. On the other hand, we also care about Him as if we were what He is. And in the end we really will be, when we are made like Him. As St. John says, "We know that when He appears, we will be like Him" [1 John 3:2]. That is how complete the fellowship of Christ and all the saints with us is.
Our sins attack Him, and His righteousness protects us. The union makes everything shared, until at last, on the last day, He destroys sin in us completely and makes us like Himself.
In the same way, by the same love, we are to be united with our neighbors, we in them and they in us.

16. On top of this, He did not set up this double form by itself alone. He gave His true, natural flesh in the bread and His natural, true blood in the wine. He did this to give us a truly perfect sacrament, or sign.

The bread is changed into His true, natural body, and the wine into His true, natural blood. Just as truly, we are drawn and changed into the spiritual body, that is, into the fellowship of Christ and all saints. Through this sacrament we are given all the virtues and mercies of Christ and His saints. It is like what was said above about a citizen who is taken into the city and made part of it, sharing in the protection and freedom of the whole community.

That is why He did not set up just one form, but two separate forms: His flesh under the bread and His blood under the wine. This shows that all of it belongs to us. His life and good works belong to us; His flesh stands for them, and He did them in His flesh. His suffering and martyrdom also belong to us; His blood stands for them, and in them He shed His blood. And because we are drawn into this fellowship, we may use and enjoy all of it.

17. All this makes it clear that this holy sacrament is nothing but a sign from God. In it, Christ and all saints are promised, granted, and given to us, with all their works, sufferings, merits, mercies, and riches. This is to comfort and strengthen everyone who is worried and sad, and who is hunted by the devil, sin, the world, the flesh, and every evil. And receiving the sacrament means nothing other than longing for all this and firmly believing that it will happen.
Next comes the third part of the sacrament: faith. Everything depends on it.
It is not enough to know what the sacrament is and what it means.

It is not enough for you to know that it is a fellowship, a gracious exchange or mixing of our sin and suffering with the righteousness of Christ and His saints. You must also long for it and firmly believe that you have received it.
This is where the devil and our own nature fight their hardest battle, so that faith will not stand firm at all.

Some people push their clever tricks and fine arguments so far that they ask where the bread goes when it is changed into Christ's flesh, and where the wine goes when it is changed into His blood. They also ask how the whole Christ, His flesh and His blood, can fit into such a small piece of bread and such a little wine.
Why does that matter?
It is enough to know that it is a sign from God, in which Christ's flesh and blood are truly present. How and where, we leave to Him.

18. Make sure you practice and strengthen your faith. Then, when you are sad or your sins trouble you, and you go to the sacrament or hear mass, you will go with a heartfelt longing for this sacrament and for what it means. Do not doubt that you have what the sacrament stands for. Be certain that Christ and all His saints come to you. They bring all their virtues, sufferings, and mercies, to live, work, suffer, and die with you. They come to be completely yours and to share everything with you.
If you practice and strengthen this faith, you will find out what a rich and joyful wedding supper and celebration your God has prepared for you on the altar.

Then you will understand what the great feast of King Ahasuerus means [Esther 1:5]. You will see what that wedding is for which God has killed His oxen and fattened calves, as it says in the Gospel [Matthew 22:2 and following]. And your heart will become truly free and confident, strong and brave, against every enemy.
Who would be afraid of any disaster if he is sure that Christ and all His saints are with him and share everything with him, bad or good?
That is why we read that Christ's disciples broke this bread and ate it with great gladness of heart.

This work is so great that our small, weak souls do not dare to long for it, let alone hope for it or expect it. So it is necessary and helpful to go to the sacrament often, or at least to practice and strengthen this faith in the daily mass. Everything depends on this faith, and the sacrament was set up for its sake.
If you doubt, you dishonor God more than in any other way. You treat Him as someone who does not keep His word, as a liar.
If you cannot believe, pray for faith, as was said earlier in the other treatise.
19. Also make sure you become a companion to every person. Never shut anyone out because of hatred or anger. This sacrament of fellowship, love, and unity cannot put up with quarreling and division.

You must let other people's weaknesses and needs weigh on your heart, as if they were your own. And you must offer them your strength, as if it were theirs. That is what Christ does for you in the sacrament.

That is what we mean when we say we are changed into one another through love. Many little pieces become one bread and one drink. Each gives up its own form and takes on a form that belongs to everyone.
That is why people who slander others, and who wickedly judge and look down on others, cannot help receiving death in the sacrament, as St. Paul writes [1 Corinthians 11:29].

They do not do for their neighbors what they want from Christ and what the sacrament points to. They wish their neighbors nothing good. They have no sympathy for them. They do not welcome them the way they want Christ to welcome them. Then they become so blind that they do not know what else to do in this sacrament, except to fear and honor Christ in the sacrament with their prayers and devotion.

Once they have done this, they think they have done all they need to do. But Christ gave His body for this purpose: that the meaning of the sacrament, which is fellowship and love for one another, would be put into practice. His own natural body is meant to count for less than His spiritual body, which is the fellowship of His saints.

What matters most to Him, especially in this sacrament, is this. He wants our faith in the fellowship with Him and His saints to be practiced rightly and to grow strong in us. And He wants us, in keeping with that faith, to practice our fellowship with one another rightly.
They do not see this purpose of Christ. In their devotion they say and hear mass every day, yet they stay the same every day. In fact, they get worse every day and do not even notice it.
So pay attention. It is more important for you to recognize the spiritual body of Christ than His natural body. And faith in the spiritual body is more important than faith in the natural body.
In this sacrament, the natural body without the spiritual body does us no good. A change has to happen, and it has to show itself through love.

20. Many people pay no attention to this change of love and faith. Instead they rely on the idea that the mass or the sacrament is, as they say, opus gratum opere operato. That means a work that pleases God all by itself, even if the people who do it do not please Him.
From this they conclude that it is still a good thing to have many masses, no matter how unworthily they are said. They think the harm falls on those who say or use them unworthily.
I let everyone have his own opinion, but I do not like such made-up stories.
If you want to talk like that, then every creature and every work pleases God by itself. As it is written, "God saw all His works, and they pleased Him."
[Genesis 1:31] But what good comes of it if someone misuses bread, wine, gold, and every good created thing, even though in themselves they please God?
None at all. The result is condemnation.
It is the same here. The more precious the sacrament is, the greater the harm that comes on the whole church family when it is misused.
It was not set up for its own sake, just to please God. It was set up for our sake, so that we would use it rightly, practice our faith through it, and through it become pleasing to God.
If it is only an opus operatum, it does nothing but harm. It must become an opus operantis.

Bread and wine do nothing but harm if they are not used, no matter how much they please God in themselves. In the same way, it is not enough for the sacrament to be prepared (that is, opus operatum). It must also be used in faith (that is, opus operantis).

We must be careful that such dangerous explanations do not turn our minds away from the sacrament's power and strength. Otherwise faith will die out completely, because people feel falsely safe once the sacrament has been carried out on the outside.
All this happens because in this sacrament they pay more attention to Christ's natural body than to the fellowship, the spiritual body.
Christ on the cross was also a finished work, and it pleased God very much. But to this day the Jews have found it a stumbling block, because they did not make it a work to be used in faith.

So make sure the sacrament is an opus operantis for you, that is, a work that is put to use. And make sure it pleases God, not because of what it is in itself, but because of your faith and the right way you use it.
God's Word also pleases God by itself. But it harms me when it does not also please God inside me.
In short, phrases like opus operatum and opus operantis are nothing but useless human words. They get in the way more than they help.

And who could list all the terrible misuses and false beliefs about this blessed sacrament that grow in number every day? Some of them seem so spiritual and holy that they could almost lead an angel astray.

To put it briefly, anyone who wants to understand these misuses only needs to keep in mind the use and faith of this sacrament described above. There must be a sad, hungry soul. It must long with all its heart for the love, help, and support of the whole communion of Christ and all saints. It must not doubt that by faith it receives them. And then, on the other side, it must make itself one with everyone.
Whoever does not arrange his hearing or reading of masses and his receiving of the sacrament in this way is making a mistake. He is not using this sacrament for his salvation.
This is also why the world is flooded with deadly diseases, wars, and other horrible disasters. With our many masses we only bring even more disfavor on ourselves.

21. Now we see how much this sacrament is needed by those who have to face death or other dangers to body and soul. They are not left alone in these dangers. They are made strong in the communion of Christ and all saints.
That is also why Christ set it up and gave it to His disciples when they were in the greatest need and danger.

Every day all of us are surrounded by all kinds of danger, and in the end we must die. So we should thank the God of all mercy humbly, with all our heart and all our strength, for giving us a gracious sign. Through this sign, if we hold on to it by faith,
He leads us and draws us through death and every danger to Himself, to Christ, and to all saints.
So it is also useful and necessary that the love and fellowship of Christ and all saints stay hidden, invisible, and spiritual. Only a bodily, visible, outward sign of it is given to us.

Suppose this love, fellowship, and help could be seen by everyone, like the everyday fellowship people have in this world. Then it would not strengthen us or train us to trust in invisible and eternal things, or to long for them. Instead, it would train us to trust only in things that we can see and that last only for a time. We would get so used to them that we would not want to let them go and keep following God. So we would never reach Him, if we followed God only as far as things we can see and touch could take us.
Everything that belongs to time and to our senses must fall away. We must learn to live without it if we are going to come to God.

So the mass and this sacrament are a sign that trains us and gets us used to letting go of all the love, help, and comfort we can see. It teaches us to trust in Christ and in the unseen love, help, and comfort of His saints.

Death takes away everything we can see. It separates us from people and from the things of this passing world. So to face death, we need the help of invisible and eternal things. The sacrament and sign point us to these things. We hold on to them by faith until we also reach them and see them with our eyes.
So the sacrament is, for us, a shallow place to cross a river, a bridge, a door, a ship, and a stretcher to carry us. In it and by it we pass from this world into eternal life.
That is why everything depends on faith.

A person who does not believe is like someone who has to cross the sea but is so fearful that he does not trust the ship. So he has to stay where he is and is never saved, because he never gets on board and crosses over.
This happens because we depend on our senses and our faith has not been tested. So it pulls back from crossing the Jordan of death. And the devil cruelly helps this along.
22. This was pictured long ago in Joshua 3 [Joshua 3:7 and following].

The people of Israel had walked through the Red Sea on dry ground, which is a picture of baptism. After that they went through the Jordan River in the same way. But the priests stood in the Jordan with the ark. The water below them flowed away, while the water above them stood up in a heap. This is a picture of this sacrament.
The priests carry and hold up the ark in the Jordan when, at the hour of our death or danger, they preach to us and give us this sacrament, Christ, and the fellowship of all saints.
If we believe, the waters below us go away. That means the visible things of this passing world do not hurt us, but run away from us.
And the waters above us stand up high, as if they were about to crash down on us. These are the horrors and ghostly sights of the other world that terrify us at the hour of death.
But if we pay no attention to them and keep going with firm faith, we will enter eternal life with dry feet and unharmed.
So we have two main sacraments in the church: baptism and the bread.
Baptism leads us into a new life on earth. The bread guides us through death into eternal life.
These two are pictured by the Red Sea and the Jordan, and by the two lands, one on the far side of the Jordan and one on this side.
That is why our Lord said at the Last Supper: "I will not drink this fruit of the vine again until the day I drink it new with you in My Father's kingdom."
[Matthew 26:29] This sacrament is meant and set up completely to make us strong against death and to let us enter eternal life.
Finally, the blessing of this sacrament is fellowship and love. They make us strong against death and every evil.

This fellowship has two sides. On one side, we share in Christ and all saints. On the other side, we let all Christians share in us, in whatever ways they and we are able. In this way the sacrament pulls up all selfish love by the roots. In its place comes love that seeks the common good of everyone. Through this love for one another there is one bread, one drink, one body, one community. That is the true union of Christian brothers.
Now let us see how the showy brotherhoods, of which there are so many today, measure up to this and how much they are like it.

blocks.x: About the Brotherhoods

s: 1. First, let us look at the evil practices of the brotherhoods.

One of them is their gluttony and drunkenness. They hold one or more masses. After that, the whole day and night, and other days as well, are handed over to the devil. They do only what displeases God.
This mad partying was brought in by the evil spirit. It is called a brotherhood, but it is really a drunken binge. It is a completely heathen way of life. In fact, it is a way of life fit for pigs.
It would be far better to have no brotherhoods in the world at all than to allow such a detestable thing.
The worldly rulers and the cities should join with the clergy to get rid of it.
For it brings great dishonor on God, the saints, and all Christians. And it turns the worship services and the feast days into a game for the devil.
Saints' days should be kept holy with good works. The brotherhood should also be a special treasure chest of good works. Instead, it has become a treasure chest of beer money.

What do the names of Our Lady, St. Anne, St. Sebastian, or other saints have to do with your brotherhoods? All you have in them is gluttony, drunkenness, wasting money, howling, yelling, chattering, dancing, and wasting time.
If a sow were made the patron saint of such a brotherhood, she would not agree to it.

So why do they cause the dear saints such pain? They misuse the saints' names in these shameful practices and sins. And with such evil practices they dishonor and blaspheme the brotherhoods named after the saints.
How terrible it will be for those who do this and those who allow it!

2. If people want to keep a brotherhood going, they should gather food and feed and serve a table or two of poor people, for God's sake. On the day before, they should fast. On the feast day they should stay sober and spend the time in prayer and other good works.
Then God and His saints would be truly honored. Things would get better, and others would be given a good example.

Or they should collect the money they planned to waste on drink and put it into a common fund, with each trade having its own. Then fellow workers in need could be helped or lent money. Or a young couple from that trade could be properly provided for from the common fund. These would be true works of brotherhood. They would make God and His saints look on the brotherhoods with pleasure, and the saints would then gladly be their patrons.
But suppose they are not willing to do this, and they keep following the old foolish show. Then I urge them not to do it on the saints' days, and not in the name of the saints or of the brotherhood.
Let them choose some other weekday. And let them leave out the names of the saints and of their brotherhoods, so that the saints do not someday show their displeasure.
There is no day that is not dishonored by such behavior. But at least the festivals and the names of the saints should be spared.
For such brotherhoods call themselves brotherhoods of the saints, while they do the devil's work.

3. Another evil in the brotherhoods is spiritual. It is a false opinion they have of themselves. They think their brotherhood should benefit no one except themselves, that is, those who are members, whose names are on the list, or who pay in.

This damnable, wicked opinion is an even worse evil than the first. It is one of the reasons why God has caused the brotherhoods to become such a mockery and blasphemy of God through gluttony, drunkenness, and the like.

For there they learn to seek their own good and to love themselves. They learn to be loyal only to one another and to look down on others. They learn to think they are better than others and to imagine that they stand higher before God than others do.
And so the communion of saints dies out. So do Christian love and the true brotherhood that was set up in the holy sacrament.

In this way a selfish love grows in them. That is, by means of these many outward brotherhoods based on works, they fight against the one brotherhood of all saints and destroy it. That brotherhood is inner, spiritual, essential, and shared by all.

When God sees this twisted state of things, He twists it even more. As Psalm 18 says, "With the twisted You will be twisted" [Psalm 18:26]. He causes them to make themselves and their brotherhoods a mockery and a disgrace. He throws them out of the common brotherhood of saints, which they oppose and do not join with. He throws them into their own brotherhood of gluttony, drunkenness, and sexual immorality. So those who have looked for and thought of nothing but what is their own will find what is their own. Then He blinds them, so that they do not see it as something detestable and shameful. Instead, they decorate their disgraceful behavior with the names of saints, as if they were doing right. Beyond this, He lets some of them fall into such a deep pit that they openly boast. They say that anyone in their brotherhood cannot be condemned. It is as if baptism and the sacrament, which God Himself set up, were worth less and were less certain than what they have made up with their darkened minds.

So their God will bring shame on them and blind them. For with their mad behavior and the piggish practices of their brotherhoods, they mock and blaspheme His feasts, His name, and His saints. This harms the common Christian brotherhood, which flowed from the wounds of Christ.
4. So if we want to understand and use the brotherhoods rightly, we must learn to tell the difference between brotherhoods correctly.
The first brotherhood is the divine, heavenly, and noblest one. It is far above all the others, as gold is far above copper or lead. It is the fellowship of all saints, which we talked about above.

In it we are all brothers and sisters. We are so closely joined that no closer relationship can be imagined. For here we have one baptism, one Christ, one sacrament, one food, one Gospel, one faith, one Spirit, one spiritual body, and each is a member of the other. No other brotherhood is so close.
Brothers by birth are, of course, brothers of one flesh and blood, of one inheritance and home. But they have to go their separate ways and join themselves to the blood and inheritance of others.

Organized brotherhoods have one membership list, one mass, one kind of good works, one feast day, one treasury. And as things are now, they also have their common beer, common feast, and common binge. But none of these ties people together so closely that they become one spirit. Only Christ's brotherhood does that.

The greater, wider, and more all-embracing Christ's brotherhood is, the better it is. So all other brotherhoods should be run in a way that keeps this first and noblest brotherhood always before their eyes. They should consider it alone to be great. In all their works they should seek nothing for themselves. They should do their works for God's sake and ask God to keep this Christian fellowship and brotherhood and make it prosper from day to day.

So when a brotherhood is formed, the members should show that they are stepping out ahead of others. They should do some special service for Christianity with their prayers, fasting, gifts to the poor, and good works. They should not do it to seek selfish profit or reward, or to shut others out. They should do it to serve as free servants of the whole community of Christians.
If people understood it rightly like this, God would restore good order. Then the brotherhoods would not be put to shame by drunken partying.

Then God's blessing would follow. A common fund could be collected, and it could be used to give material help to other people too. Then the spiritual and physical works of the brotherhoods would be done in their proper order.
If anyone will not follow this way in his brotherhood, my advice is to run from it and leave the brotherhood alone. It will harm him in body and soul.
But you may say, "If the brotherhood does not give me some special advantage, what good is it to me?"
I answer: If you are looking for some special advantage, how can the brotherhood or sisterhood help you?
Use it to serve the community and other people, as love does by its nature. Then you will receive your reward for this love without working for it or wanting it.
But if you think the service and reward of love are too small, that shows that your brotherhood is a twisted one.
Love serves freely and for nothing. That is why God also gives every blessing back to love, freely and for nothing.
Everything must be done in love if it is to please God at all. So the brotherhood also must be a brotherhood in love.
But what is done in love, by its nature, does not seek its own or its own profit. It seeks the profit of others, and above all of the community.

5. Let us come back once more to the sacrament. The Christian fellowship is also in bad shape right now, worse than ever before, and it gets worse every day, especially among the rulers. Every place is full of sin and shame. So do not pay attention to how many masses are said or how often the sacrament is celebrated. That will make things worse rather than better. Instead, pay attention to how much you and others are growing in what the sacrament means and in the faith it calls for. Only there can things get better. The more you find that you are being made part of Christ and of the fellowship of His saints, the better off you are. That is, you may find that you are growing strong in your trust in Christ and His dear saints. You may be sure that they love you and stand by you in all the troubles of life and in death. And in turn you may take to heart the failings and falls of all Christians and of the whole Church. Your love may go out to everyone. You may want to help everyone, to hate no one, to suffer with all and pray for them. If so, then the work of the sacrament is going as it should. Then you will often weep, grieve, and mourn over the miserable condition of Christendom today.

But you may find no such trust in Christ and His saints, and the needs of the Church and of every fellow human being may not trouble or move you. If so, then beware of all other good works, if you think that by doing them you are godly and will be saved.
You can be sure that they are only hypocrisy, pretense, and deception, or they are without love and fellowship. And without these, nothing is good.
For the sum of it all is this: Plenitudo legis est dilectio, "Love is what fulfills the law."
[Romans 13:10] Amen.
The text is Luke 2:1-14. In those days Caesar Augustus gave an order. Everyone in the whole world was to be registered.
This was the first registration. It took place while Quirinius was governor of Syria.
So everyone went to be registered, each person to his own hometown.

Joseph also went up from the town of Nazareth in Galilee. He went to Judea, to the town of David, which is called Bethlehem. He went there because he belonged to the house and family of David. He went to be registered together with Mary, who was promised to him in marriage. She was pregnant.
While they were there, the day came for her to give birth.
She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in baby cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them at the inn.
In that same area there were shepherds living out in the fields. At night they kept watch over their flock.
An angel of the Lord came and stood by them. The glory of the Lord shone all around them, and they were very frightened.
But the angel said to them, "Don't be afraid! Listen, I bring you good news of great joy. It is for all the people. Today in the city of David a Savior has been born for you. He is Christ the Lord."
"This will be the sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger."
Suddenly a huge crowd of heaven's angels appeared with the angel. They were praising God and saying, "Glory to God in the highest! And on earth, peace among the people he delights in."

blocks.x: I. The Birth of Jesus
The Story of How Jesus Was Born

s: 1. In Haggai 2:6-7 God says, "I will shake the heavens, and the treasures of all nations will come."
This came true today. The heavens were shaken. That means the angels in heaven sang praises to God.
The earth was shaken too. That means the people on earth were stirred up. One person traveled to this town and another to that one, all over the land, just as the Gospel tells us.
It was not a violent, bloody revolt. It was a peaceful stirring, started by God, who is the God of peace.
This does not mean that every country on earth was stirred up like this. Only the lands under Roman rule were, and they did not even make up half of the earth.

But no land was stirred up as much as Judea. That land had once been divided among the tribes of Israel. By this time, though, mostly the people of Judah lived there. The ten tribes who had been taken away as prisoners to Assyria never came back.

2. Luke says this tax, registration, or census was the first one. But in Matthew 17:24 and in other places we read that it went on from time to time. They even demanded the tax from Christ, and they tried to trap him with the tax money, Matthew
22:17. On the day he suffered, they also accused him of telling people not to pay taxes to Caesar.
The Jews did not like paying the tax. They gave in, but only unwillingly. They claimed that they were God's people and so were free from Caesar.
They argued a lot about whether they really had to pay it. But they could do nothing about it and were forced to give in.
That is why they would have liked to pull Jesus into the argument and get him in trouble with the Roman authorities.

So this tax was simply a general order across the whole empire. Every person had to pay a penny each year. The officials who collected the tax were called publicans. In German this word is wrongly translated as "notorious sinners."

3. Notice how exact the Gospel writer is. He says Christ was born in the time of Caesar Augustus, when Quirinius was governor of Syria. The land of Judea was part of Syria, just as Austria is part of the German lands.
Since this was the very first tax of its kind, it seems it had never been paid before. It began just when Christ was about to be born.
By this Jesus shows that his kingdom would not be an earthly one. It would not use worldly power or rule over people. Instead, he and his parents obey the rulers who are in charge.

Because he came right at the time of the very first registration, he leaves no doubt about this. If he had wanted to leave it unclear, he could have chosen to be born during some other registration. Then people could have said it just happened that way, without God planning it.
4. And if he had not been willing to obey, he could have been born before any registration was ordered.
Everything Jesus did teaches us something precious. So this fact can mean only one thing. By God's plan and purpose, he will not use any worldly power, but will obey it.
So this is the first blow against the pope's rule and against everything like it. That kind of rule fits with Christ's kingdom about as well as night fits with day.

5. This Gospel story is so clear that it hardly needs explaining. But we should think about it carefully and take it deep into our hearts. The people who will gain the most from it are those who come with a calm, quiet heart. They put everything else out of their minds and study it carefully.
It is like the sun. The sun shines back from calm water and gives off strong warmth. But in water that is rushing and roaring, you cannot see the sun as easily, and it cannot give off as much warmth.

So do you want light and warmth? Do you want to see the wonders of God's grace and have a heart that glows with light, love for God, and joy? Then go where you can think about this in silence. Hold on to this picture deep in your heart, and you will see one miracle after another.
But to help ordinary people get started, and to give them a reason to think about it, we will explain some of it first. After that we will go deeper.
6. First, look at how plain and ordinary these events on earth seem to us, and yet how highly heaven values them.
This is how it looks on earth. Here is a poor young woman, Mary of Nazareth. No one thinks much of her. She is one of the humblest people in the village.
No one knows about the great wonder she is carrying. She stays quiet and keeps her thoughts to herself. She sees herself as the least important person in town.

She sets out on the trip with her husband Joseph. Most likely they had no servant. He had to do the work of both master and servant, and she did the work of both lady of the house and maid. So they had to leave their home empty, or ask others to look after it.
7. They probably owned a donkey that Mary rode on, though the Gospel does not say so. It is also possible that she walked alongside Joseph.
Just imagine how people looked down on her at the inns and rest stops along the way. Yet she deserved to ride in honor in a golden chariot.

At that time there were surely many wives and daughters of important men who lived in fine rooms and great luxury. Meanwhile the mother of God is making a trip in the middle of winter, in very hard conditions.
What differences there are in this world!
The trip from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem in Judea took more than a day.
They had to go either past Jerusalem or through it, because Bethlehem is south of Jerusalem and Nazareth is north of it.

8. The Gospel writer shows that when they got to Bethlehem, they were treated as the least important and most looked-down-on people there. They had to step aside for others, until at last they had to take shelter in a stable. There they shared a room, a table, a bedroom, and a bed with the cattle. Meanwhile many a wicked man sat in the place of honor at the hotels and was treated like a lord.
No one noticed or knew what God was doing in that stable.
God passes by the big houses and expensive rooms and leaves them empty. He lets the people in them eat, drink, and have a good time. But this comfort and treasure are hidden from them.
Oh, what a dark night that was for Bethlehem! The town did not even know about that glorious light.

See how God shows that he cares nothing at all for what the world is, what it has, or what it wants. And see how the world, in turn, shows how little it knows or notices what God is, what he has, and what he does.
9. Look, this is the first picture Christ uses to put the world to shame. It shows up everything the world does and knows.
It shows that the world's greatest wisdom is foolishness. Its best actions are wrong, and its greatest treasures are really disasters.
What did Bethlehem have when it did not have Christ?
What do those people have now who had plenty back then?
And what are Joseph and Mary missing now, even though back then they had no place to sleep comfortably?
10. Some people have explained the word "diversorium" as if it meant an open archway that anyone could walk through, where a few donkeys stood. They say Mary could not reach a place to stay.
That is wrong.
The Gospel writer wants to show that Joseph and Mary had to stay in a stable. There was no room for her in the inn, the place where travelers usually stayed.
All the other guests in the inn, or travelers' lodge, were given a room, food, and a bed. Only these poor people were left out. They had to creep into a stable where cattle were usually kept.

This word "diversorium," which Luke calls "katalyma," simply means a place for guests. Christ's own words prove this in Luke 22:11. There he sent the disciples to get the supper ready and said, "Go and say to the man who owns the house, 'The Teacher wants to know: which room is for guests, where I can eat the Passover with my disciples?'"

In the same way, Joseph and Mary had no room in the katalyma, the inn. They only had room in the innkeeper's stable. Yet that innkeeper would not even have been worthy to give shelter to such a guest.
They had no money and no important friends to get them a room in the inn. So they had to stay in a stable.
Oh world, how foolish you are!
Oh mankind, how blind you are!
11. But the birth itself is even sadder.

No one felt sorry for this young wife, who was about to have her first child. No one cared about her situation. She was a stranger there, and she did not have even the smallest thing a mother needs on the night she gives birth.
There she is with nothing ready, with no lamp and no fire, alone in the dark. No one offers to help her, as women usually do for each other at such times.
The inn is full of noise and bustle. Guests have crowded in from all over the country. No one thinks about this poor woman.
Maybe she did not expect the baby to come so soon. If she had, she would probably have stayed in Nazareth.
12. Just imagine what kind of cloths she wrapped the baby in.
Maybe it was her veil, or some piece of clothing she could do without.
But the claim that she wrapped him in Joseph's trousers, which are put on display at Aix-la-Chapelle, is far too false and silly.
It is a made-up story, and there are more stories like it in the world.
Isn't it strange that Christ was born in the cold of winter, in a foreign place, and in such a poor and humiliating way?
13. Some people argue about how this birth happened. They say Jesus was born while Mary was praying and rejoicing, with no pain at all, before she even knew it.
I do not completely throw out this well-meant idea. But it was clearly made up for the sake of simple people.
But we must stick to what the Gospel says: he was born of the virgin Mary.
There is no trick here. The Word clearly says it was a real birth.
14. Everyone knows what giving birth means.
What Mary went through was no different from what other women go through. So Christ's birth was a real, natural birth. Mary was his natural mother, and he was her natural son.

So her body did what a body naturally does in giving birth. The only difference is that she gave birth without sin, without shame, without pain, and without injury, just as she had become pregnant without sin.

The curse on Eve did not fall on her. That is where God said, "You will have pain when you give birth to children" (Genesis 3:16). In every other way, it went for her just as it goes for every woman who has a baby.
15. Grace does not get in the way of nature and what nature does. Instead, grace makes it better and helps it along.

In the same way, Mary surely fed the child with milk from her own breast. She did not use another woman's milk or some method different from the one nature provides. As we sing, "ubere de coelo pleno," which means "from her breast filled by heaven," without harm or impurity.

I mention this so that we may stand firm in the faith. We should know that Jesus was a natural human being in every way, just like us. The only difference has to do with sin and grace: he did not have a sinful nature.
In him and in his mother, nature was pure in every part of the body and in everything those parts did.
No woman's body or body part ever did its natural work without sin, except for this virgin's. Here, for once, God gave special honor to nature and to what it does.
It is a great comfort to us that Jesus took on our nature and our flesh.
So we must not take away from him or his mother anything that does not go against grace. The text clearly says that she gave birth to him. And the angels said, "To you he is born."

16. How could God have shown his goodness in a greater way? He humbled himself to share our flesh and blood. He did not even look down on the most private parts of our nature. Instead, he honors nature most highly in the very part where it was so miserably put to shame in Adam and Eve. So from now on, even that part can be seen as godly, decent, and pure, though in all people it is the most ungodly, shameful, and impure.
These are true miracles of God. He could not have given us a stronger, more powerful, or cleaner picture of purity than in this birth.

Look at this birth. Think about how the great and glorious Majesty comes with deep seriousness, and with love and goodness beyond words, to the flesh and blood of this virgin. When we do, we see how every evil desire and every evil thought is driven away.
17. No woman can fill a man's mind with thoughts as pure as this virgin can. And no man can fill a woman's mind with thoughts as pure as this child can.
If we think about this birth and see the work of God in it, nothing but purity and clean living will come from it.
18. But what happens in heaven because of this birth?
As much as it is looked down on here on earth, it is honored that much in heaven, and a thousand times more.

Suppose an angel came from heaven and praised you and your work. Wouldn't that be worth more to you than all the praise and honor the world could give you? Wouldn't you gladly put up with the worst humiliation and insults for it?

Then how great is the honor when all the angels in heaven cannot hold themselves back? They burst out rejoicing, so that even poor shepherds in the fields hear them preach, praise God, sing, and pour out their joy without limit.

Compared with the joy and glory shown here, shouldn't all the joy and honor found in Bethlehem be counted as nothing but trash and filth? Yes, shouldn't all the joy and honor of all the kings and nobles on earth be counted that way too, so that no one even wants to think about them?
19. See how richly God honors people whom others look down on, and how gladly he does it.
Here you see that his eyes look down into the lowest, humblest places. As it is written, "He sits above the cherubim" and looks into the depths.
The angels could not find any princes or brave heroes to tell the good news to. They found only uneducated ordinary people, the humblest people on earth.
Couldn't they have gone to the high priests, who were supposed to know so much about God and the angels?
No, God chose poor shepherds. People thought very little of them, but heaven counted them worthy of such great grace and honor.
20. See how completely God throws down whatever is high and proud!

And yet we storm and shout for nothing but this empty honor, as if there were no honor to look for in heaven. We keep stepping out of God's sight, so that he cannot see us in the low places, the only places he looks.
21. That is enough on this for ordinary people.
Each person should keep thinking about it on his own.
If you really understand every word, it is like a fire that makes your heart glow. As God says in Jeremiah 23:29, "Isn't my Word like a fire?"
As we can see, God's Word is meant to teach us to know God and what he does, and to see that this life is nothing.
God does not live by the ways of this life. He does not have possessions or earthly honor and power. So he pays no attention to these things and says nothing about them. He teaches only the opposite.
He works against these earthly things. He looks kindly on what the world turns away from. He teaches what the world runs away from. He picks up what the world throws away.
22. We are not willing to put up with God doing things this way. We do not want to receive blessing, honor, and life like this. But that is how it must stay.
God does not change his plan. He does not teach or act any differently from what he planned.
