We must adjust ourselves to him. He will not adjust himself to us.
What is more, anyone who will not pay attention to his word, or to the way he works to comfort people, surely has no good sign that he is saved.

How could he have shown his grace in a lovelier way to the humble and despised people of the earth? He did it through this birth in poverty. The angels rejoice over it, and they tell no one about it except the poor shepherds.
23. Now let us look at the hidden meanings in this story.

In all these hidden meanings, two things stand out most: the Gospel and faith. That means what should be preached and what should be believed, who should do the preaching and who should do the believing.
We will look at this now.

blocks.x: II. The Spiritual Meaning of Jesus' Birth
A. What It Teaches About Faith

s: 24. Faith comes first. It is right for us to see faith as the most important thing in every word of God.
It does no good just to believe that this story is true as it is written. All sinners believe that, even those who are condemned.
The Scripture, God's Word, does not teach that faith is a natural human work done without grace.
The right faith, the faith of grace that God asks for, is this: you firmly believe that Christ was born for you, and that this birth happened for your good.

The Gospel teaches that Christ was born, and that he did and suffered everything for us. The angel says so here: "Listen, I bring you good news of great joy. It is for all the people. Today a Savior has been born for you. He is Christ the Lord."
In these words you can clearly see that he was born for us.
25. The angel does not just say, "Christ is born." He says, "He is born for you." He does not just say, "I bring good news." He says, "I bring good news of great joy to you."
What is more, this joy was not meant to stay with Christ alone. It is for all the people.

No condemned or wicked person has this faith, and none can have it. For the true basis of salvation, which joins Christ and the believing heart together, is this: they share everything with each other.
But what do they each have?
26. Christ's birth is pure, innocent, and holy.
People have an unclean, sinful, condemned birth. As David says in Psalm 51:5, "Look, I was born in guilt, and my mother conceived me in sin."
Nothing can fix this unholy birth except the pure birth of Christ.

But Christ's birth cannot be handed out in a physical way, and that would not help anyway. So it is given spiritually, through the Word, as the angel says. It is given to all who firmly believe, so that their impure birth will not harm them.
This is how we are made clean from the miserable birth we got from Adam.

Christ wanted to be born for this reason: so that through him we could be born again. He says this in John 3:3, and it happens through faith. St. James also says in James 1:18, "Because he wanted to, he brought us to birth through the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of first fruits of all he has made."

27. Here we see how Christ, in a way, takes our birth away from us and swallows it up in his own birth. Then he gives us his birth, so that in it we can become pure and holy, as if it were our own. So every Christian can be glad and boast about Christ's birth just as much as if he himself had been born of Mary, like Christ.
Anyone who does not believe this, or who doubts it, is not a Christian.
28. Oh, this is the great joy the angel is talking about!
This is God's comfort and his overflowing goodness. If a person believes this, he can boast about this treasure: Mary is his true mother, Christ is his brother, and God is his father.
These things really happened, and they are true, but we must believe them.
This is the main thing and the main treasure in every Gospel passage. It comes before any teaching about good works can be drawn from it.
Before anything else, Christ must become ours and we must become his. Only then can we do good works.
But this can happen only through faith. Faith teaches us to understand the Gospel rightly and to hold on to it properly.
This is the only way to know Christ rightly, so that our conscience is at peace and made glad.
From this, love and praise for God grow. In Christ he has given us gifts too great for words.
This gives us courage to act or to hold back, and, whether we live or die, to suffer anything that pleases God.
This is what Isaiah 9:6 means: "A child has been born for us! A son has been given to us!" For us, for us, for us this child is born, and to us he is given.

29. So make sure you do not enjoy the Gospel only as a story, because that does not last. And do not see it only as an example, because without faith it is worth nothing. Instead, make sure you make this birth your own, and that Christ is born in you.
This will happen if you believe. Then you will rest in the lap of the virgin Mary and be her dear child.
But you must practice this faith and pray as long as you live. You can never make it too strong.
This is our foundation and our inheritance. Good works must be built on it.

30. Suppose Christ has now become your own in this way. Through this faith he has made you clean. You have received your inheritance without earning it, only through the love of God, who gives you the treasure and work of his Son as your own. Then it follows that you will do good works. You will do for your neighbor what Christ has done for you.
Here good works teach themselves.
What are Christ's good works?
Isn't it true that they are good because they were done for your benefit? They were done for God's sake, because God commanded him to do them for you.
So this is how Christ obeyed the Father: he loved us and served us.

31. You have received enough and have become rich. So there is no other command for you, if you want to serve Christ and obey him, than this: aim your works so that they help your neighbor, just as Christ's works help you and are useful to you.
That is why Jesus said at the Last Supper, "This is what I command you: love one another, just as I have loved you."

John 13:34. Here we see that he loved us and did everything for our good, so that we would do the same. We do it not for him, because he does not need it, but for our neighbor. This is his command, and this is how we obey.
So it is through faith that Christ becomes ours, and his love is the reason we are his.
He loves, and we believe. In this way the two are joined into one.
In the same way, our neighbor trusts and expects our love. So we should love him back and not leave him waiting for it for nothing.
The one works just like the other. As Christ helps us, we help our neighbor in return, and everyone has enough.
32. From this you can see how far off the path some people have gone. They have linked good works to stone, wood, clothes, eating, and drinking.
How does it help your neighbor if you build a church entirely out of gold?
How does it help him when big church bells ring again and again?
How does he gain from all the glitter and ceremonies in the churches, the priests' robes, the holy place, and the silver images and cups?
How do all the candles and all the incense help him?
How does all the chanting and mumbling help him, or the singing of night services and masses?
Do you really think God will let himself be paid off with the sound of bells, the smoke of candles, the shine of gold, and silly ideas like these?

He never commanded any of these things. But if you see your neighbor going the wrong way, sinning, or suffering in body or soul, you must drop everything else. Help him right away in every way you can. And if you can do nothing more, help him with comforting words and with prayer.
That is what Christ has done for you, and he has given you an example to follow.

33. These are the two things a Christian should practice. The first is to draw Christ into himself. By faith he makes Christ his own, claims Christ's treasures for himself, and builds on them with confidence. The second is to bend down to his neighbor and let him share in what he has received, just as he himself shares in Christ's treasures.

Anyone who does not practice these two things will gain nothing. That is true even if he fasted until he died, went through torture, or even let his body be burned, and could do every kind of miracle. St. Paul teaches this in 1 Corinthians 13.

blocks.x: B. What This Gospel Teaches Us Spiritually

s: 34. The second hidden meaning, or spiritual lesson, is this: only the Gospel should be preached in the churches, and nothing else.

Now it is clear that the Gospel teaches only the two things we just talked about: Christ and his example. It teaches two kinds of good works. One kind belongs to Christ, and through faith it saves us. The other kind belongs to us, and through it our neighbor is helped.

So anyone who teaches something different from the Gospel leads people the wrong way. And anyone who does not teach the Gospel in these two parts leads people even further the wrong way. He is worse than the first kind of teacher, who teaches without the Gospel, because he misuses and twists God's Word. St. Paul complains about people like this.
2 Corinthians 2:17.
35. Now it is clear that human nature could never have discovered this teaching. All the cleverness, reason, and wisdom of the world could not have figured it out.
Who could ever find out by his own efforts that faith in Christ makes us one with Christ and gives us everything that belongs to Christ as our own?
Who could find out that no works are worth anything except the ones meant to help our neighbor?
Nature can teach only what the law produces.

So nature falls back on its own works. One person thinks he keeps the commandment by starting some religious foundation or order. Another thinks he does it by fasting. Another by the kind of clothes he wears. Another by going on pilgrimages. One does it this way, another that way. And yet all their works are worthless, because they help no one.

That is how things are today. The whole world is blinded and is going the wrong way because of human teachings and human works. As a result, faith and love have died out, and the Gospel along with them.
36. So the Gospel, when it is rightly understood, is a message and a light from beyond this world. It makes known only Christ.

The first thing that shows this is that no human being told others about it. Instead, an angel came down from heaven and told the shepherds that Jesus was born. No person on earth knew anything about it.

37. The second thing that shows this is that Christ was born at midnight. By this he shows that the whole world is in the dark about its future. Christ cannot be known by human reason alone. Knowledge of him must be revealed from heaven.
38. The third thing that shows this is the light that shone around the shepherds. It teaches that here we need a completely different light from the light of human reason.
Also, when St. Luke says "Gloria Dei," the glory of God, shone around them, he calls that light a brightness, or the glory of God.
Why does he say it that way?
He does it to point to the hidden meaning and to show what the Gospel is like.

The Gospel is a heavenly light that teaches nothing but Christ. In him God's grace is given to us, and all human merit is thrown out completely. So the Gospel lifts up only the glory of God. From now on no one can brag about his own strength. Instead, everyone must give God the glory and say that we are saved through Christ only because of God's love and goodness.
You see, God's honor and God's glory is the light in the Gospel. It shines around us from heaven through the apostles and their followers who preach the Gospel.
The angel here stands for all the preachers of the Gospel, and the shepherds stand for all who hear it, as we will see.

That is why the Gospel cannot put up with any teaching except its own. Human teaching is earthly light and human glory. It lifts up the honor and praise of people and makes souls brag about their own works. But the Gospel boasts in Christ and in God's grace and goodness. It teaches us to boast in Christ and to trust in him.
39. The fourth thing that shows this is the names Judea and Bethlehem, the places where Christ chose to be born.
The name Judea means confessing or giving thanks. That is what we do when we confess God, praise him, and thank him, admitting that everything we have is his gift.
A person who confesses and praises God like this is called a "Judaeus."
Christ is king of Jews like these. As the words say, "Jesus Nazarenus Rex Judaeorum," which means Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews, that is, of those who confess God.
This shows that no teaching at all can lead to such a confession except the Gospel, which teaches Christ.
40. "Beth" means house, and "Lehem" means bread. So Bethlehem means house of bread.
The town had that name because it lay in good, fruitful farmland, rich in grain. It was the storehouse for the nearby towns, or as we would say, a fertile land.
Long ago the town was called Ephrata, which means fruitful.
Both names show that the town was in a fruitful, rich land.
This pictures the fact that without the Gospel, this earth is a wilderness. There is no confessing God and no giving thanks.
41. But wherever Christ and the Gospel are, there you find the fruitful Bethlehem and the thankful Judea.
There everyone has enough in Christ and overflows with thanks for God's grace.
People may be thankful for human teachings, but those teachings cannot fill them. They leave behind a barren land and a deadly hunger.
No heart can ever be satisfied unless it hears Christ preached rightly in the Gospel.

In the Gospel a person comes to Bethlehem and finds him. He also comes to Judea and stays there, thanking his God forever. Here he is satisfied. Here God receives his praise and confession. But outside the Gospel there is nothing but ungratefulness and starvation.
42. But the angel shows most clearly of all that nothing should be preached among Christians except the Gospel. He takes on the job of a Gospel preacher himself.
He does not say, "I preach to you." He says, "I bring you good news."
I am an evangelist, and my word is an evangel, which means good news.
The word Gospel means a good, happy message that is preached in the New Testament.
What does the Gospel tell us about?
Listen! The angel says, "I bring you good news of great joy." My Gospel speaks of great joy.
Where is that joy? Listen again: "Today in the city of David a Savior has been born for you. He is Christ the Lord."
43. Here you see what the Gospel is: a joyful message about Christ, our Savior.
Whoever preaches him rightly is preaching the Gospel of pure joy.
How could anyone hear of a greater joy than this: Christ has been given to him as his very own?
The angel does not only say that Christ is born. He makes that birth ours by saying, "for you a Savior."
44. So the Gospel does not just teach the story of Christ. It also lets everyone who believes it receive it as their own. That is how the Gospel works, as we have just explained.

What good would it do me if Christ had been born a thousand times, and it were sung into my ears every day in the loveliest way, if I never heard that he was born for me and was meant to be my very own?
But if the voice gives out this sweet sound, even in simple, everyday words, my heart listens with joy. It is a lovely sound that goes deep into the soul.
If there were anything else that needed preaching, this Gospel-preaching angel, this angelic evangelist, would surely have mentioned it.

blocks.x: C. What the Signs, the Angel, and the Shepherds Mean

s: 45. The angel goes on to say, "This will be the sign for you: you will find the baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger."
The cloths are nothing other than the holy Scriptures. The Christian truth lies wrapped up in them, and the faith is described in them.
For the Old Testament contains nothing but Christ, just as he is preached in the Gospel.
That is why we see the apostles pointing to what the Scriptures say. They use the Scriptures to prove everything that should be preached and believed about Christ.
So St. Paul says in Romans 3:21 that faith in Christ, through which we are made right with God, is backed up by the law and the prophets.
And after he rose from the dead, Christ himself opened up to them the Scriptures that speak about him.
Luke 24:27.
When he was transformed in glory on the mountain, Matthew
17:3, Moses and Elijah stood beside him. This means the law and the prophets were his two witnesses, signs pointing to him.
That is why the angel says the sign by which people will recognize him is the cloths he is wrapped in. On earth there is no other witness to Christian truth except the holy Scriptures.
46. In the same way, Christ's seamless robe stands for the New Testament. It was not torn apart, but during his suffering it was gambled for and given away (John 19:23-24).

This shows that the pope, the Antichrist, would not deny the Gospel. Instead, he would lock it up by force and play games with it through false explanations, until Christ can no longer be found in it.

And the four soldiers who crucified the Lord are pictures of all the bishops and teachers in the four corners of the earth. They violently hold down the Gospel and destroy Christ and faith in him with their human teachings, as the pope and his Papists have long been doing.
47. From this we see that the law and the prophets cannot be rightly preached and understood unless we see Christ wrapped up in them.
It is true that Christ does not seem to be in them. And the Jews do not find him there.

They look like small, unimportant cloths, just simple words. They seem to speak about unimportant outward matters, and their real meaning is not recognized. But the New Testament, the Gospel, must open it up, shine its light on it, and reveal it, as we have said.
48. So first of all the Gospel must be heard. The angel's appearing and his voice must be believed.
If the shepherds had not heard from the angel that Christ was lying there, they could have seen him ten thousand times. They would never have known that the child was Christ.
That is why St. Paul says in 2 Corinthians 3:16 that the law stays dark and covered for the Jews until they turn to Christ.

Christ must first be heard in the Gospel. Then people will see how beautiful and lovely the whole Old Testament is, and how well it agrees with him. Then a person cannot help but give himself over to faith. He will be able to see the truth of what Christ says in John 5:46: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me, because he wrote about me."
49. So let us beware of all teaching that does not present Christ.
What more do you want to know?
What more do you need, if you really know Christ as described above? What more do you need, if you live by faith in God and by love for your neighbor, doing for others what Christ has done for you?
This is truly the whole Bible in its shortest form. No more words or books are needed, only life and action.
50. He lies in the manger.
Notice here that nothing but Christ should be preached in the whole world.
What is the manger? It is the Christians who gather in the churches to hear the preaching.
We are the animals in front of this manger. And Christ is laid before us, so that we can feed our souls on him.
Whoever goes to hear preaching goes to this manger. But it must be preaching about Christ.
Not all mangers have Christ in them, and not all sermons teach the true faith.
There was only one manger in Bethlehem where this treasure lay. And it was an empty, despised manger, with no feed in it.

So the preaching of the Gospel is set apart from everything else. It has nothing and teaches nothing except Christ. If anything else is taught, it is no longer Christ's manger. It is the manger of war horses, full of earthly things and food for the body.
51. Christ in his baby cloths stands for the faith in the Old Testament. To show this, we will give several examples here.
We read in Matthew
8:4 that when Christ made the leper clean, he said to him, "Go and show yourself to the priest. Offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them."
Here you see that the law of Moses was given to the Jews as a testimony, or sign, as the angel also says here. That is, this law stands for something other than itself.

What does it stand for? Christ is the priest. All people are spiritual lepers because of unbelief. But when we come to faith in him, he touches us with his hand. He gives us his merit and lays it on us. Then we become clean and whole, without any merit of our own at all.
So we should show our thanks to him. We should admit that we have not become godly by our own works, but through his grace. Then we will be on the right path before God.
We should also offer our gifts. That means giving what is ours to help others, doing good to them as Christ has done to us.
In this way Christ is served, and an offering is brought to the true priest. For it is done for his sake, to love and praise him.
Do you see how, in picture language, Christ and faith are wrapped up in the simple words of Scripture?
Here it becomes clear that Moses in the law only bore witness to Christ and explained him.
The whole Old Testament should be understood this way. It should be seen as the baby cloths, a sign that points to Christ and makes him known.

52. Again, it was commanded that the Sabbath be kept strictly and that no work be done. This shows that not our works, but Christ's works should live in us. For it is written that we are not saved by our works, but by the works of Christ.
Now these works of Christ are of two kinds, as shown before.
First, there are the works Christ did himself, without us. These are the most important, and we believe in them.
Second, there are the works he does in us, in our love for our neighbor.

The first can be called the evening works, and the second the morning works. So evening and morning make one day, as it is written in Genesis 1:5. For the Scriptures begin the day in the evening and end it in the morning. That is, the evening with the night is the first half, and the morning with the daytime is the second half of the whole natural day.
The first half is dark and the second half is light. In the same way, Christ's first works are hidden in our faith. But the others, the works of love, are meant to be seen and openly shown to others.
So here you see how the whole Sabbath is kept and made holy.
55. Do you see how beautifully Christ lies in these cloths?
How beautifully the Old Testament shows the faith and love of Christ and of his Christians?
Now, baby cloths usually come in two kinds. The outer one is made of rough wool, and the inner one of linen.
The outer, rough wool cloth stands for the testimony of the law. But the linen stands for the words of the prophets.

For example, Isaiah says in 7:14, "Look, a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and will call his name Immanuel." There are other passages like it. They would not be understood as being about Christ if the Gospel had not revealed it and shown that Christ is in them.
54. So here we have these two things, the faith and the Gospel. These, and nothing else, should be preached in all of Christendom.
Now let us see who should be the preachers and who should be the learners.
The preachers should be angels, that is, God's messengers. They should live a heavenly life and always be busy with God's Word, so that they never preach human teaching.
It makes no sense at all to be God's messenger and not spread God's message.
"Angelus" means a messenger, and Luke calls him God's messenger ("Angelus Domini").
The message is also more important than the messenger's life.

If he lives a wicked life, he only harms himself. But if he brings a false message instead of God's message, he leads astray and harms everyone who hears him. He causes idolatry among the people, because they accept lies as truth, honor people instead of God, and pray to the devil instead of to God.

55. There is no more terrible plague, disaster, or cause of grief on earth than a preacher who does not preach God's Word. Sadly, the world today is full of them. And yet they think they are godly and doing good. In fact their whole work is nothing but murdering souls, blaspheming God, and setting up idolatry. It would be much better for them if they were robbers, murderers, and the worst criminals, because then they would know they were doing wrong.

But now they go around with spiritual titles and outward show, as priest, bishop, pope. At the same time they are vicious wolves in sheep's clothing. It would be good if no one ever heard them preach.
56. The learners are shepherds, poor people out in the fields.
Here Jesus does what he says in Matthew
11:5: "And the poor have the good news preached to them." And in Matthew
5:3: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for the kingdom of heaven is theirs."
Here there are no learned people, no rich people, no powerful people. Such people usually do not accept the Gospel.
The Gospel is a heavenly treasure. It will not put up with any other treasure, and it will not get along with any earthly guest in the heart.
So whoever loves the one must let go of the other, as Christ says in Matthew
6:24: "You cannot serve God and mammon."

The shepherds show this by being out in the field, under the open sky, and not in houses. This shows that they do not hold on tightly to earthly things. Also, they are in the fields at night. The world does not know them and looks down on them. The world sleeps at night, and by day it loves to walk around so that it will be noticed. But the poor shepherds do their work at night.
They stand for all the humble people on earth. They are often despised and unnoticed, but they live only under heaven's protection. They long for the Gospel.
57. The fact that there were shepherds means that no one should hear the Gospel for himself alone. Everyone should tell it to others who do not know it.

For whoever believes has enough for himself. He should try to bring others to the same faith and knowledge. In this way one can be a shepherd to another, caring for him and leading him into the pasture of the Gospel in this world, during the night of this earthly life.

At first the shepherds were very frightened by the angel. For human nature is shocked when it first hears in the Gospel that all our works are nothing and are condemned before God. It does not easily give up its prejudices and its proud ideas.
58. Now let everyone examine himself in the light of the Gospel. Let him see how far he is from Christ, and what his faith and love are really like.

Many people are stirred with dreamy devotion when they hear about Christ's poverty. They are almost angry with the people of Bethlehem. They condemn their blindness and ingratitude. They think that if they had been there, they would have served the Lord and his mother better. They would not have let them be treated so miserably.
But they do not look right beside them to see how many people need their help. They leave them in their misery without help.
Who on earth does not have poor, miserable, sick, straying, or sinful people around him?
Why doesn't he show his love to them?
Why doesn't he do for them what Christ has done for him?
59. It is completely wrong to think that you have done much for Christ if you do nothing for those needy people.
If you had been in Bethlehem, you would have paid as little attention to Christ as they did. But now that it is known who Christ is, you claim to serve him.
If he came now and laid himself in a manger, and sent you word that it was he, the one you now know so much about, you might do something for him. But you would not have done it before.

Suppose the rich man in the Gospel had been told for certain how highly Lazarus would be raised up, and suppose he had been convinced of it. Then he would not have let him lie there and die as he did.
60. So if your neighbor were now what he will be in the future, and lay before you, you would surely pay attention to him.
But now, since that is not how it is, you are beating the air. You do not recognize the Lord in your neighbor. You do not do for him what he has done for you.
That is why God lets you be blinded and deceived by the pope and false preachers. So you waste on wood, stone, paper, and wax what you could have used to help others.

blocks.x: III. What the Angels' Song of Praise Means

s: 61. Finally we must also talk about the angels' song, which we use every day in our worship: "Gloria in excelsis Deo."
There are three things to look at in this song: glory to God, peace to the earth, and good will to people.
The good will could be understood as God's own good will toward people through Christ.
But we will take it to mean the good will that is given to people through this birth. That is how it is put in the words "en anthropis eudokia, hominibus beneplacitum."
62. The first is glory to God.

This is also where we should begin. In all things the praise and glory should be given to God, as the one who does, gives, and owns all things. No one should take credit for anything or claim any merit for himself.
For the glory belongs to no one but God alone. It cannot be made common by being shared with any person.

63. Through the evil spirit Adam stole the glory and took it for himself. So all people have fallen into disgrace with him. This evil is so deeply rooted in all people that no vice in them is as great as vanity.
Everyone is very pleased with himself. No one wants to be nothing, and they want nothing. This spirit of vanity is the cause of all the trouble, fighting, and war on earth.

64. Christ has brought the glory back to God. He did this by teaching us that all we have or can do is nothing but wrath and displeasure before God. So we should not boast or be pleased with ourselves. Instead we should be filled with fear and shame. In this way our glory and self-satisfaction are crushed, and we are glad to be rid of them. Then we can be found and kept safe in Christ.
65. The second is peace on earth.
Where God's glory is not found, there must be fighting, as Solomon says in Proverbs 13:10: "By pride comes nothing but quarreling." In the same way, where God's glory is, there must be peace.

Why would they quarrel when they know that nothing is their own? All they are, all they have, and all they can want comes from God. They leave everything in his hands and are content to have such a gracious God.
He knows that all he has is nothing before God. He does not look for his own honor. Instead he thinks of the one who is something before God, that is, Christ.

66. So it follows that where there are true Christians, there is no fighting, quarreling, or discord. As Isaiah says in 2:4, "They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will not lift up sword against nation, and they will not learn war anymore!"

67. That is why our Lord Christ is called a king of peace. He is pictured by King Solomon, whose name means "rich in peace." Inwardly, he wants to give us peace in our conscience toward God through faith. Outwardly, he wants us to show love to our fellow people. So through him there may be peace everywhere on earth.
68. The third is good will toward people.
Good will here does not mean the will that does good works. It means the good will and peace of heart that accepts equally whatever may happen, whether good or bad.
The angels knew very well that the peace they sang about does not reach beyond the Christians who truly believe. Such people certainly have peace among themselves.
But the world and the devil will not be corrected. They do not let them have peace, but persecute them to death. As Christ says in John 16:33, "In me you may have peace.
In the world you have trouble."

69. So it was not enough for the angels to sing about peace on earth. They added the good will toward people. That means that they take pleasure in all that God does, see all his dealings with them as wise and good, and praise and thank him for it.
They do not complain, but they gladly submit to God's will.

They know that God can do all things, and they have received him through faith in Christ as a gracious Father. So they celebrate and rejoice even when they are persecuted, as St. Paul says in Romans 5:3: "We also rejoice in our troubles."
They see all that happens to them as being for the best, because they are so richly satisfied in Christ.
70. See, this is the good will, the pleasure, the good opinion in all things, good or bad, that the angels want to express in their song. For where there is no good will, peace will not last long.
Unbelievers put the worst meaning on everything. They always make the bad bigger and double every misfortune.

So they do not like the way God deals with them. They want it to be different. And what is written in Psalm 18:25-26 comes true: "With the merciful you show yourself merciful, with the perfect man you show yourself perfect; with the pure you show yourself pure." That means: whoever takes pleasure in all that you do, you and all who are yours will take pleasure in him too. "And with the perverse you show yourself contrary." That means: since you and all you do do not please him, he does not please you or any who are yours.
71. About this good will St. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10:33, "Just as I also please everyone in everything."
How does he do that?
If you are content and satisfied with everything, you will in turn please everyone.

It is a short rule: If you want to please no one, be pleased with no one. If you want to please everyone, be pleased with everyone. But only as far as you do not go against God's Word. For there all pleasing and displeasing stops.

But whatever can be left undone without doing violence to God's Word may be left undone. In this way you can please everyone and at the same time be faithful to God. Then you have this good will that the angels sing about.
72. From this song we can learn what kind of beings the angels are.
Do not pay attention to what the great masters dream up about them. Here they are all painted in such a way that you can see their hearts and their own thoughts.

First, they sing joyfully and give the glory to God. This shows how full of his light and fire they are. They do not praise themselves. They know that all things belong to God alone. So with great earnestness they give the glory to him, to whom it belongs.
So if you want to picture a humble, pure, obedient, and joyful heart that praises God, think of the angels.
This is their first step, the way they serve God.
73. The second is their love for us, as has been shown.

Here you see what great and kind friends we have in them. They care for us no less than for themselves. They rejoice in our well-being just as much as in their own. In fact, in this song they give us a very comforting reason to see them as the best of friends.

This is the right way to understand the angels. Not by what they are in their being, which the masters boldly try to describe, but by their inner heart, spirit, and mind. Though I do not know what they are, I know what they most desire and what they are always doing. In this way you look into their heart.
That is enough about this Gospel.
What Mary, Joseph, and Nazareth mean will be explained in Luke 1.

blocks.x: The Armor of This Gospel

s: 74. This Gospel is the foundation of the article of our faith where we say, "I believe in Jesus Christ, born of the virgin Mary."
This article is also founded on other passages of Scripture, but on none as clearly as on this one.
St. Mark says no more than that Christ has a mother. It is the same with St. John. Neither of them says anything about his birth.
St. Matthew says he was born of Mary in Bethlehem, but he leaves it at that. He does not gloriously proclaim that Mary was a virgin, as we will hear in due time.
But Luke describes it clearly and carefully.
75. Long ago it was also announced by the patriarchs and prophets. For example, God says to Abraham in Genesis 22:17, "And in your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed."
And he says to David in Psalm 89:4 and 132:11, "Jehovah has sworn to David in truth, and he will not go back on it: from the fruit of your body I will set someone on your throne."
But those words are unclear compared with the Gospel.
76. It is also pictured in many figures. One is the rod of Aaron. Although it was a dry piece of wood, it budded in a supernatural way (Numbers 7:5).
In the same way Mary, without any natural conception, gave birth in a supernatural way to a real and true natural son. Just so the rod bore natural almonds and still remained a natural rod.
Another figure is Gideon's fleece (Judges 6:37). It was wet with the dew of heaven while the ground around it stayed dry. There are many similar figures that we do not need to list.
These figures do not conflict with faith. Instead they adorn it. For it must first be firmly believed before I can believe that the figure helps to illustrate it.
77. There is a great deal in this article that we would not want to lose in times of temptation. For the evil spirit attacks nothing as fiercely as our faith.
So it is very important for us to know where in God's Word this faith is taught. Then in times of temptation we can point to that, for the evil spirit cannot stand against God's Word.

78. There are also many moral teachings in this Gospel, such as meekness, patience, poverty, and the like. But these have been touched on enough, and they are not points of dispute. For they are fruits of faith and good works.
Death comes to every one of us, and no one can die in someone else's place.
Each person has to fight his own battle with death, by himself and alone.
We can shout into each other's ears. But in the end, each person must be ready to face death alone.
I will not be with you then, and you will not be with me.
So each of you must know the main truths of the Christian faith for yourself. You must be armed with them.
They are the same truths, my dear friends, that you heard from me a long time ago.
First, we must know that we are children of wrath. All our works, plans and thoughts are worth nothing at all.

To prove this, we need a clear, strong Bible verse. There are many such verses in the Bible, but I will not overload you with them. I only ask you to remember this one: "We are all children of wrath."
[Eph. 2:3] And please don't brag back at me, saying, "I have built an altar," or "I have paid for masses to be said," and so on.

Second, God has sent us His only Son so that we may believe in Him. Whoever puts his trust in Him will be free from sin and will be a child of God. John says this in the first chapter: "He gave them power to become God's children—everyone who believes in His name."
[John 1:12] We should all know our Bibles really well here. We should be ready with many verses to face the devil.
On these two points, nothing seems to be missing or wrong. They have been preached to you correctly. I would be very sorry if it were not so.
In fact, I know well, and I dare to say it, that you know more about this than I do. There are not just one, two, three or four of you, but maybe ten or more, who have this wisdom and understanding.
Third, there must also be love. Through love we must treat one another the way God has treated us through faith.

Without love, faith is nothing. As St. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 2, "Even if I could speak with the tongues of angels, and talk about the highest things of faith, if I did not have love, I would be nothing."
[1 Cor. 13:1] And here, dear friends, haven't you failed badly?
I see no sign of love among you. And I notice that you have not thanked God for His rich gifts and treasures.
Let us watch out, or Wittenberg will become another Capernaum.
I notice that you talk a lot about the teaching you hear preached—about faith and about love.
That is no surprise. Even a donkey can almost chant the Bible readings. So why shouldn't you be able to repeat the teachings and the formulas?
Dear friends, the kingdom of God—and we are that kingdom—is not about talk or words. It is about deeds, works and practice.
God does not want people who only hear words and repeat them. He wants people who do what they hear and follow it. He wants people who practice the faith that works through love.
A faith without love is not enough. In fact, it is not faith at all [1 Cor. 13:12]. It is a fake faith. It is like a face you see in a mirror: it is not a real face, only the reflection of one.
Fourth, we also need patience.
Anyone who has faith, trusts God and shows love to his neighbor, doing it day after day, is sure to suffer persecution.
For the devil never sleeps. He keeps bothering us all the time.
But patience works in us and produces hope. Hope gives itself freely to God and finds comfort in Him [Rom. 5:4].
In this way faith keeps growing through much trouble and persecution. It becomes stronger day by day.
By God's grace, a heart can receive these good qualities. Such a heart must always stay busy. It must freely give itself to help and serve the other believers, just as it has received from God.

And here, dear friends, no one should insist on his own rights. Instead, he should look for what is useful and helpful to his brother. As St. Paul says, "Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia expediunt"—"Everything is permitted for me, but not everything is helpful."

[1 Cor. 6:12] We are not all equally strong in faith. Some of you have stronger faith than I do. So we must not look at ourselves, or our strength, or our position. We must look at our neighbor. For God said through Moses, "I have carried you and fed you, just like a mother with her child."
[Deut. 1:31] How does a mother feed her child?
First she feeds it milk, then porridge, then eggs and soft food.
If she stopped nursing it and right away gave it ordinary, rough food, the child would never grow well.

That is how we should treat our brother too. We should be patient with him for a while. We should put up with his weakness and help him carry it. We should give him milk too [1 Peter 2:2], just as others did for us, until he also grows strong. Then we will not travel to heaven alone. We will bring with us our fellow believers who are not yet on our side.
If all mothers left their children, where would we be now?
Dear brother, if you have had milk long enough, don't suddenly cut off the breast. Let your brother be fed too.
If I had been here, I would not have gone as far as you have.
What you did was good, but you went too fast.
There are brothers and sisters on the other side too. They belong to us, and we still need to win them.
Let me give you a picture. The sun has two qualities: light and heat.
No king is strong enough to bend or steer the sunlight. It stays straight, right where it shines.
But heat can be turned and directed, and yet it always stays around the sun.
In the same way, faith must always stay pure and unmoved in the heart. It must never waver. But love can move and be directed, depending on how well our neighbors can understand it or follow us.
Some people can run. Others have to walk. Still others can hardly crawl.
So we must not look at our own strength, but at our brother's. Then the one who is weak in faith, and tries to follow the strong, will not be destroyed by the devil.
So, dear brothers and sisters, obey me.
I have never been one who tears things down. And I was the very first one God called to this work.
I cannot run away either. I must stay as long as God wants me to.
I was also the first one God showed this to, so that I would preach His Word to you. And I am sure that you have the pure Word of God.
So let us handle this matter with fear and humility. Let us throw ourselves at one another's feet, join hands, and help each other.
I will do my part. That is no more than my duty, because I love you as much as I love my own soul.
For here we are not fighting against the pope or the bishop, but against the devil [Eph. 6:12]. Do you think he is asleep?
He is not asleep. He sees the true light rising. To keep it from shining into his eyes, he would attack us from the side. And he will succeed if we are not on guard.
I know him well. And I hope that, with God's help, I am stronger than he is.
But if we give him even an inch, we will soon have to figure out how to get rid of him.
So everyone who agreed to get rid of the mass, and helped to do it, made a mistake. Getting rid of it was a good thing in itself, but it was not done in an orderly way.
You say it was right according to the Bible.
I agree. But what about order?
It was done wildly and carelessly, with no respect for proper order, and it upset your neighbor.
If you had first called on God in serious prayer, and had gotten the help of the authorities, then people could be sure it had come from God.
I would have worked toward the same goal too, if it had been a good thing to do. And if the mass were not such an evil thing, I would bring it back again.
For I cannot defend what you did, as I just said.
I could defend it to the pope's followers and to those blockheads. I could say to them, "How do you know if it was done with good or bad motives, since the act itself was really a good act?"
But I can find no answer to give the devil.

The devil will come to those who started this, when they lie on their deathbeds. He will remind them of verses like these: "Every plant that My Father has not planted will be pulled up by the roots" [Matt. 15:13], or "I did not send them, but they ran anyway" [Jer. 23:21]. How will they be able to stand against him then?
He will throw them into hell.

But I have a weapon to wave in the devil's face, and it will make the whole wide world too small for him. I know that I was properly called by the Council to preach here, even though I did not want to.
And I wish you had the same certainty that I have. You could so easily have asked me about this.
I was not so far away that you could not reach me with a letter. And I had not gotten in your way at all.
Did you want to start something and then leave me to carry the blame?
That is more than I can take on, and I will not do it.
This shows that you do not have the Spirit, even though you know the Bible so well.
Pay attention to these two words: "must" and "free."

A "must" is something that is truly necessary. It can never bend or give way. Faith is an example. I will never let anyone take it away from me. I must always keep it in my heart and openly confess it before everyone.
But "free" is something where I have a choice. I may use it or not use it. But I must use it in a way that helps my brother, not myself.
Now don't turn something "free" into a "must," the way you have done. Otherwise you will have to answer for those who were led astray because you used your freedom without love.
Suppose you talk someone into eating meat on Friday. Then on his deathbed he is troubled about it, and he thinks, "Oh no! I have eaten meat, and now I am lost!"
God will hold you responsible for that soul.
I would like to start many things, but only a few people would follow me. So what would be the use?
I know that those who started this thing will not be able to hold out when things get serious. They will be the first to back down.
What if I led the people into battle? What if I had been the first to urge others on, and then I ran away and did not face death bravely?
How the poor people would be fooled!
So let us feed others too with the milk we received, until they also become strong in the faith.
There are many people who agree with us on other things. They would gladly accept this one thing too, but they do not fully understand it yet. And we are driving all these people away.
So let us show love to our neighbors, or our work will not last.
We must be patient with them for a while. We must not throw out the person who is weak in faith. Even more, love should decide what we do and what we don't do, as long as our faith is not harmed.
We must pray to God seriously and act carefully in this matter. If we do not, I think all the misery we have started to bring on the pope's followers will come down on us.
That is why I could not stay away any longer. I had to come and tell you these things.
That is enough about the mass. Tomorrow we will talk about the images.
Dear friends, yesterday you heard what a Christian is like: his whole life is faith and love.

Faith is aimed at God. Love is aimed at people and at our neighbor. Love means giving our neighbor the same kind of love and service that we have received from God, even though we did nothing to earn it.

So there are two kinds of things. The first kind is the most needed. It must be done in one way and no other. The second kind is a matter of choice, not of necessity. We may keep it or not keep it, and it does not put our faith at risk or send us to hell.
In both kinds of things, love must treat our neighbor the same way God has treated us. Love must walk the straight road. It must not wander off to the left or to the right.
Some things are "musts." They are necessary, like believing in Christ. But even in these things, love never uses force or pushes people too hard.
So the mass is an evil thing, and God is not pleased with it. That is because it is performed as a sacrifice and as a work to earn merit with God.
So it must be done away with.
There is no question about this. It is as clear as asking whether you should pray to God.
We all agree on this: the private mass must be done away with, just as I have said in my writings.
I truly wish it would be done away with everywhere. I wish that only the gospel mass for all the people would be kept.
But Christian love should not be harsh here or force the issue.
We should preach and teach, by speaking and by writing, that holding mass in this way is a sin. But no one should be dragged away from it by force.
We should leave the matter to God. His Word alone should do the work, without our work.
Why? Because I do not have the power to shape people's hearts the way a potter shapes clay. I cannot do with them whatever I want.
I can reach people's ears, but no farther. I cannot reach their hearts.
And since I cannot pour faith into their hearts, I cannot force anyone to believe. And I should not try.
That is God's work alone. He is the one who makes faith come alive in the heart.
So we should let the Word run freely, and not add our own works to it.
We have the right to speak the Word (the jus verbi), but not the power to make it happen (the executio). We should preach the Word, but what comes of it must be left up to God and what pleases Him.

Now suppose I rushed in and got rid of the mass by force. Many people would be forced to go along with it without really knowing what they thought. They would say, "I don't know if it is right or wrong. I don't know where I stand. I was forced to go along with the majority."
This forcing and ordering people around leads to nothing but a joke. It is only an outward show, a foolish game, rules made up by people, fake saints and hypocrites.
If the heart is not right, I don't care at all about the outward act.
First we must win people's hearts.

That happens when I teach only God's Word and preach the gospel. I say, "Dear lords or pastors, stop holding the mass. It is not right. You are sinning when you do it. I cannot keep from telling you this."
But I would not make it a rule for them or push for a law for everyone. Whoever wanted to follow me could do so. Whoever refused would stay out.
If someone refused, the Word would still sink into his heart and do its work.

Then he would become convinced and admit he was wrong, and he would leave the mass. Tomorrow someone else would do the same. In this way God would do more with His Word than if you and I combined all power and authority into one.
If you have won the heart, you have won the whole person. Then the mass will finally fall by its own weight and come to an end.

If everyone's heart and mind agree on this goal, then do away with the mass. But if not everyone is fully for doing away with it, then please leave it in God's hands. I beg you. Otherwise things will not turn out well.
I don't mean that I would bring the mass back. I let it lie, in God's name.
Faith must not be chained up or locked in prison. It must not be tied to any work by a rule.
This is the principle you must follow.

I am sure you will not be able to carry out your plans. And if you do carry them out with laws like these for everyone, then I will take back everything I have written and preached, and I will not stand with you. So I ask you plainly: What harm can the mass do to you?
You have your faith in God, pure and strong. The mass cannot hurt you.
So love requires you to have compassion on the weak, as all the apostles did.

Once Paul came to Athens, a powerful city. In the temple he found many altars. He went from one to the next and looked at them all [Acts 17:16 ff.]. But he did not touch a single one of them, not even with his foot.
Instead he stood in the middle of the marketplace. He said they were all works of idol worship, and he begged the people to leave them behind. But he did not destroy a single one by force.
When the Word took hold of their hearts, they left their idols on their own. And so idol worship fell by itself.
Now, if I had seen them holding mass, I would have preached to them about it and warned them.

If they had listened to my warning, they would have been won. If not, I still would not have dragged them away from it by the hair or used any force. I would simply have let the Word do its work, while I prayed for them.
The Word created heaven and earth and everything. The Word must do this work, not us poor sinners.
To sum up: I will preach it, teach it and write it. But I will not force anyone, because faith must come freely, without being forced.
Look at me as an example.
I have stood against the indulgences and against all the pope's followers, but never by force.
I just taught, preached and wrote God's Word. I did nothing else.
And while I slept, or drank Wittenberg beer with my Philip and with Amsdorf, the Word weakened the papacy so much that no prince or emperor ever did it so much damage.
I did nothing. The Word did it all.
If I had wanted to stir up trouble, I could have caused a lot of bloodshed in Germany. Yes, I could have started such a little game at Worms that even the emperor would not have been safe.
But what would that have been?
A fool's game. I did nothing. I left it to the Word.
What do you think goes through Satan's mind when people try to do things by violence?
He sits back in hell and thinks, "What a great show these fools will put on for me!"
But it upsets him when we only spread the Word and let the Word alone do the work.
For the Word is all-powerful. It captures hearts. And once the hearts are captured, the evil practice will fall by itself.
Let me give an example.
Long ago there were also groups who disagreed: Jewish Christians and Gentile Christians. They disagreed about the law of Moses on circumcision.
The Jewish Christians wanted to keep it, and the Gentile Christians did not [1 Cor. 7:18 ff.].

Then Paul came and preached that it could be kept or not kept. It made no difference either way. They should not make a "must" out of it, but leave it to each person to choose. Keeping it or not did not matter.
Later Jerome came along. He wanted to make a "must" out of it, and he wanted laws and rules to forbid it.
Then St. Augustine came. He held to St. Paul's view: it could be kept or not, as each person wished. St. Jerome had missed St. Paul's meaning by a hundred miles.
The two church teachers bumped heads pretty hard over this question.
But when St. Augustine died, St. Jerome got his way.
After that came the popes. They wanted to add something of their own, and they made laws too.
So one law led to a thousand laws, until they buried us completely under laws.
And the same thing will happen here. One law will soon become two, two will grow to three, and so on.
That is enough for now about the things that are necessary. And let us be careful not to lead astray people whose consciences are weak.
We have heard about the things that are most necessary in the Christian life. We have also heard what must follow from them: getting rid of the private mass.
The works that are necessary are the ones God has either commanded or forbidden, as the Majesty on high has decided.
But no one should be dragged to them by the hair or kept from them by force. I cannot drive anyone to heaven with a club.
I said this clearly enough, and I believe you understood me.

Now we will look at the things that are not necessary. God leaves these up to our free choice, and we may keep them or not. For example: whether a person should marry or not, or whether monks and nuns should leave the monasteries.
These things are a matter of choice. No one may forbid them. If someone does forbid them, that is wrong, because it goes against what God has decided.

In things that are free, like being married or staying single, you should act like this: If you can control yourself without weighing down your conscience, then by all means do so. But there must be no law for everyone. Each person must be completely free.
Any priest, monk or nun who cannot control the desires of the body should marry. That will take the weight off his conscience.
But make sure you are well armed and prepared. Then you can stand before God and the world when you are attacked—especially when the devil attacks you in the hour of death.
It is not enough to say, "This man or that man did the same thing. I followed the crowd. I did what the provost preached, or Dr. Carlstadt, or Gabriel, or Michael."
No! Each person must stand on his own feet and be ready to fight the devil.
If you want to pass the test, you must stand on a strong and clear Bible verse.
If you can't do that, you will never hold out. The devil will pick you off like a dry, dead leaf.

So the priests who have married, and the nuns who have married, must stand firmly on a clear Bible verse to keep their consciences safe. There are many such verses, but here is one from St. Paul: "In the last times some will fall away from the faith. They will pay attention to spirits that lead people astray, and to teachings of devils (I think Paul uses plain words here!). They will forbid marriage and command people to stay away from foods, which God has made."
The devil will not be able to knock down or swallow up this verse. Instead, it will knock him down and swallow him up.

So any monk or nun who is too weak to keep the vow to stay unmarried and pure should examine himself honestly. If his heart and conscience are strong, so that he can defend himself with a clear conscience, then let him marry.

I wish to God that all monks and nuns could hear this sermon and understand this matter properly. I wish they would all leave the monasteries, so that every monastery in the world would disappear. That is my deep desire.

But right now they don't understand it, because no one preaches it to them. They hear that in other places many people are leaving the monasteries—people who are well prepared for such a step. So they want to follow their example. But they have not yet made their consciences strong, and they don't know that this is a matter of freedom.
That is bad, although it is better for the evil to be outside the monastery than inside.
So I say: what God has made free must stay free. If someone forbids it, you must not obey—just as the pope, the Antichrist, has forbidden it.
If someone can wear a monk's hood or a shaved head without harm, and out of love for his neighbor, he may do so. It will not hurt his faith. Wearing a hood will not kill him.
So, dear friends, this is clear enough. I believe you should understand it and not turn freedom into a law. Don't say, "This priest has married, so all priests must marry."
Not at all. Or, "This monk or that nun has left the monastery, so they must all come out."
Not at all. Or, "This man has smashed the images and burned them, so all images must be burned." Not at all, dear brother!
Or the other way around: "This priest has no wife, so no priest is allowed to marry."
Not at all! Those who cannot stay pure without marriage should marry. And for others who can live pure lives, it is good for them to hold back, as people who live by the spirit and not by the flesh.
They should also not be troubled about the vows they have made, like the monks' vows of obedience, chastity and poverty (though the monks are rich enough anyway).
We cannot make a vow to do anything that goes against God's commands.
God has made it a free choice to marry or not to marry. And you fool, do you try to turn this freedom into a vow against God's own order?
So you must leave freedom alone and not turn it into something forced. Your vow goes against the freedom God gives.
Suppose I made a vow to hit my father in the mouth, or to steal someone's things. Do you think God would be pleased with that vow?

I should not keep a vow to hit my father in the mouth. In the same way, I should not stay away from marriage just because I am tied by a vow of chastity. In both cases God has ordered things differently.
God has decided that I am free to eat fish or meat, and that there should be no command about them.
So all the Carthusian monks, and all other monks and nuns, turn away from the order and freedom God has given when they believe that eating meat makes them unclean.
But now we must come to the images. It is true of them too that they are not necessary. We are free to have them or not, although it would be much better if we did not have them.
I am not fond of them.
A great fight broke out over images between the Roman emperor and the pope. The emperor said he had the right to get rid of the images. But the pope insisted they must stay. Both of them were wrong.
Much blood was spilled, but the pope came out the winner and the emperor lost.
What was all this about?
They wanted to make a "must" out of something that is free. And God cannot put up with that.
Do you want to change what the Majesty on high has ordered?
No, you will not do any such thing.
You read in the Law, in Exodus 20, "Do not make any carved image for yourself, or a picture of anything in the sky above, on the earth below, or in the water under the earth."
[Ex. 20:4] That is where you take your stand. That is your firm ground.
Now let's see!

Our opponents will say, "The first commandment is aimed at this: that we should worship one God alone and not any image. That is why it says right afterward, 'Do not bow down to them or serve them.'" They will argue that worshiping images is forbidden, but not making them. And so they shake our foundation and make it unsteady.
And if you answer, "The text says, 'Do not make any images,'" they reply, "It also says, 'Do not worship them.'"
With so much uncertainty, who would be bold enough to destroy the images?
Not me. But let's go further.
They say, "Didn't Noah, Abraham and Jacob build altars?"
And who will deny that?
We have to admit it.
Again, didn't Moses set up a bronze snake [Num. 21:9], as we read in his fourth book?
How can you say Moses forbids making images when he makes one himself?
It seems to me that a snake like that is an image too.
How should we answer that?
Again, don't we read that two birds were set up on the mercy seat, the very place where God wanted to be worshiped?

[Ex. 37:7] Here we must admit that we may make images and have images. But we must not worship them. And when people do worship them, the images should be removed and destroyed, just as King Hezekiah smashed to pieces the snake Moses had set up [2 Kings 18:4].
And who will be bold enough to say, when he is asked to prove it, "They worship the images"?
They will answer, "Are you the man who dares to accuse us of worshiping images?"
Don't think they will admit it.
Of course it is true, but we cannot make them admit it.
Remember how they acted when I condemned works done without faith.
They said, "Do you think we have no faith? Do you think our works are done without faith?"
All I can do then is put my flute back in my pocket. Give them a hair's width, and they will take a hundred miles.
So it should have been preached that images are nothing, and that setting them up does not serve God. Then they would have fallen by themselves.
That is what I did. That is what Paul did in Athens, when he went into their churches and saw all their idols.
He did not strike at any of them. Instead he stood in the marketplace and said, "Men of Athens, you are all idol worshipers."
[Acts 17:22] He preached against their idols, but he did not knock down a single one by force.
And you want to rush in, cause an uproar, smash the altars and tear down the images?
Do you really think you can get rid of the images this way?
No, you will only make them stand more firmly.
Even if you tore down the images here, do you think you have torn down the ones in Nuremberg and in the rest of the world?
Not at all. St. Paul, as we read in the Book of Acts, sat in a ship that had the Twin Brothers painted or carved on its front.
He got on board and did not worry about it at all. He did not break them off either.
Why did Luke have to describe the Twins here?
No doubt he wanted to show that outward things cannot harm faith, as long as the heart does not cling to them or trust in them.
This is what we must preach and teach. And we must let the Word alone do the work, as I said before.
First the Word must capture people's hearts and give them light. We cannot do it.
That is why the apostles boasted about their service (ministerium), and not about its results (executio).
Let this be enough for today. Let us pray to God for His grace.
Dear friends, we have heard about the things that are necessary—for example, that the mass is treated as a sacrifice.
Then we looked at the things that are left to our freedom, like marriage, life in a monastery, and getting rid of images.
We have dealt with these four subjects. And we have said that in all these matters, love is the captain.

About images in particular, we saw that they should be removed if people are going to worship them, but not otherwise. Still, I wish they were removed everywhere, because they are misused. There is no point denying it.
Whoever puts an image in a church thinks he has done God a service and a good work. That is plain idol worship.
This is the biggest, most important and highest reason for getting rid of images. But you ignored it and picked up the very weakest reason.
I suppose there is hardly anyone who does not understand that the crucifix over there is not my God. My God is in heaven. The crucifix is only a sign.
But the world is full of the other misuse. Who would put an image of silver or wood in a church unless he thought he was doing God a service by it?
Do you think Duke Frederick, the bishop of Halle and the others would have put so many silver images in the churches if they thought it meant nothing to God?
No, they would not have done it.
But that is not a good enough reason to remove, destroy and burn all the images. And why not?
Because we have to admit that there are still people who do not think wrongly about images. For them, the images may be useful.
There may be only a few of them. But we cannot and should not condemn anything that still helps anyone to worship.

But you should have taught that images are nothing. God does not care about them. He is not served or pleased when we make an image for Him. It would be better to give a poor man a gold coin than to give God a golden image. For God has forbidden the golden image, but not the gift to the poor.
If people had heard this teaching—that images count for nothing—they would have stopped on their own. And the images would have fallen without any uproar or riot, as was already starting to happen.
So we must be on our guard. The devil is after us, through his apostles, with all his tricks and cunning.
It is true, and no one can deny it, that images are evil because they are misused. Still, we must not reject them for that reason. We must not condemn anything just because it is misused.
That would lead to total chaos.
God has commanded us not to lift up our eyes to the sun, and so on.
[Deut. 4:19] He said this so that we would not worship them, because they were created to serve all nations.
But there are many people who worship the sun and the stars.
So should we try to pull the sun and stars out of the sky?
No, we will not do that.
Again, wine and women bring many men to misery and make fools of them.
So should we kill all the women and pour out all the wine?
Again, gold and silver cause a lot of evil. So should we condemn them?

No. If we wanted to drive away our one worst enemy, the one who harms us most, we would have to kill ourselves. We have no greater enemy than our own heart. As Jeremiah says, "The human heart is crooked" [Jer. 17:9]. Or, as I understand it, "always twisting to one side or the other."
And what good would that do us?
Anyone who wants to paint the devil black needs good charcoal. For the devil also wears fine clothes and goes to the fair.

But I can catch him by asking, "Don't you put the images in the churches because you think it is a special way of serving God?" When he says yes, as he must, you can conclude that he has turned what was meant to serve God into idol worship by misusing the images. He eagerly went after what God has not commanded, and he ignored what God clearly did command: to help our neighbor.
But I have not caught him yet. He slips away from me by saying, "I help the poor too. Can't I give to my neighbor and also put images in churches?"
That is not true. For who would not rather give his neighbor a gold coin than give God a golden image!
No, he would not bother putting images in churches if he believed they did not serve God.
So I freely admit that images are neither here nor there. They are neither evil nor good. We may have them or not, as we like.
You caused this trouble. The devil would not have managed it with me. For I cannot deny that you can find someone for whom images are useful.

And if someone asked me about it, I would admit that none of these things bother me. And if even one person on earth used images in the right way, the devil would quickly turn that against me: "Why do you condemn something that is still useful in worship?"
I could not answer that challenge. He would have beaten me.
He would not have gotten nearly this far if I had been here.
He played a bold game and won, although it does no harm to God's Word.
You wanted to paint the devil black, but you forgot the charcoal and used chalk.
If you want to fight the devil, you must know the Bible well. And you must also use it at the right time.
Let's move on and talk about eating foods.
It is true that we are free to eat any kind of food—meat, fish, eggs or butter.
No one can deny this.
God has given us this freedom.
That is true. But we must know how to use our freedom. And we must treat the weak brother differently from the stubborn one.
So pay attention to how you must use this freedom.
First: Maybe you cannot give up meat without hurting yourself, or maybe you are sick. Then you may eat whatever you like. And if anyone is offended, let him be offended.

Even if the whole world were offended, you would still not be sinning. God can excuse you. He has kindly given you this freedom, and your health needs it. Going without meat would put your health in danger.

Second: Someone may push you to eat fish instead of meat on Friday. Or they may push you to eat fish and stay away from eggs and butter during Lent, and so on. That is what the pope has done with his foolish laws. When that happens, you must never let yourself be pulled away from the freedom God has given you. Instead, do exactly the opposite, just to spite him. Say to him: "You forbid me to eat meat. You dare to turn my freedom into a law. So I will eat meat, whatever you say."
You must do the same in all the other things where we are free.
Here is an example. Suppose the pope, or anyone else, tried to force me to wear a monk's hood exactly the way he orders. Then I would take the hood off, just to spite him.
But since it is left up to me, I wear it or take it off, just as I like.
Third: Some people are still weak in faith. They need to be taught, and they would gladly believe as we do.
But they do not know any better, and that holds them back. If this were preached to them faithfully, as it was to us, they would be one with us.
We must treat these well-meaning people in a completely different way from the stubborn ones.

We must be patient with them and not use our freedom. Holding back does not put body or soul in any danger or do them any harm. In fact, it is good for us. And on top of that, we do our brothers and sisters a great service.
But suppose we use our freedom when there is no need, and we offend our neighbor on purpose. Then we drive away the very person who would have come to our faith in time.
That is why St. Paul circumcised Timothy. Some simple Jewish people had been offended [Acts 16:3]. Paul thought, "What harm can it do? They are only offended because they do not know better."

But in Antioch some people insisted that he had to circumcise Titus. They said he must do it. Then Paul stood up against all of them. And to spite them, he refused to have Titus circumcised [Gal. 2:3].
He did not give in.
Paul did the same when St. Peter used his freedom in a way that gave people who had not been taught a wrong idea [Gal. 2:11ff.].
This is what happened. When Peter was with the Gentiles, he ate pork and sausage with them. But when the Jews came in, he would not touch that food, and he stopped eating with the Gentiles.
Then the Gentiles who had become Christians thought, "Oh no! We must be like the Jews too. We must not eat pork, and we must live by the law of Moses."

But Paul saw that this would damage the freedom of the Gospel. So he corrected Peter in front of everyone and gave him an apostle's lecture. He said, "You are a Jew, yet you live like the Gentiles. So why do you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?"

[Gal. 2:14] We should live the same way. We should use our freedom at the right time. Then Christian freedom will not be damaged. And we will not offend our weak brothers and sisters who do not yet know about this freedom.

chapters.title: Sermon Five: A Sermon on the Sacrament (Thursday after Invocavit)

s: We have heard about the necessary things, such as the mass, which people treat as a sacrifice. We have also heard about the things that are not necessary, such as monks leaving their monasteries, priests getting married, and the images.
We have seen how we must handle these matters. We must not force them or make laws about them. No one should be dragged away from them by the hair. We must let the Word of God alone do the work.
Now let us think about how we should treat the blessed sacrament.

You have heard how I preached against the pope's foolish law and opposed his rule. His rule says that no woman may wash the altar cloth that the body of Christ has lain on—not even a pure nun—unless a pure priest has washed it first.
In the same way, when anyone touches the body of Christ with his hand, the priests come running and scrape his fingers. And there is much more of the same kind.
But when a priest lives an unchaste life, the pope looks the other way.
If the woman has a baby, he lets that go too.
But the altar cloth and the sacrament must not be touched!

We have preached against foolish laws like these. We have taught that there is no sin in breaking the pope's foolish rules. A layperson does not sin if he touches the cup or the body of Christ with his hands.
You should thank God that you understand this so clearly. Many great men have not understood it.
But now you have become just as foolish as the pope. You think you must hold the sacrament in your hands. You want to prove you are good Christians by touching the sacrament with your hands.
The sacrament is our greatest treasure. Yet you have treated it in such a way that it is a wonder you were not struck down by thunder and lightning.
God would have put up with the other things you did. But forcing people in this matter—
that He will never put up with.

If you do not turn back from this, no emperor or anyone else will need to drive me away from you. I will leave without being asked. In fact, I dare to say this: my enemies have caused me a lot of sorrow, but none of them has hurt me the way you have hurt me in this matter.
Suppose you could prove you are good Christians by handling the sacrament and bragging about it to everybody. Then Herod and Pilate would be the greatest and best Christians of all!
After all, I think they handled the body of Christ when they had Him nailed to the cross and killed.
No, my dear friends. The kingdom of God is not made of outward things that can be touched or seen. It is made of faith [Luke 17:20].
But you may say, "We live by the Scriptures, and we should. And God set up the sacrament so that we take it with our hands. For He said, 'Take and eat, this is my body.'"

[Matt. 26:26] Here is my answer. I am completely sure that the Lord's disciples took it with their hands. And I admit that you may do the same without sinning. But I still cannot make it a rule. And I cannot prove that it is the only way.
Here is why. The devil comes after us and argues, "Where have you read in the Scriptures that 'take' means 'grab with the hands'?" How could I prove it or defend it?

In fact, how could I answer him when he quotes the Scriptures to show the very opposite? He can prove that "take" does not only mean to receive with the hands. It also means to receive something in other ways.
He says, "Look, my good friend. Three Gospel writers use the word 'take' when they describe how the Lord took the gall and vinegar [Matt. 27:34; Mark 15:23; Luke 23:26].
You have to admit that the Lord did not touch it or hold it with His hands. His hands were nailed to the cross."
That verse is a strong argument against me.
Then he quotes another passage: Et accepit omnes timor—"And fear took hold of all" [Luke 7:16]. Here again we have to admit that fear has no hands.

So I am backed into a corner. Even though I do not want to, I have to agree that "take" does not only mean to receive with the hands. It also means to receive something in any other way it can be done.
So you see, dear friends, we must stand on solid ground if we want to stand up to the devil's attack.
I have to admit that you did not sin when you touched the sacrament with your hands. But I must still tell you that it was not a good thing to do, because it offended people everywhere.
For everywhere, the custom is to receive the blessed sacrament straight from the priest's hands.
Why won't you serve those who are weak in the faith in this too, and hold back from using your freedom?
Doing it does not help you, and not doing it does not hurt you.
So no new practices should be started until the Gospel has first been fully preached and understood, the way it has been among you.
For this reason, dear friends, let us be serious and wise about the things of God. God will not be mocked.
You may make fun of the saints, but it is a very different matter with God.
So I beg you, stop doing this.
Now let us talk about the two kinds.
I believe the sacrament should be received in both kinds, the way the Lord set it up. But it still must not be forced on anyone or made into a law for everyone.
We must busy ourselves with the Word. We must practice it and preach it.
