As for the results, we should leave them completely to the Word. And we should let everyone have his freedom in this matter.
If we do not do that, the sacrament turns into an outward ritual and a show of fake religion. That is exactly what the devil wants.
But when the Word is allowed to run freely and is not tied to any ritual, it takes hold of one person today and sinks into his heart. Tomorrow it touches someone else, and so on.
In this way it will do its work quietly and calmly. And no one will know how it all happened.
I was glad when someone wrote to tell me that some people in this city had started to receive the sacrament in both kinds.
You should have left it that way and not turned it into a law.
But now you rush at it without thinking, and you force everyone to do it.
Dear friends, you will not succeed that way.
Suppose you want people to see you as better Christians than others because you take the sacrament in your hands and receive both kinds. Then you are poor Christians indeed!
If that were enough, even a pig could be a Christian. After all, she has a snout big enough to take in the sacrament on the outside.
We must be serious about such high things.
Dear friends, this must not be treated as a joke. If you will listen to me, stop doing it.
If you will not listen to me, no one needs to drive me away from you. I will leave you without being asked. And I will be sorry that I ever preached even one sermon here.

We could let the other things go, but not this one. You have gone so far that people are saying, "There are very good Christians in Wittenberg. They take the sacrament in their hands and hold the cup. Then they go off to their brandy and drink until they are drunk."
This drives away the weak and simple people. They would come to us if they had been taught as much as we have been taught.
But suppose someone is so foolish that he just has to touch the sacrament with his hands. Then let him have it brought to his house. There he can handle it as much as he likes.
But in public he should hold back. That will not hurt him. And it will keep us from offending our brothers, sisters and neighbors. Right now they are so angry with us that they are ready to kill us.
I can honestly say that none of the enemies who have fought against me so far have caused me as much grief as you have.
That is enough for today. We will continue tomorrow.
In talking about the main things, we have come to receiving the sacrament. We have not finished that yet.
Today we will see how we should behave here. We will also see who is worthy to receive the sacrament and who belongs there.

Here it is very important that your hearts and consciences are well taught. Then you can clearly tell the difference between receiving the sacrament outwardly and receiving it inwardly and spiritually.
Receiving it with the body, on the outside, means this: a person takes the body and blood of Christ with his mouth.
Anyone can receive the sacrament this way. It can be done without any faith or love.
But receiving it that way does not make a person a Christian. If it did, even a mouse would be a Christian! A mouse can also eat the bread and drink from the cup.
It is such an easy thing to do.
But the true, inward, spiritual receiving is something very different. It means using the sacrament rightly and receiving its fruits.
First of all I would say this: the true inward receiving is receiving in faith.
We Christians have no other outward sign that sets us apart from others except this sacrament and baptism. But just receiving it on the outside, without faith, is worth nothing.
There must be faith. Faith makes a person well prepared to receive it and makes him acceptable to God. Without faith it is all fake, just an outward show. And that is not Christianity at all.
Christianity is a matter of faith. And faith is never tied to any outward action.

We all need faith if we want to come to the sacrament in a worthy way. And faith is a firm trust. It trusts that Christ, the Son of God, stands in our place. It trusts that He has carried all our sins on His shoulders. It trusts that He is the payment for our sin forever and brings us back to peace with God the Father.
Whoever has this faith belongs at this sacrament. Then no devil, no hell and no sin can hurt him.
Do you ask why?
Because God protects and defends him.
When I have this faith, I am sure that God is fighting for me. Then I can stand up against the devil, death, hell and sin, and against all the harm they threaten me with.
This is the great treasure that God has given us in Christ. It is worth more than anyone can count, and human words cannot describe it.
Only faith can take hold of the heart. And not everyone has that kind of faith.

So this sacrament must not be made into a law. But that is what the most holy father, the pope, has done with his foolish command. It says all Christians must go to the sacrament at holy Easter time. And anyone who does not go will not be buried in holy ground.
Isn't that a foolish law the pope has made?
Do you ask why? Because we are not all the same. We do not all have the same faith. One person's faith is stronger than another's.
So the sacrament can never be made into a law. In fact, the worst sins are committed at Easter, only because of this unchristian command that drives everyone to the sacrament.

Imagine all the stealing, all the greedy moneylending, all the sexual sin and all the other sins piled up in one big heap. This sin would be bigger than the whole pile. And it happens at the time and place where it seems the silliest of all.
And why? Because the pope cannot look into anyone's heart to see whether he has faith or not.

But suppose you believe that God is with you. Suppose you believe He puts all His treasures and His blood on the line for you. It is as if He were saying: "Come and follow right behind Me. Do not be afraid, and do not wait. Then let anything come that tries to hurt you. Let the devil, death, sin, hell and all creation try it. I will go ahead of you. I will be your captain and your shield. Trust Me and depend on Me completely." Whoever believes like this cannot be hurt by the devil, hell, sin or death. If God is fighting for him, what can you do to him?
Whoever has this kind of faith is ready for the altar. He receives the sacrament as a promise, a seal or a sign. It makes him sure of God's promises and grace.
But we do not all have this kind of faith. I wish to God that even one out of ten Christians had it!

Look: God in His grace pours out these rich treasures on us, more than can be measured. But not everyone can have them. They belong only to those who suffer hardship in body or in spirit. Hardship in the body comes when people persecute them. Hardship in the spirit comes when their conscience is in despair. It comes from outside or from inside—when the devil makes your heart weak, fearful and discouraged, so that you do not know where you stand with God, and when he throws your sins in your face.
God wants to live only in hearts like these, hearts that are terrified and trembling. That is what the prophet Isaiah says [Isa. 66:2].

Some people have never felt this battle inside themselves. Their sins do not trouble them, and they do not fight against them every day. They do not want anyone to protect them, defend them and stand in front of them like a shield. People like that are not ready for this food yet.
This food is for someone who is hungry and longing for it. It loves to come into a hungry soul—a soul that is always fighting its sins and wants to be free of them.
Whoever is not prepared like this should stay away from this sacrament for a while. This food is not for a heart that is already stuffed and full. If it comes to a heart like that, it does harm.

So if we think about these things and feel this trouble of conscience and the fear of a timid heart, we will come with all humility and respect. We will not rush at it carelessly, with pride and without fear and humility.
We are not always ready for it. Today I have the grace and I am ready. But tomorrow I may not be. In fact, I may go six months without wanting it or being ready for it.

So the most worthy people are those who are always troubled by death and the devil. It is the best time for them to receive it. It reminds them that nothing can hurt them, and it makes them strong in that faith. For now He is with them, and no one can take them away from Him. Let death or the devil or sin come—they cannot hurt them.
That is what Christ did when He got ready to set up the blessed sacrament.

He filled His disciples with pain and made their hearts tremble when He told them He was going away [Matt. 26:2]. And they were tormented again when He said, "One of you will betray me" [Matt. 26:21].
Don't you think that cut them to the heart?
Yes, they heard those words with great fear. They sat there as if every one of them were a traitor against God.
He made them all shake with fear and sorrow. Only then did He set up the blessed sacrament to comfort them, and He cheered them up again.
For this bread is comfort for those who are sad. It is healing for the sick and life for the dying. It is food for everyone who is hungry, and a rich treasure for all who are poor and in need.
That is enough for now about the right way to use this sacrament.
I put you in God's care.

Yesterday we heard how to use the holy and blessed sacrament. We saw who is worthy to receive it. It is those who are afraid of death, whose consciences are fearful and in despair, and who live in fear of hell.
All these people come ready to share in this food. It makes their weak faith stronger and comforts their conscience.

That is the true and right way to use this sacrament. If someone does not find himself in this condition, he should stay away. He should wait until God takes hold of him too and draws him through His Word.
Now we will talk about the fruit of this sacrament. That fruit is love. It means we should treat our neighbor the same way God has treated us.

God has given us nothing but love and kindness. Christ has promised us His righteousness and given it to us, along with everything He has. He has poured out on us all His treasures. No one can measure them, and no angel can understand them or get to the bottom of them. For God is a blazing furnace of love that reaches all the way from the earth to the heavens.
Love, I say, is a fruit of this sacrament.
But I do not see it yet among you here in Wittenberg. You hear a lot of preaching about love, and you should practice it more than anything else.
Love is the main thing. It is the only thing that truly suits a Christian.
But no one is eager to love. Instead you want to do all kinds of things that are not needed and do not matter.

If you do not want to show you are Christians by your love, then do not bother with the other things either. For St. Paul says in 1 Corinthians, "If I speak in the languages of people and of angels, but I do not have love, I am only a noisy piece of brass or a jingling cymbal."
[1 Cor. 13:1] These are frightening words from Paul.
And he goes on: "If I have the gift of prophecy and understand all God's secrets and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but I do not have love, I am nothing.
And if I give away everything I own to feed the poor, and if I give up my body to be burned, but I do not have love, it does me no good at all."
[1 Cor. 13:2–3] You have not come that far yet. And yet God has given you great and rich gifts, especially an understanding of the Scriptures.

It is true that you have the pure Gospel and the true Word of God. But none of you has given his things to the poor yet. None of you has been burned yet. And even those things would be worth nothing without love.
You want to take all of God's good gifts in the sacrament. But you do not want to pour them out again in love.

No one will lend anyone else a helping hand. No one thinks of others first. Everyone looks out for himself and what he can get. He only cares about his own things and lets everything else go however it goes. If someone happens to get help, fine.
No one takes care of the poor or tries to find ways to help them.
It is sad. You have heard many sermons about this. All my books are full of it. They have only one goal: to urge you to faith and love.
If you will not love one another, God will send a great disaster on you. Let this be a warning to you. God will not show His Word and have it preached for nothing.
My friends, you are testing God too far.
If someone had preached the Word to our ancestors long ago, maybe they would have acted differently.
Or if the Word were preached today to many of the poor children in the monasteries, they would receive it with much more joy than you do.
You pay no attention to it at all. Instead you give yourselves to other things that are not needed and are foolish.
I put you in God's care.

chapters.title: Sermon Eight: A Short Summary of Dr. M. Luther's Sermon on Private Confession, Preached on Reminiscere Sunday

s: We have now heard about all the things we needed to think about here, except confession.
Now we will talk about that.
First, there is a kind of confession that is based on the Scriptures. It is for when someone sins in public, or in a way other people know about, and he is accused in front of the church.
If he turns away from his sin, the church prays to God for him.
But if he will not listen to the church, he is put out of the church and sent away. Then no one will have anything to do with him.
God commands this kind of confession in Matthew 18: "If your brother sins against you (so that you and others are offended), go and point out what he did wrong, just between the two of you."
[Matt. 18:15] But you cannot find even a trace of this kind of confession anymore. In this matter the Gospel has been pushed aside here.
Anyone who could bring it back would be doing a good work.
This is where you should have put in the effort. You should have brought back this kind of confession and let the other things go.
No one would have been offended by that, and it could have been done without any trouble.

This is how it should be done. When you see someone who lends money at unfair interest, or who cheats on his marriage, or who steals, or who gets drunk, go to him privately. Warn him to give up his sin.
If he will not listen, take two other people with you. Warn him once more, like a brother, to give up his sin.

But if he laughs that off, tell the pastor in front of the whole church. Bring your witnesses with you. Accuse him before the pastor with all the people there. Say: "Dear pastor, this man has done this and that. We warned him like brothers to give up his sin, but he would not listen.
So I am accusing him, together with my witnesses who were there."

Then, if he will not give up his sin and willingly admit his guilt, the pastor should put him out. In front of the whole gathering, he should shut him out of the church's fellowship. This is done for the good of the church. It lasts until the man comes to his senses and is welcomed back again.
That would be Christian.
But I cannot take this on and carry it out all by myself.
Second, we need to confess when we go off into a corner by ourselves. There we confess to God Himself and pour out all our faults to Him.
This kind of confession is also commanded.
That is where the well-known saying from Scripture comes from: "Facite judicium et justitiam"—"Do judgment and righteousness."
[Gen. 18:19] To do judgment means to accuse and condemn ourselves. To do righteousness means to trust in God's mercy.
As it is written, "Happy are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times."
[Ps. 106:3] Judgment is simply this: a person sees himself as he is, judges himself and condemns himself. That is true humility, bringing yourself low.
Righteousness is simply this: a person knows himself and prays to God for mercy and help. And through that mercy and help, God lifts him up again.

That is what David means when he says, "I have sinned. I will confess my wrongs to the Lord" [Ps. 32:5f.]. He also says, "You forgave the guilt of my sin. That is why all Your holy people will pray to You."

Third, there is also a kind of confession where one person takes another aside. He tells him what is troubling him, so that he can hear a word of comfort from him. This is the kind of confession the pope has commanded.
What I condemned when I wrote about confession was this pushing and forcing. I refuse to go to confession just because the pope wants it and has ordered it.
I want him to keep his hands off confession. He should not turn it into something forced or commanded. He does not have the power to do that.
Still, I will not let anyone take private confession away from me. I would not give it up for all the treasures in the world. I know how much comfort and strength it has given me.
No one knows what it can do for him unless he has fought hard against the devil.
Yes, the devil would have killed me long ago if confession had not held me up.
A person has many doubts that he cannot settle by himself. So he takes a brother aside and tells him his trouble.

What harm is there in that? He humbles himself a little in front of his neighbor and lets himself be ashamed. He looks to him for a word of comfort. Then he takes that word for himself and believes it, as if he heard it from God Himself. We read about this in Matthew 18: "If two of you agree about anything they ask for, it will be done for them." [Matt. 18:19]
We need many absolutions. They make our fearful consciences and hopeless hearts strong against the devil and against God.
So no one should forbid confession. No one should keep anyone away from it or drive anyone away from it.

Maybe someone is struggling with his sins. He wants to be free of them and is looking for some promise from the Scriptures to make him sure. Let him go and confess to another person in private. And whatever is said to him there, let him receive it as if it came straight from God's own mouth.
If someone has a strong, firm faith that his sins are forgiven, he can skip this kind of confession and confess to God alone.
But how many people have such strong faith?
So, as I said, I will not let anyone take this private confession away from me.
But I would not force anyone to do it. I leave it up to each person's free choice.

Our God is not stingy. He has not left us with just one comfort or one source of strength for our conscience, or just one absolution. No, we have many absolutions in the Gospel, and He pours them out on us richly.
For example, we have this in the Gospel: "If you forgive other people when they wrong you, your Father in heaven will forgive you too."
[Matt. 6:14] We have another comfort in the Lord's Prayer: "Forgive us our trespasses" [Matt. 6:12], and so on.
A third comfort is our baptism. I reason like this: "Look, my Lord, I am baptized in Your name, so I can be sure of Your grace and mercy."
Next we have private confession. I go and receive a sure absolution, as if God Himself were speaking it. Then I can be sure that my sins are forgiven.

Finally I receive the blessed sacrament for myself. I eat His body and drink His blood as a sign that I am free of my sins and that God has set me free from all my weaknesses. To make me sure of this, He gives me His body to eat and His blood to drink. So I will not despair, and I cannot despair. I cannot doubt that God is kind to me.
So we see that confession must not be looked down on. It is a true comfort.

We need many absolutions and comforts, because we have to fight against the devil, death, hell and sin. So we must not let any of our weapons be taken away. We must keep the whole set of armor and equipment that God has given us to use against our enemies.
You do not know yet how hard it is to fight the devil and beat him.
But I know it well. I have eaten salt with him once or twice.
I know him well, and he knows me well too.
If you only knew him, you would not throw out confession like this.
I put you in God's care. Amen.
Text: Romans 12:16-21.
16 Do not be wise in your own opinions.
17 Do not pay anyone back evil for evil.
Be careful to do what is honorable in the eyes of everyone.
18 If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.
19 Dear friends, do not take revenge yourselves. Instead, make room for the wrath of God. For it is written: Vengeance belongs to me; I will pay back, says the Lord.
20 But if your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him something to drink. For by doing this you will heap coals of fire on his head.
21 Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
"Do not be wise in your own opinions."
64. The reading used in church ends here.
So we will only look briefly at the rest.

"Your own opinions" here means a stubborn attitude about earthly things. It is the attitude of a person who does not want to be taught. He thinks he knows best about everything. He gives in to no one, and he calls good whatever fits his own ideas.
A Christian should be more willing to give in on earthly matters.
He should not be quarrelsome but ready to give way. After all, God's Word and faith are not at stake here. It is only a matter of personal honor, of friends, and of worldly things.
"Do not pay anyone back evil for evil."
65. Earlier (verse 14) the writer of the letter said, "Do not curse." There he was thinking of people who cannot take revenge or pay back evil for evil.
These people have no other choice but to curse, to call down evil on those who oppress them.

But here he is talking about people who have equal power to pay each other back evil for evil and spite for spite. They can do this by what they do or by what they fail to do. And usually it is by what they fail to do.
But a Christian should pay back good for evil, and not fail to do it.
God lets his sun shine on the evil and on the good.
Matthew 5:45.
"Be careful to do what is honorable in the eyes of everyone."

66. This command is like the one he gives the Thessalonians (1 Thess 5:22): "Stay away from every appearance of evil." It is also like what he tells the Philippians (4:8): "Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is well spoken of. If there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things."
This is only about how we act outwardly.
Paul does not want Christians to think they are free to do whatever they please, without caring whether others approve.
Only in matters of faith does a Christian have that freedom.

His outward behavior should be above blame and acceptable to everyone. This fits the teaching of 1 Corinthians 10:32-33: we should please everyone and give offense to neither Jews nor Gentiles. It also follows Peter's advice (1 Pet 2:12): "Keep your behavior proper among the Gentiles."
"If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone."
67. Here Paul means outward peace among people. This is peace with Christians and pagans, with the godly and the wicked, with people of high and low rank.
We must not give anyone a reason to fight. Instead, we should patiently put up with every evil. We should never let peace be broken because of us.
We must not pay back evil for evil or blow for blow. Whoever does that starts quarrels.
Paul adds, "As far as it depends on you."
We should avoid hurting anyone, so that we are not the ones who start a quarrel.
We must be friendly to everyone, even if they are not friendly to us.
It is impossible to keep the peace all the time.
As the saying goes, "I can only live in peace as long as my neighbor wants to."
But it is in our power to leave others in peace, both friends and enemies, and to put up with everyone's quarrels.
"Oh yes," you say, "but then where would we be?" Listen:
"Dear friends, do not take revenge yourselves. Instead, make room for the wrath of God. For it is written: Vengeance belongs to me; I will pay back, says the Lord."
68. Notice this: the apostle forbids us to pay back blow for blow or to take revenge. In this way he shows that if we want to enjoy peace, we must quietly put up with the trouble others cause us.
He does not only assure us that we will be avenged. He also frightens us away from taking over God's office, for vengeance and payback belong to God alone.

In fact, he rather grieves over what will happen to the Christian's enemies, who put themselves in the path of God's wrath. He wants to move us to pity them, because we must make room for wrath and let them fall into God's hands.

God's vengeance and wrath come in many ways. They come through the government and through the devil. They come by sickness, hunger, and plague, by fire and water, and by war, hostility, and disgrace. And they come by every kind of misfortune on earth.
Any creature can serve as God's rod and weapon when he means to punish.
As the Wisdom of Solomon says (5:17): "He shall ... make the creature his weapon to take revenge on his enemies."
69. So Paul says, "Make room for wrath."
I have added the words "of God" to make the meaning of the text clearer. The wrath of God is meant, not human wrath.
The idea is not that we should make room for the anger of our enemies.
It is true that there may be times for that too. But here Paul is not talking about human anger.
Clearly he means misfortunes and plagues, which are seen as expressions of God's wrath.
Maybe the apostle left out that phrase so that no one would think he meant only God's final wrath. That is his anger on the last day, when he will punish without using any other means.
Paul wants to include here all the wrath that God shows in his punishments, whether in this life or forever.
This is a way of speaking from the Old Testament.
Phinehas says (Josh 22:18), "Tomorrow he will be angry with ...
Israel." And in several places Moses speaks of God's anger flaring up.
See Numbers 11:1, 10, 33.

I mention these things to teach this: when the government uses the sword to punish its enemies, we should see it as an expression of God's wrath. And the words in Deuteronomy 32:35, "Vengeance is mine," do not refer only to punishment that God brings directly, without any other means.
"But if your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him something to drink. For by doing this you will heap coals of fire on his head."
70. This teaching supports what I have already said: the Christian's enemies deserve pity, because they are under the wrath of God.
So it is not Christian to harm them. Instead, we should do them favors.
Here Paul quotes Solomon.
Proverbs 25:21-22. I think heaping coals of fire on someone's head means doing favors for the enemy.
Our kindness sets him on fire. In the end he becomes unhappy with himself and friendlier toward us.
Here the coals are kindnesses, or favors.
In the same way, the coals in the incense burner stand for God's favors, or blessings. They are a picture of our prayers, which should rise up with fervor.

Some say that the coals stand for God's Law and judgments (see Psalm 18:8, "Coals were kindled by it"). They reason that the Christian's kindness forces his enemy to blame himself and to feel the weight of God's Law and his judgments.
I do not think a Christian should want punishment to fall on his enemy. Still, this explanation of the verse is not a bad one.
In fact, it fits well with the command "Make room for wrath." That means: do good, and then wrath—the coals—will easily fall on the enemy.
"Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good."
71. It seems to me that with this final counsel Paul himself explains the words "coals of fire." He explains them in line with the first idea: an enemy's malice is to be overcome with good.
Overcoming by force is the same as giving yourself over to evil and wronging the enemy who wrongs you.
If you do that, your enemy overcomes you, and you become evil like him.
But if you overcome him with good, he will become righteous like you.
Here a spiritual victory is meant. The attitude, the heart, and the soul are overcome—yes, even the devil who stirs up the evil.
Text: Romans 13:8-10.
8 Do not owe anyone anything, except to love one another. Whoever loves his neighbor has done all that the law requires.
9 Take these commands: Do not commit adultery. Do not kill. Do not steal. Do not covet. If there is any other command, it is summed up in this one word: Love your neighbor as yourself.
10 Love does nothing bad to a neighbor. That is why love is the fulfilling of the law.
1. This reading, like the two epistle readings before it, is a word of warning and encouragement. It turns our attention to the fruits that faith produces.
But here Paul sums up all the fruits of faith in one short word: love.

In the verses just before this, he told us to obey the government. We are to pay taxes and duties, and give respect and honor wherever they are owed, because all power to govern is set in place by God.
Then comes our reading: “Do not owe anyone anything,” and the rest.
2. People usually come up with all sorts of explanations for this command: “Do not owe anyone anything, except to love one another.” I will leave them all aside.
To me its meaning is clear and simple. The debts we owe should be owed as Christians, not merely as ordinary people.
What we owe should be the free debt of love.
It should not be something forced on us or ordered by law.
Paul shows us two kinds of debt. One comes from the law. The other comes from love.
Debts of law make us owe things to other people. For example, one person may have the right to collect money that another person owes him.
The taxes and fees, the obedience and honor we owe to the government, are this kind of legal debt.

For a Christian, these things are not what really matter. They do not make him right with God or make him any more righteous. But he still has to live here on earth. So in his outward life he must do these things just like everyone else. In general, he must help keep order and peace in the world.
Christ himself paid the tax money as a debt (Matthew 17:27). Yet he had told Peter that he did not have to pay it, and that it would not have been a sin before God to leave it unpaid.
3. The other kind of debt is love. This is when a Christian freely makes himself a servant of everyone.
Paul says (1 Corinthians 9:19), “I was free from everyone, and yet I made myself a slave to everyone.”
Human laws do not require this. If someone fails to do it, no one blames him or punishes him for breaking the law.
The world does not know about the command to love. It does not know that we owe it to others to put ourselves under them and serve them.
You can see this very plainly.
Take a rich man. As long as he does not disgrace his neighbor’s wife, take his neighbor’s things, ruin his good name, or hurt him, the law says he is a good man.
No law punishes him for being greedy and stingy. No law punishes him for refusing to lend, to give, or to help, or for not helping a neighbor who has been wronged to get justice.
Laws are made to control what people do on the outside. They deal only with evil deeds, which they forbid and punish.
Good deeds are left for people to do freely.
The laws of the land do not force good deeds out of people with threats and punishment. Instead they praise and reward them, just as the Law of Moses does.

4. Paul wants to teach Christians how to behave toward other people and toward the government. They should give no one a reason to complain about them or blame them for not paying what the law of the land says they owe.

He does not want them to fall short of what the law requires. He wants them to go beyond it. They should freely make themselves debtors, and serve people who have no right to demand anything from them.
About this Paul says (Romans 1:14), “I owe a debt to both Greeks and Barbarians.”
The debt of love makes a person able to do more than he is actually required to do.
So a Christian always gladly gives the state and each person every service that the rules of this world require. He makes sure no one can say he owes them anything in this area.
5. So Paul’s command could be put like this: Owe everyone, so that you owe no one. Owe everything, so that you owe nothing.
That sounds like a contradiction. But one kind of debt is the debt of love, which we owe to God.
The other kind is what we owe to the law of the land, a debt in the eyes of the world.

Think of someone who makes himself a servant and takes on the debt of love toward everyone. He goes so far that no one dares to complain that he has left something undone. In fact, he goes farther than anyone could ask.
In this way he is set free.
He owes nothing to anyone, simply because he has made himself owe everything to everyone.
The Spirit would back up this way of speaking about other duties too. For example: Do no good work, so that you may do only good works.
Never be godly and holy, if you want to always be godly and holy.
As Paul says (Romans 12:16), “Do not think yourselves wise.” Or (1 Corinthians 3:18), “If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this world, let him become a fool, so that he may become wise.”
This is what we mean when we say: Owe everyone, so that you owe no one. Or: “Do not owe anyone anything, except to love one another.”
6. This advice is given with the two kinds of debt in mind.
Anyone who wants to do works that are truly good in God’s sight must watch out for works that look dazzling to the world. By such works people think they can make themselves righteous.
Anyone who wants to be righteous and holy must watch out for the kind of holiness people get from works without faith.
In the same way, anyone looking for wisdom must turn away from human wisdom, the wisdom of nature, wisdom that does not come from the Spirit.
And so, anyone who wants to owe no one must put himself in debt to everyone, in every way.
When he does this, he keeps no claims for himself.
As a result, he soon rises above every law. The law only has a hold on people who still have claims of their own.
The saying is right: “Qui cedit omnibus bonis, omnibus satisfecit,” which means, “Whoever gives up all he owns has satisfied everyone.”
How can someone owe anything when he does not own anything, and cannot own anything?
Love’s way is to give everything.
So the best way to owe no one is to put yourself, through love, in debt to everyone in every way.

In this sense we can say: If you want to live, die. If you do not want to be locked up, lock yourself up. If you do not want to go to hell, go down there. If you do not want to be a sinner, be a sinner. If you want to escape the cross, take it up yourself. If you want to conquer the devil, let him defeat you. Do you want to overcome a wicked person? Let him overcome you.
What all this means is that we should be quick to give way to God, to the devil and to people, and gladly let them have their way. We should insist on nothing, but accept everything as it happens.
That is why Paul says, “Do not owe anyone anything,” and so on. He does not just stop with the command before it in verse 5, “So pay everyone whatever is due to them,” and so on.

blocks.x: Love Keeps the Whole Law.

s: “Whoever loves his neighbor has done all that the law requires.”
7. We have often talked about what love is like and what fruit it bears, so there is no need to go into that here.
That subject is covered well enough in the epistle reading for the Sunday before Lent.
We will look at the command to love as it stands in God’s Law.
There are countless, endless books and teachings written to tell people how to live.
And still people keep making more books and more laws, with no end.
Just look at all the rules of the church and of the state, and all the religious orders and ranks.

We could put up with these laws and teachings, and even welcome them more, if they were built on the one great law of love and carried out by it. Love is the one rule and measure. That is how the Scriptures do it. They give many different laws, but all of them are born from love, all are included in love, and all are under love.
And whenever these laws clash with love, they must give way and no longer count.
The Scriptures give many examples that show love has the higher authority.
Christ speaks about this in Matthew 12:3-4, where David and his men ate the holy bread that was set out before God.
There was a law that only the priests could eat this holy food. But here Love was the empress, and she was free.
Love stood above the Law and made the Law obey her.
When David was hungry, the Law had to step aside for the moment and lose its force.
The Law had to accept this ruling: “David is hungry and must be helped, because Love commands, Do good to your neighbor who is in need.
So step aside, Law.
Do not stop this good thing from being done.
Better yet, do it yourself.
Help him in his need.
Do not get in the way with your rules.”
In the same story, Christ teaches that we should do good to our neighbor on the Sabbath. We are to help him as his need requires, no matter what the Law’s Sabbath rules say.
For when a brother’s need calls out, Love is in charge, and the Sabbath law does not count.
8. If laws were made and carried out in love, it would not matter much how many laws there were.
A person might not hear or learn all of them. But from the one or two he did know, he would learn the rule of love that all of them teach.
And even if he knew every law, he would not find the rule of love any more easily than in just one.

Paul teaches this way of understanding and mastering the law when he says: “Do not owe anyone anything, except to love one another.” “Whoever loves another has done all that the law requires.” “If there is any other commandment, it is summed up in short in this saying: Love your neighbor as yourself.” “Love does nothing bad to a neighbor.” “Love is the fulfilling of the law.”
Every word in this epistle reading proves that Love rules over all law.
9. What is more, there is no greater disaster, wrong and misery on earth than teaching and enforcing laws without love.

When that happens, laws are nothing but a curse that ruins people. They prove these sayings true: “summum jus, summa injustitia,” which means, “The strictest justice is the worst injustice.” And Solomon’s words (Ecclesiastes 7:17), “Noli nimium esse justus,” which means, “Do not be more righteous than you should be.”
This is where we do not notice the log in our own eye, and go ahead to take the speck out of our neighbor’s eye.
Laws without love make the conscience fearful. They fill it with terror and despair that make no sense, and this does great harm to body and soul.
So a lot of trouble and hard work is spent for nothing.
10. A good example is the story we mentioned earlier, about David when he was hungry.
1 Samuel 21:6.

Suppose the priest had wanted to refuse David the holy bread. Suppose he had blindly held on to the Law’s rules and failed to see that Love had authority. Suppose he had kept this food from a hungry man. What would have happened?
As far as the priest’s help went, David would have had to starve to death. And the priest would have been guilty of murder for the sake of the Law.
Here the saying would truly fit: “summum jus, summa injustitia”—the strictest justice would have been the worst injustice.

And if you looked into the heart of a priest foolish enough to do that, you would find something utterly disgusting. He makes a sin out of something that is not a sin. He troubles his conscience where there is no reason for it.
He thinks eating the bread is a sin, when really it is an act of love and of doing right.
On top of that, he thinks his act of murder—letting David starve—is not a sin at all, but a good work and a service to God.
11. Who could ever fully describe this blind, twisted, disgusting foolishness?
It is an evil so great that the devil himself could not do worse.
It makes sin where there is no sin. It troubles the conscience for no reason.
It steals away grace, salvation, goodness, and God himself with all his blessings. And it does this for no reason, falsely and by trickery.
It flatly denies God and condemns him.
It also turns murder and injustice into a good work and a service to God.
It puts the devil and his lies in God’s place.
It sets up the worst kind of idol worship. It ruins both body and soul, destroying the body by hunger and the soul by a terrified conscience.
It turns God into the devil and the devil into God.
It turns heaven into hell and hell into heaven. It turns sin into righteousness and righteousness into sin.
This is what I call turning things upside down—when the strictest justice becomes the worst wrong.

Ezekiel speaks about this wickedness (13:18-19): “This is what the Lord Jehovah says: How terrible it will be for the women who sew pillows for everyone’s elbows, and make head coverings for people of every height, in order to hunt souls!
Will you hunt down the souls of my people, and keep souls alive to benefit yourselves?

You have dishonored me among my people for a few handfuls of barley and some pieces of bread. You kill souls that should not die, and you keep alive souls that should not live, by lying to my people, who are willing to listen to lies.”

What else can this mean? The blind teachers of the Law terrify the conscience. They put sin and death in place of grace and life, and they put grace and life where there is only sin and death. And all for a handful of barley and a bit of bread!

Put simply, these teachers give all their attention to laws about purely outward things, things that are used up and gone, like a drink of water and a bite of bread. They completely ignore love, and they torment people’s consciences with the fear that sin will bring them eternal death. As Ezekiel goes on to say (verses 22-23): “You have used lies to make the hearts of good people sad, when I had not made them sad. And you have made the wicked bolder, so that they will not turn from their wicked ways and be saved. So you will no longer see false visions or tell fortunes. I will set my people free from your hands, and you will know that I am Jehovah.”

12. Notice this: to load good people with sins when their works are good is to make their hearts sad. And to call the works of wicked people good when those works are nothing but sin is to make the wicked bolder.
About this we read (Psalm 14:5): “They were terrified there, because God is among those who do right.”
This means that the sting of conscience makes them afraid, when there is no reason to be afraid or to have a troubled conscience.
People are afraid that something is a sin when it is really a noble service to God.

The meaning of that last verse is this: When they should call on God and serve him, they are afraid that doing so is a sin and not a service to God. But when they ought to be afraid of a service that is not from God at all, they feel safe and have no fear.
Isaiah says the same thing (29:13): “The way they fear me is just a rule made by people, which they have been taught.”
These twisted people always spoil everything.
They boldly call on God where there is only the devil. And they are too afraid to call on God where God really is.
13. Take note: this is the miserable state of people who are blindly busy with laws and works. They do not understand what law is for, or that Love rules over it.
And look at our miserable clergy and their followers. See how stubbornly they hold on to the rules they made up themselves!
Even if the whole world is ruined, their schemes must stay in place. They must be kept going, even if bodies get sick and die, and souls suffer and are ruined.
They even think that such destruction and ruin is a service to God. They feel no fear and no guilt in their conscience.
In fact, they are dug in so deep in their wickedness that they will never turn away from it.

And suppose one of these poor people is allowed to ease the suffering of his body and soul—to eat meat, or to get married. He is afraid. His conscience bothers him. He is unsure about sin and the law, about death and hell. He does not call on God or serve him. And all this even though his body should die ten deaths and his soul go to the devil a hundred times.

14. So look at the state of the world. See how little flesh and blood can do, even at their very best. See how dangerous it is to try to rule by law alone. In fact, it is impossible to guide and teach souls with laws alone, without great danger, if love and the Spirit are left out. For the full power of every law is in their hands.
It is written (Deuteronomy 33:2), “In his right hand was a law of fire for them.”
This means the law of love in the Spirit.
It is to rule all the laws at the left hand, that is, the outward laws of the world.

We are told (Exodus 28:30) that the priest had to wear “the Urim and the Thummim” on his chest, in the breastplate. These words mean Light and Perfection. They show that the priest’s job was to shed light on the Law—to explain its true meaning—and to keep it and teach it without fault.
15. When laws are thought up, set in place and kept, the goal should never be to push the laws for their own sake, or to promote works. The goal should be to put love into practice.
That is the real purpose of law, as Paul says here: “Whoever loves his neighbor has done all that the law requires.”
So when a law hurts our neighbor instead of helping him, we should set it aside.
The same law may help our neighbor at one time and hurt him at another.
So it should be used according to how much good it does him.
Law should serve people in the same way that food, clothes and the other things we need to live serve them.
We do not think about the food and clothes for their own sake. We think about how they help our neighbor in need.
And we stop handing them out as soon as we see they are no longer helping him.

16. Imagine you met someone so foolish that the only thing he could think was that food and clothing are truly good things. So he stuffs a needy person with endless food and drink until the man chokes. He piles clothes on him until he cannot breathe. And even then he does not stop.

Suppose someone tells him, “Stop! You have smothered him. You have already overfed him and put too many clothes on him. It is all wasted effort now.” And suppose the foolish man answers: “You heretic! Do you want to forbid good works?
Food, drink and clothing are good things. So we must not stop giving them out. We can never do too much.”
And suppose he kept on forcing food and clothes on the man.
Tell me, what would you think of someone like that?
He is worse than a fool. He is crazier than craziness itself.

But that is pretty much what our clergy are like today. The same goes for everyone who is so blind in using the law that they act as if works were all that mattered. They smother both body and soul, because they do not know that the only purpose of law is to call love into action.
They put works above love, like putting a servant girl above the lady of the house.
This twisted thinking is so widespread that it is painful even to think about. It is worse to hear and see it, and worse still to do it and allow it ourselves.
17. The commandment to love is not long. It is short.
It is one command, not many.
It is not even a commandment, and yet at the same time it is every commandment.
It is short and all of one piece, so its meaning is easy to understand.
But when it is put into practice, it reaches very far, because it includes and directs every commandment.
As far as ordering specific works goes, it is not a commandment at all. It does not name any one particular work.
Yet it stands for all the commandments, because keeping all the commandments really means keeping this one.
The commandment to love sets every commandment aside, and yet it keeps them all in force.
Its whole point is that we should accept no commandment and no work unless love calls for it.
18. We cannot live on earth without doing works. So there have to be various commandments that deal with works.
But Love rules over all these requirements. Love decides whether a work should be done or left undone, depending on what serves love best. And love allows no works that go against it.
Here is a picture of it. A wagon driver holds the reins and steers the horses and the wagon wherever he wants.

Suppose he were happy just to hold the reins and did not care whether the horses stayed on the road. Then the whole thing—horses, wagon, reins and driver—would soon be wrecked. The driver would end up drowned in a ditch or a pond, or with a broken neck from going over stumps and rocks.
But if he skillfully steers the rig to fit the road, watching where it is safe and where it is not, he will travel safely because he drives wisely.
But suppose he were so full of himself that he drove straight ahead, trying to make the road follow the wagon wherever he pleased. He would soon see how beautifully that plan would work!
19. It is the same when people are ruled by laws and works, and the laws are not fitted to the people.
It is like the driver who wants the road to follow the wagon.
It is true that the road often fits the wagon going straight ahead.
But it is just as true that in some places the road is crooked and bumpy. Then the wagon has to follow the road’s turns and fit its condition.
People must fit themselves to laws and rules wherever they can, and wherever the laws do good.
But where laws turn out to hurt people, the laws must give way.
A ruler must be wise and make room for love, setting works and laws aside.
That is why philosophers say that prudence—or carefulness, or good judgment, as the clergy call it—guides and directs all the virtues.
20. We read in a book about the ancient church fathers that once, when they met together, someone asked, Which work is really the noblest?
They gave different answers.
One said prayer, and another said fasting. But St. Anthony thought that of all works and virtues, good judgment is the best and surest way to heaven.
But these were childish, unspiritual ideas about works they had picked for themselves.
A Christian sees the matter in a completely different and wiser way.
He decides that neither good judgment nor rashness counts for anything with God.
Only faith and love count with him.
But love is the true good judgment. Love is the driver, and the true good judgment, in works that are right.

Love always looks out for what is good for its neighbor and how to make his life better. In the same way, the good judgment of the world looks out for the welfare of the people when it adjusts the laws of the land.
That is enough on this point.

21. But here a question comes up. How can love fulfill the Law, when love is only one of the fruits of faith? We have often said that only faith in Christ takes away our sins, makes us right with God and meets every demand of the Law.
How can both of these be true?
Christ also says (Matthew 7:12): “So whatever you want people to do for you, do the same for them. For this is the law and the prophets.”
In this way he shows that loving your neighbor fulfills both the Law and the prophets.
He also says (Matthew 22:37-40): “Love the Lord your God ... your neighbor as yourself.
The whole law and the prophets hang on these two.”
So where does Paul stand? He says (Romans 3:31): “Does faith mean we cancel the law?
Not at all! Instead, we make the law stand firm.”
And again (Romans 3:28): “We conclude, then, that a person is declared righteous by faith, apart from doing the works of the law.”
And again (Romans 1:17), “The one who is righteous will live by faith.”
22. My answer is this. As we have often said, we must make a proper distinction between faith and love.
Faith has to do with the heart, and love has to do with works.
Faith takes away our sins, makes us acceptable to God, and makes us right with him.
And once we ourselves have been accepted and made right with God, love is given to us in the Holy Spirit, and we enjoy doing good.
Now, the Law by its nature goes after us personally and demands good works. It will keep on demanding until it gets what it wants.
Without the Spirit and love, we cannot do good works.
The Law forces us to see ourselves as we are, with all our flaws. It makes us see that we need to become completely different people if we are ever to satisfy the Law.
The Law does not ask as much from the heart as from works. In fact, it asks for nothing but works and pays no attention to the heart.
It leaves each person to figure out, from the works it requires, that he has to become a completely different person.
But when faith comes, it creates a nature that is able to do the works the Law demands.
And so the Law is fulfilled.
So what Paul says about this is beautiful and just right.
The Law demands works from us. It has to be fulfilled by works.
So we cannot say in every sense that faith fulfills the Law.
But faith prepares the way and makes us able to fulfill it. For the Law does not demand us, but our works.
The Law puts pressure on us. It teaches us that we must be changed before we can do its works. It makes us see that, just as we are, we cannot do them.
On the other hand, love and works do not change us, and they do not make us right with God.
We ourselves must be changed and made right with God before we can love and do good works.
Our love and our works are proof that we have been made right with God and changed. They cannot happen until a person has been set free from sin and made righteous.

23. I give this explanation to help us see what the Law, faith and love really are, and to give each one its own proper job. It also helps us rightly understand how the statements of Scripture fit together. Faith makes us right with God, but it does not fulfill the Law. Love does not make us right with God, but it does fulfill the Law.
The Law requires love and works, but it says nothing about the heart.
The heart feels the Law, but love does not.

Before there is faith, the Law demands works. That is a sign to a person. It leads him to see that he has no faith and no righteousness at all, and to admit that he is beaten. In the same way, after faith has come, love fulfills the Law. That is a sign and a proof to the person that he has faith and righteousness.
So the Law and love both act as witnesses to him, telling him whether he is unrighteous or righteous.
Once faith has come, love is the proof of righteousness.
Before faith, a person feels the Law pressing down on him, because he knows he does not have what the Law requires.
And the Law does not ask for a changed heart, but for works.
Love and works do not cause the Law to be fulfilled. They themselves are its fulfilling.
24. Now, even though faith does not fulfill the Law, it holds what makes the Law fulfilled. It gains the Spirit and love, and these get the job done.
On the other hand, love does not make us right with God, but it shows the faith by which we are made right.
To put it briefly, as Paul says here, “Love is the fulfilling of the law.”
What he means is this: fulfilling the Law is one thing, and causing or providing that fulfilling is another.
Love fulfills the Law in the sense that love itself is the fulfilling. But faith fulfills it in the sense that faith supplies what fulfills it.
For faith loves and works, as Galatians 5:6 says: “Faith goes to work through love.”
The water fills the pitcher, and so does the servant who pours it.
The water fills it by itself. The servant fills it by means of the water. As the sophists would say, “effective et formaliter implere.”
25. Faith is always the doer, and love is the deed.
The law demands the deed, and that forces the doer to be changed.
So the Law is fulfilled by the deed, but the doer has to do it.

In this way Paul rejects the made-up ideas of the sophists. When it comes to love, they want to separate the outward work from the inner feeling. They say, “Love is an inner feeling that loves our neighbor when we wish him well in our heart.”
But they call the way love shows itself in works the fruit of love.
But we will not argue about this idea.
Notice that Paul calls love not just a feeling, but a loving good deed.
Faith and the heart are the doer and the fulfiller of the Law.
Paul says, “Whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.”
And love is the deed, the fulfilling, because he says, “Love is the fulfilling of the law.”
26. Another question comes up. How can love for our neighbor be the fulfilling of the Law, when we are told to love God most of all, even more than our neighbor?
My answer: Christ answers this question himself when he tells us (Matthew 22:39) that the second commandment is like the first.
He makes love for God and love for our neighbor one and the same love.
The first reason is this: God does not need our works and our gifts for himself. So he tells us to do for our neighbor what we would do for God.
All he asks for himself is our faith, and that we acknowledge him as God.
We proclaim his honor and give him praise and thanks here on earth so that our neighbor may be converted and brought into fellowship with God.
This kind of service is called love for God, and it is done out of love for God. But it is carried out only for our neighbor’s good.

27. Here is the second reason why God makes love for our neighbor a duty equal to love for himself. God has made the wisdom of this world foolish. From now on he wants to be loved in the middle of crosses and troubles.
Paul says (1 Corinthians 1:21), “In God’s wisdom, the world did not come to know God through its own wisdom. So it pleased God to use the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe.”
So on the cross he gave himself up to death and misery, and he required the same surrender from all his disciples.
People who would not love him before, when he gave them food and drink, blessing and honor, must now love him in hunger and sorrow, in hard times and in shame.
So all our works of love must be aimed at our poor, needy neighbors.
In these lowly people we are to find God and love him. In them we are to serve him and honor him. This is the only way we can do it.
The command to love God is completely wrapped up in the command to love our neighbors.
28. These facts hold back those slippery, high-flying spirits who look for God only in great and glorious projects.
This shuts the mouths of people who try to be great like him, who want to force their way into heaven, and who think they can serve and love him with their dazzling works.
But they miss him, because they walk right past him in their neighbor here on earth, the very one in whom God wants to be loved and honored.
So on the last day they will hear the sentence (Matthew 25:42), “I was hungry, and you did not give me anything to eat,” and so on.
For Christ set aside his divine nature and took on the form of a servant. He did this for the very purpose of bringing our love for him down to earth and pointing it toward our neighbor.
And yet we leave the Lord lying here in his lowliness, while we stare up into heaven with our mouths hanging open and make a big show of loving and serving God.

blocks.x: Every Commandment Summed Up in Love.

s: “Take these commands: Do not commit adultery. Do not kill. Do not steal. Do not covet. If there is any other command, it is summed up in short in this one word: Love your neighbor as yourself.”
29. Love is the main thing in every law. So, as we have shown clearly enough, it includes all the commandments.
Its only concern is to help people and not to hurt them. That is why it easily finds the way.
Love sees that people, because they love themselves so much, try to look after their own interests and avoid anything that would harm them. So love tries to do the same for others.
Let us look at the commandment we just quoted, and notice how cleverly and wisely it is put together.
It brings out four ideas.
First, it tells us who has the duty to love: you. That is the nearest, noblest and best person any of us can command.
No one can keep God’s Law for someone else. Each person must do it for himself.
As Paul says (Galatians 6:5), “Each person will carry his own burden.”

And (2 Corinthians 5:10): “All of us must be shown for what we are before the judgment seat of Christ. Then each one will receive back what he did while in the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad.”
So it says, “You, you yourself, must love.” It does not say, “Let someone else love for you.”
We can and should pray that God will be kind to someone else and help him. But no one will be saved unless he himself keeps God’s command.
It is not enough just to pray that someone will escape punishment, as the people who sell indulgences teach. Much more, we should pray that he will become righteous and obey God’s commands.
30. Second, the commandment names the noblest virtue of all: love.
It does not say, “Feed your neighbor, give him something to drink, give him clothes,” even though all of these are wonderfully good works. It says, “Love him.”
Love is the greatest virtue, the spring that all the other virtues flow from.
Love gives food and drink. It clothes people, comforts them, urges them on, relieves them and rescues them.

What can we say about it? Look: the one who loves gives himself, body and soul, his belongings and his honor, all his powers inside and out, for the good of his needy neighbor, whether that neighbor is a friend or an enemy. He holds back nothing that he could use to serve someone else.
No virtue is like love. You cannot give it just one special job, the way you can with smaller virtues like purity, mercy, patience, gentleness and so on.
Love does everything.
It will suffer in life and in death, in every situation, and it will do this even for its enemies.
No wonder Paul says here that all the other commandments are summed up in short in this command: “Love your neighbor as yourself.”
31. Third, the commandment names the place where our love is to work. It is the noblest field and the dearest friend: our neighbor.
It does not say, “Love the rich, the powerful, the educated, the saint.”
No, the boundless love named in this most perfect commandment does not share itself out among just a few people.
It does not play favorites.
False, selfish, worldly love does play favorites. It loves someone only as long as it hopes to get something out of it.
When that hope ends, that love ends too.

But the commandment in our text asks us for a love that is free and willing. It is for all people, whoever they are, friend or enemy. It is a love that does not look for gain, and gives only what is good for others.

This kind of love is most active and strongest when it serves the poor, the needy, the sick, the wicked, the simple and those who are against us. Among such people you always have to suffer and put up with things, serve and do good, no matter what.
32. Notice here that this commandment makes all of us equal before God. It pays no attention to the differences between us in our place in life, who we are, our positions or our jobs.

This commandment is for everyone, for every human being. So a king, if he is a human being, must admit that the poorest beggar and the most miserable leper is his neighbor and his equal in God’s eyes.
This commandment says the king must not just give a little help. He must serve that neighbor with everything he has and everything under his control.
If he loves him the way God commands here, he must put the beggar ahead of his crown and his whole kingdom. And if the beggar’s need calls for it, he must give his life.
He must love his neighbor, and he must admit that such a person is his neighbor.
33. Isn’t this a high and noble commandment, which makes the most unequal people completely equal?

Isn’t it wonderfully comforting for the beggar to have such honored people as his servants and as those who love him? Isn’t it amazing that his poverty can call on a rich king to serve him? That the crown of riches and the sweet fragrance of royal splendor must bow to his sores and wounds?
But how strange it would look to us to see kings and queens, princes and princesses, serving beggars and lepers, as we read that St. Elizabeth did!
Yet even this would be a small thing compared with what Christ has done.
No one can ever match the obedience with which he has lifted this commandment high.
He is a king whose honor is greater than that of all other kings. In fact, he is the Son of God.
And yet he puts himself on the same level as the worst sinners, and serves them so fully that he even dies for them.
If ten kings on earth served one beggar with all they had, that would be remarkable. But what would it mean compared with the service Christ has given?
The kings would be completely ashamed and would have to admit that their service was not worth mentioning.
34. So learn what condition the world is in. See how far it is, not only from Christ’s example, which no one can measure, but also from the commandment in this verse.

Where can you find anyone who understands what the little words “your neighbor” mean? And this is so even though, besides this commandment, the natural law of service is written in the hearts of all people.

There is not a single person who does not see, and who is not forced to admit, that the natural law is right and true. That law is described in the command (Matthew 7:12): “All the things you would want people to do to you, you must also do to them.”
The light of this law shines in the reason that every person is born with.
If people would only pay attention to it, what need would they have for books, teachers or laws?
Deep in their hearts they carry a living book with them. It can teach them fully what to do and what not to do, what to accept and what to turn down, and what to decide.
Now, the command to love our neighbors as ourselves means the same as that other command: “All the things you would want people to do to you,” and the rest.
Every person wants to be loved and not hated. And each one also feels and sees that he has a duty to have the same attitude toward others.
Carrying out this duty means loving someone else as himself.
But evil desire and sinful love darken the light of the natural law. They blind a person, until he no longer sees the guidebook in his heart and no longer follows the clear command of reason.
So he has to be held in check and pushed back by outward laws and written books, by the sword and by force.
He has to be reminded of the natural light he has, and his own heart has to be shown to him.
But warning him does not help. He does not see the light.
Evil desire and sinful love make him blind.
So he still has to be held back from the outside, by the sword and by the laws of the state. That keeps him from actually committing crimes.
35. The fourth thing the commandment shows us is the measure we are to use for our love. It is an excellent model.
Instructions and commandments that give examples are especially valuable.
This commandment holds up an example that is truly alive: “yourself.”
It is a better model than any example the saints have given us.
The saints are dead and what they did is in the past. But this example is always alive.

Everyone has to admit that he knows he loves himself. He knows how eagerly he cares for his life here on earth. He knows how carefully he feeds his body and gives it food, clothing and every good thing. He knows how he runs from death and keeps away from evil.
This is self-love. It is something we know is in us.
So what does the commandment teach?
To treat someone else the way you treat yourself. To value his body and his life just as much as your own body and life.
How could God have pointed you to an example that is dearer, more pleasing and more fitting than this one: the deep instinct of your own nature?
In fact, how deep your character goes is measured by this command that is written in your heart.
36. How will things go for you with God if you do not love your neighbor?
You feel this commandment written inside your heart, so your conscience will condemn you.

Your whole way of living will be an example that speaks against you. It will show that you did not do to others what the natural instinct of your own being taught you to do. And that instinct taught you more forcefully than all the examples of the saints.
But how will it go especially for the clergy? I mean the churchmen with their singing and praying, their monks’ hoods and shaved heads, and all their tricks.
I will not even mention that they have never kept the commandment.

But I do ask this: When has their monkish fanaticism ever given them the time and the chance to notice this law in their hearts even once? When has it let them become aware of the example their own human instinct gives them? When has it let them even read this command in books or hear it preached?

Poor, miserable people! Do you really dare to think that God will cancel this commandment of love? It is pressed so deeply and clearly into the heart. It is shown so beautifully and so plainly in your own nature, and also in the many words that have been written and spoken. Do you think God will cancel it because of your monks’ hoods and shaved heads? Do you think he will pay attention to what you have been making up and doing?
37. How sad it is! How shamelessly the world has ignored this beautiful and powerful commandment! It so skillfully shows the person, the task, the model and the field where the work is done.
And on the other hand, how shameful it is that the world keeps busy with the exact opposite of what this commandment teaches!

Its whole way of doing things and its whole aim seem to be to put our responsibility on other people. Monks and priests must be righteous for us and pray in our place, so that we ourselves can be let off.
In place of the noblest virtue, love, we put works we have made up ourselves. In place of our neighbors we put wood and stone, clothing and food, and even dead souls: the saints in heaven.
These are what we serve. These are what keep us busy. They are the field where we put in all our effort.
Instead of the noblest example, “as yourself,” we look to the legends and works of the saints.

We dare to copy such outward examples. Meanwhile we leave out the duty that our own nature and life set before us, and that God’s command describes. Yet that duty gives us more to do than we could ever carry out.
Even if we could do everything it sets before us, we would still not be equal to Christ.

blocks.x: Love Does Only Good to Its Neighbor.

s: “Love does no harm to its neighbor. So love is the fulfilling of the law.”
38. The Ten Commandments forbid us to do evil to our neighbor: “Do not kill. Do not commit adultery,” and so on.
The apostle uses similar words. He says that love keeps all these commands and harms no one.
And not only that: it does good to everyone.
If we can help our neighbor out of danger and we leave him in it, that is almost the same as doing evil to him. This is true even if we had no part in putting him there.
If he is hungry and we do not feed him when we are able to, we are in effect letting him starve to death.
We should see it the same way whenever our neighbors are in any danger or any kind of trouble.
Now we have heard how love fulfills the Law.
Text: Colossians 3:12-17.

12 God has chosen you. You are holy, and he loves you. So put on a heart full of compassion, along with kindness, humility, gentleness and being slow to anger. 13 Put up with one another. If anyone has a complaint against someone, forgive each other. Forgive just as the Lord forgave you. 14 And above all these things, put on love. Love is the perfect bond.
15 Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts. You were called to this peace together, in one body. And be thankful.
16 Let the Word of Christ live in you richly. Use all wisdom as you teach and warn one another with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. Sing to God with grace in your hearts.
17 Whatever you do, whether you speak or act, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus. Give thanks to God the Father through him.
1. This text is also a letter of warning and encouragement. It teaches what kind of fruit should grow out of faith.
Paul treats the Colossians kindly.
He does not give orders, push or threaten them. Teachers of the Law have to do that with people who live under the Law.
Instead, he wins them over with loving words. He reminds them of the blessing and grace they have received from God, and he points them to Christ's own example.
Christians should act willingly and cheerfully. They should not be moved by fear of punishment or by wanting a reward. We have said this many times before.
This encouragement was repeated so often in the last epistle reading that I trust we now know what makes someone a Christian.
So we will only touch on the subject briefly.
“So put on.”
2. In the epistle for New Year's Day we explained well enough what “putting on” means. By faith we put on Christ, and he puts on us. In love we put on our neighbor, and our neighbor puts on us.
Christians wear two kinds of clothing: faith and love.
Christ wore two kinds of garments. One was whole, and it pictures faith. The other was divided, and it pictures love.
Here Paul is talking about the second garment, love.
He wants to teach us Christians what kind of jewelry and clothing we should wear in the world. He does not mean silk or precious gold.
Peter (1 Peter 3:3) and Paul (1 Timothy 2:9) forbid women to wear these things.
Love for our neighbor is a garment that suits us well. It is the kind of love that makes us care about our neighbor and his troubles.
This love is called the jewel of a Christian's character. It is a jewel that people can see.
3. Notice how tender and holy the apostle's way of warning is. This is how he usually speaks to us.
He does not drive us with laws. Instead, he wins us over by reminding us of God's grace, which is too great for words. He calls us “chosen by God,” “holy” and “loved.”
He wants to bring out the fruits of faith. He wants them to come from a willing, cheerful and happy spirit.

Suppose someone truly believes and trusts that God sees him as loved, holy and chosen. That person will think about how to live up to these honors and titles, and how to behave in a way that is worthy of them. Even more, he will love God so warmly that he can cheerfully do anything, give up anything, or suffer anything. And he will never feel that he has done enough.
But someone who doubts that God feels this way about him will not see how strong these words are.
He will not feel the power of the truth that God sees us as holy, loved and chosen.

4. So let us pay no attention to the “saints” who choose themselves and love themselves. They decorate themselves with the works of the Law. They keep fasts and strict rules. They care about clothing and rank. They do this because they refuse to be sinners before God.
Our jewels are not like theirs. They have nothing to do with such mockery.
Our jewels are honesty, sincerity, good works and serving our neighbor.
We are free from laws about food, clothing, special days and so on.
We are holy in God's eyes. No one can be holy before God until he sees that he is a sinner and gives up his own righteousness.
But the people I just mentioned are holy only in their own opinion. So they always stay wicked. In God's eyes they are sinners.
God loves us because we look down on ourselves. We judge and condemn ourselves, and we turn away from loving ourselves.
The others love themselves and think highly of themselves. So in God's eyes they are hateful and not acceptable.
Also, God has chosen us because we look down on ourselves as filth.
God chooses people like that. He has chosen them from eternity.
These would-be saints choose themselves, so God will reject them. In fact, he has rejected them from eternity.
This is what Paul means by these words:
“A heart of compassion.”

5. These words describe part of the Christian's jewelry. It is a beautiful, lovely Christian jewel. In God's eyes it looks better on us than pearls, precious stones, silk and gold look on us in the eyes of the world.
“A heart of compassion” is a sign of a true Christian.
Paul means: “Do not be merciful only in what you do on the outside, or only in how things look. Be merciful deep in your heart.”
He means the sincere, whole-hearted mercy of a father and mother who see their child in trouble. They would gladly risk their lives or give up everything they own for that child.
A Christian's mind and heart should always be set on acts of mercy. He should be so eager about this that he does not even notice he is doing good and kind things.
6. With this one phrase, Paul condemns the works and made-up rules of hypocritical saints. They are so harsh that they will not spend time with sinners.
Their strict laws must rule everything.
All they do is force and push.
They show no mercy. They only scold, criticize, condemn, blame and bluster, over and over.
They cannot put up with any imperfection.
But among Christians many are sinners, and many are weak.
In fact, Christians spend time only with people like this, not with “saints.”
Christians reject no one. They put up with everyone.
They truly care about sinners, just as much as they would care about themselves if they were the weak ones.
They pray for sinners. They teach, warn and persuade them. They do everything they can to win them back.
That is what a true Christian is like.
This is how God, in Christ, has treated us, and how he always treats us.
This is how Christ treated the woman caught in adultery (John 8:11). He rescued her from the people who tormented her. His kind words moved her to repent, and he let her go.
We read that St. Antony said Paphrutius knew how souls are saved. Paphrutius had rescued a man from his fellow brothers, who were attacking and bullying him because of his sin.
See the book “Lives of the Fathers.”
If God treated us as strictly as his laws demand, we would all be lost.
But in his mercy he sets the Law aside.
Isaiah says (9:4): “The yoke that weighed him down, the bar across his shoulder, the rod of the one who oppressed him—you have broken them.”
Now God only persuades.
7. Look how tangled up in the Law and in hypocrisy some people still are. They think of themselves as great saints, yet they cannot stand the weaknesses of Christians.

They expect perfect holiness—a miracle of purity—in people who have Christ and know the Gospel. If they do not find it, then nothing is right. To them it seems the sky is about to fall and the earth is about to be destroyed.
All they can do is judge, criticize and make fun. They say: “Oh, yes, he is a real evangelical! Sure, he is a wild dreamer!”
This shows how completely blind they are.
They always have a beam in their own eye, and so they show how little they know about Christ.

So when you meet someone who is quick to criticize and condemn, and who demands that Christians be perfect, know this: that person is only an enforcer of the Law. He is a low hypocrite and a merciless jailer. He does not truly know Christ.
Among Christians there is no law; everything is love. So there can be no judging, condemning or criticizing either.
And whoever calls someone else a wild dreamer is surely ten times more a wild dreamer himself.
He condemns himself for the very thing he judges and condemns in someone else.
He pays no attention to mercy and cares only about the Law. So he finds no mercy with God. In fact, he has never experienced or tasted God's mercy.
To him, both God and his neighbor taste as bitter as gall and wormwood.
8. But this tender mercy is to be shown only to Christians and only among Christians.
