We must treat those who reject and persecute the Gospel differently.
My love should not be so loose that it puts up with false teaching.
When it comes to false faith and false teaching, there is no room for love or patience.
I must fight hard against these things and not give in even a hair's width.
But in other matters, when faith is not in danger, I must always be kind and merciful to everyone, no matter how weak their lives are.
I may not criticize, crush or push them. I must persuade, plead with and put up with them.
A flawed life does not destroy Christianity. It gives it exercise.
But flawed teaching—false belief—destroys everything good.
So when it comes to false teaching, there is no place for putting up with it or showing mercy. Only anger, resistance and death are fitting. But this must always be done according to the Word of God.
9. On the other hand, those who are treated with mercy must not think their beliefs and actions are right just because no one criticizes or forces them.
They must not take this mercy as permission to become lazy and careless and to keep on in their error.
Mercy is not shown to them for that reason.
The goal is to give them a chance to get their eagerness and strength back.
But if they want to stay as they are, fine. Leave them alone.
They will not stay that way for long. The devil will lead them further away, until in the end they fall away completely. They will even become enemies of the Gospel.
That is how they will end up if they let mercy be poured out on them for nothing.
We must not be lazy and sleepy about our false teachings. We must not count on the fact that people do not look down on us or force us.
We especially need to be active and hard-working, because the devil never sleeps or rests.
We need to be careful that he does not lead us to a place where we will never have God's mercy.
“Kindness, humility, gentleness, being slow to anger.”
10. These words name the other parts of Christian character.
You will find kindness explained in the second epistle reading for the early Christmas service.
Kindness shows in the way a person behaves when he is gentle and caring toward everyone. He does not push anyone away with an unfriendly face, harsh words or rude behavior.
We Germans would call such a person pleasant and friendly.
Kindness is not a virtue that shows up only in certain deeds. It shapes a person's whole life.
A kind person is helpful to everyone. He is not annoyed with anyone, and everyone is drawn to him.
The opposite are those odd people who enjoy nothing but their own ideas. They insist that others fit in with them and their ways, but they give way to no one.
People like that are called “rude.”
11. But the generosity of kindness must not reach as far as false teaching.
It is to be used only when it comes to how people live and what they do.
As I have often said before, love with all its works and fruits has no place when it comes to false teaching.
I must love my neighbor and be kind to him, no matter how imperfect his life is.
But if he refuses to believe or teach sound teaching, I cannot love him or be kind to him. I do not dare to.
Paul says (Galatians 1:8-9) that I must treat him as cut off and cursed, even if he were an angel from heaven.
This shows how very different faith and love are, and how separate.
Love will be kind, and must be kind, even to the worst enemy, as long as he does not attack faith and teaching.
But love will not and cannot put up with someone who does attack them, even if it is your father, your mother or your dearest friend.
Deuteronomy 13:6-8. So love must be practiced toward our neighbor's life and works, not toward his teaching and faith.
Faith is the opposite. It is concerned not with his works and life, but with his teaching and belief.
12. By now I think we must know what “humility” of mind means. It means thinking of yourself as the least and of others as greater.
Christ gives a picture of it: taking the lowest seat at the wedding, and doing it cheerfully.
We are to serve even when no one wants our service. We are to serve even our enemies.
That is how Christ humbled himself before Judas, who betrayed him, and before all of us.
He did not come to be served, but to serve.
It is no surprise that humility is rare, because every Christian virtue is rare.
These virtues are especially missing in people who claim to know the most about Christ, yet find something to criticize in every Christian.
Paul calls Christianity a mystery of God, and it will probably stay that way.
13. “Gentleness” is the opposite of anger.
A gentle person is not quick to get angry. He does not curse, hit, hate or wish harm on anyone, not even an enemy.
Holding back like this is an art. Hypocrites—in fact, the whole world—can be gentle toward friends and toward people who treat them well.
But true gentleness and humility will be found only among God's chosen and loved saints, as Paul hints here.
Even among them, many are missing all of the Christian virtues, or at least a large part of them.
So hypocrites can find something to criticize and be offended by in God's loved and chosen saints.
And the true saints get a chance to practice mercy, humility, gentleness and tolerance.
Paul calls them God's chosen and loved saints, even though they are a little lacking in humility, gentleness and tolerance. That does not make them unholy. They are not rejected or looked down on.
14. Paul makes a difference between being slow to anger and tolerance, as in Romans 2:4: “Do you look down on the riches of his goodness and tolerance and slowness to anger?”
The idea of being slow to anger is what God expresses here and there in the Psalms and in other places with the Hebrew words “arich apaim,” meaning “slow to anger.”
God patiently puts up with evil.
In fact, he holds back his punishment again and again. He seems more ready to forgive than to punish, even when he is greatly provoked and has good reason to punish.
Being slow to anger goes further than patience.
Patience puts up with evil and unfairness. But being slow to anger holds back punishment.
It does not plan to punish. It will not take quick revenge.
It is not like people who want revenge. It wishes no one harm.
We see many people who suffer a lot and are patient, but at the same time they are counting on getting even in the end.
But a Christian who is slow to anger is against revenge. He wants the sinner to change his ways.
“Put up with one another, and forgive each other if anyone has a complaint against someone. Forgive just as the Lord forgave you.”
15. With this verse, all law is done away with among Christians.
No one is allowed to go to court to get his property back.
He must forgive and give way.
Christ's example teaches this rule, because he has forgiven us.
And how far does his forgiveness go?

He forgives the sins we have already done, but that is not all. As John says (1 John 2:1-2), “If anyone sins, we have someone to speak for us before the Father: Jesus Christ, the righteous one. He is the sacrifice that turns away God's anger for our sins.”
16. Notice that Paul is describing true Christian saints. Yet he sees them as weak enough to offend one another and complain about one another.
This is not at all the way Christians and saints should behave.
That is why I say Christ's kingdom is a mystery. It is so hidden that our preaching and teaching can never fully explain it.
You cannot get unbelievers to do good works, but you cannot stop believers from doing them.
Some would not believe, and some would not love.
This is true of Christ's kingdom: his Christians are not perfectly holy.
They have started to be holy and are still growing.
Among them you can still find anger, wrong desires, unholy love, worry about worldly things and other sad weaknesses. These are what is left of the old Adam.
Paul calls these things burdens that we must carry for our neighbor (Galatians 6:2). In Romans 15:1 he tells us to “bear the weaknesses of the weak.”
In the same way, Christ loved his apostles very much and suffered much from them. And every day he still puts up with his own people.

17. Some people list the fruits of the Spirit named in Galatians 5:22-23. They say a Christian should be kind, gentle, slow to anger and pure. They see this passage as a law that commands these fruits.
So they refuse to accept anyone as a Christian who does not have these fruits perfectly.
People like this cannot believe that there is a Christ, even though it is certainly true.
They judge with spite and complain that there are no Christians.
They are offended at Christ because he is wiser than they are.
For Christ has given us authority in Scripture to recognize Christians by their fruits.
He says (Matthew 7:16), “By their fruits you will recognize them.”
They put great weight on this.
18. Can you see where such a person goes wrong?
He goes wrong because he understands nothing at all about Christ's kingdom.
He gets the passages about Christians wrong.

He hears that Christians should be kind and gentle, and he thinks it means they must never get angry. They must put up with anything and never be impatient with anyone. If they fail at this, he says, they cannot be Christians, because they do not have the fruits.
Dear man, what could lead him to think that except his own blindness?
He imagines that Christianity is a holy order of perfection with no weakness at all. He thinks it is perfect, like heaven among the angels.
But tell me, where does the Bible talk about Christians like that?

But someone who sees Christianity as something still growing, still at its beginning, will not be offended when a Christian is sometimes harsh, unkind or impatient. He remembers that Christians are commanded to carry one another's burdens and weaknesses.
He knows that the list of the fruits of the Spirit is not a list of laws that must be kept or else Christ is denied.
He knows that the passage means Christians are to try hard to be kind. That is the goal they aim at.
Even though they have made a start and some progress in this virtue, they are often unkind. They produce fruits that are the exact opposite of the fruits of the Spirit.
It is true that the text says we should be kind. But it does not say we are kind.
We are moving toward it. We are growing. But while we grow, much of our old nature, which has not yet been changed, is still mixed in.
19. So know this: in a mysterious way, Christ lives in his saints. Be careful not to judge or condemn anyone unless you know for sure that he believes and teaches against the Gospel.
But if someone does oppose the Gospel, you can safely judge that he is without Christ and under the devil's control.
Pray for such a person and warn him, hoping that he will turn back to God.
But when someone supports and honors the Gospel, pay attention to what Paul says (Romans 14:4): “Who are you to judge someone else's servant? Whether he stands or falls is up to his own master.
And he will stand, because the Lord has the power to make him stand.”
And again (1 Corinthians 10:12): “So if you think you are standing, watch out that you do not fall.”
Christ wants to be hidden and shown at the same time, found and not found.
He allows some weaknesses to be mixed in with the fruits of the Spirit. He does this to hide himself, and so that spiteful judges will be offended.
“And above all these things, put on love. Love is the perfect bond.”
20. The apostle sets love apart from being slow to anger and gentleness, and from the other jewels of spiritual beauty we have already heard about. Yet all of them are included in love.
Faith is the main part of Christian character. In the same way, love is the main fruit of the Spirit, the most beautiful jewel of all.
That is why Paul says, “Above all these things, put on love.”
Love goes beyond mercy, kindness, gentleness and humility.

Paul calls love “the perfect bond” because it joins human hearts together. This is not a partial unity, based on being alike or closely related. It is a complete unity among all people and in every kind of relationship.
It gives us one mind, one heart and one desire.
It does not let anyone start his own special kind of teaching or faith.
Everyone who loves believes the same thing.
So the poor and the rich, rulers and the people they rule, the sick and the healthy, the high and the low, the honored and the disgraced all share the same purpose of heart.
A loving heart lets everyone share in the good it has. Even more, it shares in everyone's troubles and treats them as its own.
Where there is love, there is perfect unity and fellowship in everything that happens, good or bad.
It is the most perfect bond.
21. Where there is no love, hearts are united and share the same goals in only a few things. In most things people disagree.
For example, robbers have a bond with each other. But it is only a shared plan to rob and murder.
Worldly friends agree only when it comes to their own interests.
Monks are united only when it comes to their order and their honor.
Herod and Pilate agreed, but only about Christ.
Most of the time it is unusual for one monk, priest or ordinary church member to agree with another.
The bond that holds them together is weak. They are like chaff tied together with straw.
“And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts. You were called to this peace.”
22. Many things threaten to break the bond of love.
The devil never sleeps. He keeps stirring up fights and unrest.
Paul does not deny that the bond is under attack.
But he urges us to fight back, remembering that love has to be exercised against opposition.
He tells us to let the peace of Christ rule in our hearts.
The meaning of the verse is this: The peace of the world and the flesh does not last. You will have to watch forces that cause fighting and division. Even so, let your hearts have peace in Christ.
We talked about the peace of God in the epistle reading for the Fourth Sunday in Advent, Philippians 4:7.
This is the peace the Gospel calls us to. It is not the peace of the world, the flesh or the devil. It is the peace that goes far beyond all our understanding, as Paul tells us.
We are to hold on to God's peace not only when everything is going well, but also when sin, death, the flesh, the world and every kind of disaster are raging.
“And be thankful.”

23. “Thankfulness” here can be understood in two ways. First, it can mean thankfulness toward God. Then Paul's thought is: Remember all that God has done for you, and let that make you grateful for his grace and mercy. Love and peace will follow from that gratitude.
Second, we can understand it as thankfulness toward people—gratitude for all the good things we receive from others.
In another place (2 Timothy 3:2) the apostle says that in the last days, among other sins, people will be “unthankful” toward one another.
Each person can choose for himself which of the two meanings to take.
In my opinion, Paul means gratitude toward other people here. He talks about thankfulness to God later, and here he is dealing with love for our neighbor. So that is my opinion.
I think this is what he means.
People are glad when others show them love. They are happy to receive good things from others and to be treated according to the Gospel.
But they do not feel like showing love to others. The kindness shown to them is wasted on their ungratefulness.

Ungratefulness does not defeat love, because love bears all things (1 Corinthians 13:7). Still, ungratefulness makes people tired and unwilling. And it is a low, unfair and shameful thing when someone who is always helping others gets no help in return.
24. Paul speaks about this (Galatians 6:6): “The one who is taught the Word should share all good things with the one who teaches him.”
He also says (1 Timothy 5:17) that those who work hard at the Word and at teaching deserve double honor.

In the ninth chapter of First Corinthians he talks at length about how teachers have a right to be supported. He says you should not muzzle the mouth of an ox while it is threshing grain. That would be terrible ungratefulness.
Here he is hinting at that kind of ungratefulness.
It is true today, and it has always been true: preachers of God's Word usually have to find their own bread. They get ungratefulness as their reward for the wonderful blessings they bring.
If their job were to hold masses and offer indulgences, people would be grateful. They would give them great gifts and service to show their thanks.
But the Levites were treated just as ungratefully under the old Law, while the priests of idols and sacred groves were treated with favor.
“Let the Word of Christ live in you richly. Use all wisdom as you teach and warn one another with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. Sing to God with grace in your hearts.”
25. This verse fits well right after the command to be thankful.
Paul means: Be sure to honor your teachers and preachers. Be grateful that they work with the Word and can share it richly with you.
I do not think Paul means God giving his Word from heaven. People do not have the power to give it that way. Only God can give it to us.
He has done that, and he keeps doing it.
Every time he lets the Gospel be preached, he pours the message out on us richly. He holds back nothing we need to know.
But once it is given, we should be thankful. We should faithfully read it and hear it, sing it and speak it, and think about it day and night.
And it is our job to get enough teachers to bring it to us generously and without stopping.
That is what it means to let the Word of God live among us richly.
26. People who are full and lazy soon grow tired of their pastors and send them away to go wherever they want.
Then the pastors have to earn a living by doing other work. So God's Word is neglected. It becomes rare, like seed scattered thinly across the land.

Nehemiah (13:10) complains that the Levites were not supported. So they had to leave their worship and the temple and run off to the fields. Or they had to start false worship and made-up stories to lead the people astray.
Then they got enough to live on. In fact, they became rich.

The same thing has happened in the Christian Church. Every time supporting godly pastors and teachers became a burden, as Augustine sadly says it did, one of two things happened. Either the pastors had to neglect the Word and work to support themselves, or they had to invent the miserable, cursed worship that is now found all over the world. Through it the preachers have become like lords.
Now that the Gospel has come back, this money problem is coming back too, and it will keep coming back.

Today no one can raise one hundred dollars to support a good schoolmaster or preacher. Yet in the past people gave a thousand dollars—no, sums too big to count—for churches, institutions, masses, vigils and such things.

Once again God punishes ungratefulness. Sometimes he lets his preachers leave the ministry completely and work to support themselves. Or he sends the people even greater lies than ever before, which cheat them out of their money and destroy body and soul.
This happens because they refuse to let the Word of God live among them richly.
Paul adds a phrase that explains it further:
“In all wisdom.”

27. Suppose we had the Word of God so richly that it rang out on every street corner and all the children sang it everywhere. That is what those people wanted who brought the church's official prayers, singing and reading into the pulpits and the readings. But what good would all this do without an understanding mind, without wisdom?
For God gave his Word to make us wise.
He meant for us to understand it. He meant for it to be preached and sung in a way people could understand.
And those who serve the Word, who sing it and speak it, should be wise. They should understand everything that has to do with saving souls and honoring God.
That is what it means to have the Word of God live among us in all wisdom.
With these few words Paul knocks down the loud practices of the churches and monasteries. There is so much preaching and reading there, yet the Gospel is not understood.

He seems to have seen ahead to a time when the Word of God would spread freely, but no wisdom would come from it. People would grow more ignorant and fanatical every day, until they became complete fools. They would have so little wisdom that they would call shouting and bragging the worship of God, and think that was preaching the salvation of souls.
28. We have often explained what it means to teach and to warn.
Here Paul makes teaching a duty for all Christians: “teaching and warning one another.”
That means that besides the regular work of preachers, everyone is to teach himself and others. In this way we use the Word of God every day, in public and in private, in general and in particular.

29. This is how I see the difference between the apostle's three words—psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. “Psalms” really means the songs of David and others that make up the Book of Psalms. “Hymns” means the songs of the prophets that are mentioned here and there in the Bible. These include the songs of Moses, Deborah, Solomon, Isaiah, Daniel and Habakkuk, along with the Magnificat, the Benediction and others like them, which are called “Canticles.” “Spiritual songs” are songs that are not written in the Bible but are made by people every day.
Paul calls these last songs “spiritual” even more than psalms and hymns, though he knows that psalms and hymns are spiritual too.
He forbids worldly, sensual and improper songs. He wants us to sing about spiritual things.
Then our songs will help and teach us, as he says.
30. But what does Paul mean by the phrase “with grace”?

My explanation is that he means the grace of God. He means that spiritual songs should be sung freely, without force, from the heart, cheerfully and out of love. They should not be forced out of people by authority and law, the way singing in our churches is today.
No one sings, preaches or prays because he knows he has received mercy and grace.

Instead, people do it because they hope to gain something, or because they fear punishment, harm and shame. Or the holiest people bind themselves to obedience, or are forced into it, in order to win heaven. They do not do it at all to spread the knowledge of God's Word—to understand it richly and in all wisdom, as Paul wants it understood.
I think Paul is thinking of the charm of music and the beauty of poetry that go with singing.
He says in Ephesians 4:29: “Do not let any rotten talk come out of your mouth. Say only what is good for building others up, as the need arises, so that it gives grace to those who hear.”
In the same way, songs should be made to bring grace and blessing to those who hear them.
Dirty, impure and useless words do not belong in them. Neither does anything unfitting—anything without meaning, without goodness or life.
Hymns should be full of meaning, pleasant and sweet, so that everyone who hears them enjoys them.
In Hebrew, singing songs like these is rightly called singing “with grace,” just as Paul says.
The psalms and hymns of the Bible are songs of this kind. They are good thoughts put into pleasing words.
Some songs use lovely words but are worldly and fleshly. Others have good thoughts but put them in words that are unfitting, unattractive and without grace.
“Sing to God with grace in your hearts.”
31. Paul does not tell us to keep our lips silent.

He wants the words of our mouth to come from the heart, sincerely and warmly, not like a hypocrite. Isaiah talks about this (29:13) when he says: “These people come near to me, and they honor me with their mouth and with their lips, but they have put their heart far away from me.”

Paul wants the Word of God to live among all Christians. He wants it spoken, sung and thought about richly everywhere. And he wants this done with understanding, producing spiritual fruit, with everyone treasuring the Word.
He wants people to sing heartfelt praise and thanks to the Lord in this way.
He says let the Word “live” among you.
He does not mean it should just stay as a guest for a night or two. It should stay with you forever.
He is always worried about human teachings.
“Whatever you do, whether you speak or act, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus. Give thanks to God the Father through him.”
32. Christians' works are not limited by name, time or place.
Whatever Christians do is good. Whenever they do it, it is the right time. Wherever they do it, it is the right place.
That is why Paul does not name any particular work.
He makes no difference between works. He says all works are good, whether eating or drinking, speaking or keeping quiet, being awake or sleeping, going or staying, resting or doing something else.
All these acts are highly worthy, because they are done in the name of the Lord Jesus.
That is what Paul teaches here.
Our works are done in the name of the Lord Jesus when by faith we hold on to this truth: Christ is in us, and we are in him. That means we no longer do the work, but he lives and works in us.
Paul says (Galatians 2:20), “I no longer live; it is Christ who lives in me.”
But when we do a work as if it came from ourselves, it is done in our own name, and there is nothing good in it.
33. People often say “in the name of God” or “Go in the name of Jesus” falsely and out of pure hypocrisy.
There is a saying: “All misfortunes rise up in the name of God.”
For false teachers usually sell their goods in the name of God.
They even come in the name of Christ, as he himself said they would.
Matthew 24:24. To speak and work sincerely and seriously in Jesus' name, your heart must agree with what your mouth says.
When your lips say “in the name of God,” your heart must be sure, with firm faith, that God is leading and doing the work.
Peter teaches the same thing (1 Peter 4:11): “If anyone serves [does anything], let him serve with the strength God provides.”
Then the work will go well.
No Christian should try to do anything by his own power and led by his own judgment.
Instead, he should be sure that God is working with him and through him.
Paul says (1 Corinthians 9:26): “So I run, but not without a goal. I fight, but not like someone punching the air.”
34. This attitude leads to praise and thanks to God, because all honor and praise for every good thing belong to him.
That is what Paul teaches, and Peter too.
Right after Peter says that we are to work with the strength God gives, he adds: “so that God may be honored in everything through Jesus Christ.”
But whoever does anything by his own power is lying and deceiving, no matter how much he praises God with his lips. He is like the hypocrite in the Gospel.
So thankfulness is the only service we can give to God. And we cannot give it by ourselves. We give it through Jesus, our go-between.
Without him no one can come to the Father, and no one can be accepted.
We have often talked about this.
Text: 1 Corinthians 13.
1 Suppose I can speak in the languages of people and even of angels. If I do not have love, I have become nothing more than a banging piece of brass or a crashing cymbal.
2 Suppose I have the gift of prophecy and understand every mystery and know everything. Suppose I have so much faith that I could move mountains. If I do not have love, I am nothing.
3 Suppose I give away everything I own to feed the poor, and I even give my body to be burned. If I do not have love, it does me no good at all.

4 Love is very patient, and it is kind. Love does not envy. Love does not show off. It is not puffed up with pride. 5 It does not act in a rude or shameful way. It does not look out only for itself. It is not provoked to anger. It does not keep score of evil. 6 It is not glad about what is wrong, but it is glad along with the truth. 7 It puts up with everything, believes everything, hopes everything, and endures everything.
8 Love never fails. As for prophecies, they will be done away with. As for tongues, they will stop. As for knowledge, it will be done away with.
9 For we know only in part, and we prophesy only in part. 10 But when what is perfect comes, what is only in part will be done away with.
11 When I was a child, I talked like a child, I felt like a child, and I thought like a child. Now that I have grown up, I have put away childish things.
12 For now we see in a mirror, and the picture is dark. But then we will see face to face. Now I know only in part. But then I will know fully, just as I was fully known.
13 So now faith, hope and love remain, these three. And the greatest of these is love.
1. In this chapter Paul wants to quiet proud Christians down and make them humble. He is speaking especially to teachers and preachers.
The Gospel gives us a lot of knowledge about God and about Christ. It also brings many wonderful gifts, as Paul lists in Romans 12 and in 1 Corinthians 12.
He tells us that some people have the gift of speaking, some of teaching, and some of explaining Scripture. Others have the gift of leading, and so on.
Christians have great riches of spiritual knowledge. They have great treasures of spiritual gifts.
Everyone can clearly see what God, Christ, the conscience, this life and the life to come, and other such things really mean.
But you will find very few people who use these gifts and this knowledge in the right way. Very few humble themselves to serve others, the way love tells them to.
Each person looks for his own honor and his own gain. Each one wants to get ahead of others and be placed above them.
2. Today we see how the Gospel has given people more knowledge than the world ever had before. It has also given them new abilities.
All kinds of gifts have been poured out on them and shared among them, and these gifts have brought them honor.
But they carry on without paying attention.
No one stops to think how he could serve other people with Christian love and do them good.
Each one looks for glory and honor, gain and wealth for himself.

If someone could arrange to be the only person who was learned and powerful in the Gospel, with everyone else small and useless, he would gladly do it. He would love it if he alone were seen as Mister Smart.
At the same time he pretends to be very humble and to think very little of himself. And he preaches about love and faith.
But in real life he would hate to lift even his little finger to do what he preaches.
That is why the world is so full of fanatics and people who split churches apart. It is why every man wants to be the boss and rank above everyone else.
People like this are prouder than the ones who taught them.

Here Paul attacks these people who are so eager to be admired. He judges them to be worth nothing at all, no matter how great their knowledge is and how much greater their gifts are, unless they humble themselves and use their gifts to serve others.

He talks to these rough and small-minded people with many words and a long speech. In other places he deals with the same subject in just a few words. For example, he says in Philippians 2:3-4, "In humility of mind, let each one think of the other as better than himself. Do not each look out for your own things, but each of you look out also for the things of others."

To make his point, he pictures himself as guilty of this fault and passes judgment on himself. He does this to warn others all the more strongly, since they fall far short of where he stands. He says,
"If I speak in the languages of people and of angels."

4. That is: Suppose I could teach and preach with more power than any man or angel. Suppose my words were perfectly charming, and my message was full of truth and excellence. Even if I could do this, "but do not have love [charity]," and I only look for my own honor and gain and not my neighbor's, "I have become nothing more than a banging piece of brass or a crashing cymbal."
In other words, "Maybe I could teach others something that way. I could fill their ears with sound. But before God I would be nothing."

A clock or a bell cannot hear its own sound, and it gets nothing out of its own ringing. In the same way, the preacher who has no love cannot himself understand anything he says. And he does not improve his standing before God by it.
Yes, he knows a lot. But because he does not use his knowledge to serve love, something is wrong with the kind of knowledge he has.
1 Corinthians 8:1-12.

It would be far better for him to be unable to speak, or to have no gift for words, as long as he teaches with love and gentleness. That is better than speaking like an angel while looking out only for himself.
"And if I have the gift of prophecy."
5. According to chapter 14, to prophesy means being able to understand and explain the prophets and the Scriptures correctly, because the Holy Spirit gives that ability.
This is a truly excellent gift.

To "know mysteries" means being able to grasp the spiritual meaning of the Scriptures, or the deeper pictures hidden in them. Paul does this in Galatians 4:24-31. There he makes Sarah and Hagar stand for the two covenants, and Isaac and Ishmael stand for the two peoples—the Jews and the Christians.

Christ does the same thing in John 3:14. There he makes the bronze snake of Moses a picture of himself on the cross. It is the same when Isaac, David, Solomon and other people in Bible history are shown to be pictures of Christ.
Paul calls this a "mystery." It is the hidden, secret meaning that lies under the plain sense of the story.
But "knowledge" means understanding practical matters, such as Christian freedom, or knowing that the conscience is not tied down.

So Paul means this: "Someone may understand the Scriptures, both their plain meaning and their hidden meaning. He may know all about Christian freedom and about living the right way. But if he does not have love, and if he does not use that knowledge to serve his neighbor, it is all completely useless. In God's eyes he is nothing."
6. Notice how strongly, and yet how kindly, Paul holds back the shameful sin of empty pride.
He sets aside even those high gifts, those gifts that are so refined, charming and excellent. Such gifts easily make people proud and arrogant, while they win the admiration and respect of others.
Wherever there is such wisdom and such understanding of the Scriptures, who would not think that the Holy Spirit must be living there for all to see?
Paul's two letters to the Corinthians are aimed almost entirely at this one sin, because it causes a lot of trouble wherever it rules.
In Titus 1:7 the first quality he names for a bishop is that he be "non superbus," which means not proud.
In other words, a bishop must not lift himself up because of his office, his honor and his understanding, and look down on others by comparison.
But then Paul says something strange,
"If I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing."

blocks.x: Love Is the Fruit of the Spirit We Receive by Faith.

s: 7. We believe, and it is certainly true, that it is faith that makes us right with God and makes us clean.
But if faith makes us right with God and pure, then love must be there too.
The Spirit cannot help giving love along with faith.
In fact, where there is true faith, the Holy Spirit lives. And where the Holy Spirit is, there must be love and every good quality.
So why does Paul talk as if faith without love were possible?
Our answer is this: This one verse cannot be taken to overturn and fight against all the other verses that say we are made right with God by faith alone.
Even the hair-splitting scholars have not said that love makes us right with God. That is not possible, because love is a result, or fruit, of the Spirit, and we receive the Spirit through faith.
8. There are three ways to answer this question.
First, Paul is not talking here about Christian faith, which always comes with love. He is talking about a general faith in God and his power.
That kind of faith is a gift, just like the gift of tongues, the gift of knowledge, the gift of prophecy, and so on.
There is reason to think that Judas did miracles even though he did not have Christian faith. John 6:70 says, "One of you is a devil."

This general faith has no power to make a person right with God or to make him clean. It lets the old sinful self stay, with all its sins, just as the gifts of a good mind, good health, good speaking or riches do.

9. A second answer is this: Paul is talking about true Christian faith. But he has in mind people who really did come to faith and did miracles with it, but who fall from grace through pride and so lose their faith.
Many start but do not keep going.
They are like the seed that fell on rocky ground.
They quickly fall away from faith.
The temptation to be admired is stronger than the temptation that comes with hard times.
Someone who has true faith and can also do miracles may chase after honor and grab it so eagerly that he falls away from both love and faith.
10. A third answer is this: To show how necessary love is, Paul imagines something that is impossible.
For example, I could say it like this: "Even if you were a god, if you had no patience you would be nothing."
That means patience belongs so completely to being divine that there could be no divinity at all without it. And that statement is simply true.

So Paul does not mean that faith could exist without love. He means the opposite. Love is so much a part of faith that even faith that moves mountains would be nothing without love—if we could pull the two apart even in our minds.
I like the third answer by far the best. But I do not reject the other two, especially the first.
For Paul's very first statement is already impossible: "if I speak in the languages of angels."
A human being cannot speak in the language of angels. Paul clearly points out that this is impossible by making a difference between the languages of people and those of angels.
There is no angel language. Angels may speak to us in a human language, but people can never speak in the language of angels.

11. We understand the first part—"If I speak in the languages of angels"—to mean: "Suppose it were possible for me to speak in the languages of angels, though it is impossible." In the same way we should understand the second part—"If I have all faith, so that I could move mountains"—to mean: "Suppose it were possible to have such faith, though it is impossible."
Understanding all mysteries is just as impossible. We must take it to mean: "Suppose someone could understand all mysteries—which, however, no one can."
In the last chapter of his Gospel, John says that the world could not hold all the books that could be written about the things of the kingdom.
For no one can ever get to the bottom of these mysteries.

Paul is simply speaking in a very common way. It is like saying, "Even if I were a Christian, if I did not believe in Christ I would be nothing." Or, "Even if you were a prince, if you did not rule over people or own any property, you would be nothing."
"And if I give away everything I own to feed the poor."

12. In other words, "Suppose I did all the good works in the world, but I did not have love. Suppose I was only looking for my own honor and gain in them, and not my neighbor's good. Then I would still be lost."
When Paul speaks of outward works as great as giving up your property and your life, he includes every work a person could possibly do. Anyone who would do these would do any work at all.
In the same way, when he mentions tongues, he includes all good words and teachings. And when he mentions prophecy, understanding and faith, he includes all wisdom and knowledge.
Some people may risk their body and their property to win glory in this world.
The Romans and other pagans did that. But because they had no love and were only looking out for themselves, in the end they really gave nothing.
In general, people cannot give away all their property and have their bodies burned. So the meaning must be: "Suppose I could give all my goods to the poor, and my body to be burned."

13. The hair-splitting scholars reason falsely, and their reasoning will not hold up. With bad intent, they take this verse and draw from it the idea that Christian faith is not able to wipe out sin and make us right with God.
They say that before faith can make us right with God, it must be decorated with love. But they do not understand what it means to be made right with God, or what goes with it.
Being made right with God must come before love.
No one loves until he has become godly and righteous.
Love does not make us godly. But when someone has become godly, love is the result.
Faith, the Spirit, and being made right with God produce love as their result and fruit. Love is not just a decoration or an extra added on.
We hold firmly that faith alone makes us right with God and saves us.
But God does not want us to fool ourselves and trust in a false faith. So he asks us for love as the proof of our faith. That way we can be sure that our faith is real faith.

blocks.x: What Christian Love Is Like.

s: "Love is very patient, and it is kind."
14. Now Paul begins to describe what love is like. This helps us see where real love and faith are found.
A proud teacher does not have the good qualities that the apostle lists.
Since proud people lack these, they have no love, no matter how many gifts they have received through the Gospel.
First, love "is very patient."
That is, it waits patiently. It is not quick to flare up in anger. It does not rush to take revenge, lose its patience, or fly into a blind rage.
Instead, it patiently puts up with bad people and weak people until they give in.
Proud teachers can only judge, condemn and look down on others, while they defend themselves and lift themselves up.
15. Second, love is "kind."
In other words, it is pleasant to be around. It does not have a stern, frightening look. It does not ignore anyone. It is kind to everyone, in its words, its actions and its attitude.
16. Third, love "does not envy." It is not jealous or upset when other people do better than it does. It does not resent anyone's property or honor.
Proud teachers, however, are jealous and unkind.
They resent it when anyone else has honor or possessions.
They may say something different with their mouths, but you can clearly see these traits in what they do.
17. Fourth, love "does not show off."
It hates dishonest tricks, sly schemes and two-faced behavior.
Proud and deceitful people cannot stop acting this way. But love deals honestly and fairly, face to face.
18. Fifth, love is not "puffed up," like false teachers, who puff themselves up like poisonous snakes.

19. Sixth, love "does not act in a rude or shameful way." It does not behave like people who are hot-tempered, impatient and stubborn. Such people think they are always right. They oppose everyone and give in to no one. They demand that every single person give in to them. If not, they set the world on fire. They rage and fume, scream and complain, and long for revenge.
That is where the swelling pride and arrogance we just talked about lead.
20. Seventh, love "does not look out only for herself."
She does not chase after more money. She does not chase after honor, profit or comfort, or even try to protect her body and life.
Instead she risks all these things in her ... is no such thing as the Church of Christ or as true Christians.
Many misguided spirits, especially those who loudly pretend to ...
21. Eighth, love "is not [easily] provoked to anger" by wrongs and ungratefulness. It is gentle.
False teachers cannot put up with anything. They look out only for their own gain and honor, and they hurt others to get it.
22. Ninth, love "does not keep score of [does not think] evil."
It is not suspicious. It takes everything in the best possible way and accepts everything in good faith.

Proud people, on the other hand, are suspicious beyond measure. They are always worried that someone will think too little of them. So they take everything in the worst possible way, just as Joab twisted the meaning of what Abner did.
2 Samuel 3:25.
This is a shameful sin, and people who have it are hard to deal with.
23. Tenth, love "is not glad about what is wrong [wicked]."
These words can be understood in two ways. First, they could mean a person enjoying his own evil deeds.
Solomon, in Proverbs 2:14, speaks of people who "enjoy doing evil."

Such people must either be very wild and shameless, like prostitutes and crooks. Or else they must be hypocrites who do not see how wicked their behavior is—people like heretics and those who split the church, who are glad when their dirty tricks succeed in the name of God and of the truth.
I do not accept this explanation. I take the other one.

Paul means that false teachers are so spiteful that they love nothing better than hearing that someone else has done wrong, made a mistake and been put to shame. Their only reason is that they want to look good and godly themselves.
That was how the Pharisee treated the tax collector in the Gospel.
But love's compassion goes far beyond its own sins, and it prays for others.
24. Eleventh, love "is glad along with [in] the truth."
This shows that the phrase before it is about being spitefully glad when someone else sins and falls.
Being glad in the truth simply means being delighted when someone else does right and lives with integrity.
In the same way, love is sad when someone else does wrong.
But for proud people, it is painful to hear that someone else is doing right. They imagine that someone else's goodness takes away from their own gain and honor.
25. Twelfth, love "puts up with everything."
It excuses every fault in everyone, no matter how weak, unfair or foolish someone may seem. No one can do a wrong so big that love cannot overlook it.

But in the eyes of proud people, no one can ever do anything right. They always find something to put down and criticize as too much to put up with, even if they have to go digging around an old fence to find something to be hurt by.
26. Thirteenth, love "believes everything."
Here Paul is not talking about faith in God, but about trust in people.
He means that love is very trusting.
A person who has love believes and trusts everyone. He thinks they are fair and honest, just as he is.

He does not expect sly or crooked behavior. Instead he lets himself be fooled, tricked, mocked and taken advantage of by anyone who wants to. And he asks, "Do you really think people are that wicked?"
He judges all other hearts by his own heart, and he makes mistakes with the greatest cheerfulness.
But making such mistakes does him no harm.
He knows that God cannot abandon him, and that whoever deceives love is only deceiving himself.
Proud people, on the other hand, trust no one, will not believe anyone, and cannot stand being fooled.
27. Fourteenth, love "hopes everything."
Love does not give up on anyone, no matter how wicked he is.
It hopes for the best.
As this verse suggests, love says, "We really must hope for better things."
From this it is clear that Paul is not talking about hope in God.
Love is a virtue that is especially about caring for your neighbor. In its thoughts and actions, its goal is his well-being.
Just like its faith, the hope that love has is often let down. But it never gives up.
Love turns no one away. It does not give up on any cause.
But proud people quickly give up on people in general and throw them away as worthless.
28. Fifteenth, love "endures everything."

It endures whatever harm comes its way and whatever hurt it suffers. It endures when its faith and hope in people have been let down. It endures when it suffers damage to its body, its property or its honor.
It knows that no harm has been done, because it has a rich God.
False teachers, however, put up with nothing—least of all with betrayal and broken promises.
29. Sixteenth, love never fails. That means it lasts forever, even in the life to come.

It never gives up. It never lets itself be stopped or beaten by people's wickedness or ungratefulness. Worldly people and false saints act differently. As soon as they notice they are being looked down on or treated ungratefully, they pull back and refuse to do good to anyone ever again. They make themselves completely heartless and become total people-haters, like Timon, who had that reputation among the Greeks.
Love does not act like that.
It does not let the wickedness of people make it wicked, and it does not let anything stop it from doing good.
It keeps doing good everywhere—teaching and warning, helping and serving—even though its kind deeds and services are paid back not with good, but with evil.
Love stays steady and cannot be moved. It keeps going and endures, in this life on earth and also in the life to come.
The apostle adds, "As for prophecies, they will be done away with. As for tongues, they will stop. As for knowledge, it will be done away with."
He praises love above all other gifts, because it is a gift that can never pass away, even in the life to come.
Those other gifts, which the false apostles brag about, are given only for this present life, to help in carrying out the work of the ministry.
Prophecy, tongues, knowledge—they all must end. For in the next life each person will see perfectly for himself, and no one will need to teach anyone else.
In the same way, all differences and all inequalities will be gone.
No knowledge and no variety of gifts is needed. God himself will be everything in every soul.
1 Corinthians 15:28.
30. Here Paul points out the difference between the life of faith here on earth and the life in heaven, where we will see God.
He wants to teach that we have the same things in this life and in the next. It is the same God and the same treasures—here we have them by faith, and there we will have them by sight.
The things themselves are no different. The difference is in how we know them.
We have the same God in both lives, but we have him in different ways.
In this life, the way we have God is by faith.
Faith is an incomplete, unclear way of seeing. That is why we need the Word. And the Word, in turn, spreads through the ministry, tongues and prophecy.
Without the Word, faith cannot live.
But in the life to come, the way we have God is not by faith but by sight.
That is perfect knowledge. Then we will not need the Word anymore, or preaching, tongues and prophecy either.
So these things must pass away. Paul goes on,
"We know only in part, and we prophesy only in part."
31. "We know only in part." That means that in this life our knowledge is incomplete, because it comes by faith and not by sight.
And we "prophesy only in part." That means incompletely, because what our prophecy is made of is the Word and preaching.
Still, both knowledge and prophecy show us nothing less than what the angels see—the one God.
"But when what is perfect comes, what is only in part will be done away with."
He proves this with a picture, comparing a child with a grown man.
Children are still weak, so they need to play. For them, play takes the place of a job and work.
In the same way, in this present life we are far too weak to look at God.
Until we are able to, we need to use the Word and faith, which fit our limits.
"For now we see in a mirror [through a glass], and the picture is dark. But then we will see face to face."
32. Paul tells us that faith is like a mirror, like a riddle.
The real face is not in the glass. There is only a picture of it.
In the same way, faith does not give us the shining face of the eternal God. It gives us only a picture of him, a picture that comes to us through the Word.
A dark riddle points to something more than it says. In the same way, faith hints at something clearer than what it can see.
But in the life to come, the mirror and the riddle, faith and its proof, will all be gone.
God's face and our own face will be clearly shown to each other.
Paul says, "Now I know only in part. But then I will know fully, just as I was fully known [know just as I am known]."
That means God knows me perfectly right now, clearly and plainly. There is no dark veil over me.
But when it comes to him, a dark veil hides him from me.
Then I will know him just as perfectly and clearly as he knows me now—without a veil.
The veil will be taken away, not from him, but from me. For there is no veil on him.

blocks.x: Love Is the Greatest Christian Virtue.

s: "So now faith, hope and love remain, these three. And the greatest of these is love."
33. The hair-splitting scholars have gone wrong about this verse in a truly masterful way.
They have made faith far less important than love, because Paul says that love is greater than faith and greater than hope.
As usual, their crazy reasoning blindly grabs hold of the bare words.
They chop out one piece and ignore the rest.
So they miss what Paul means. They do not see that Paul's idea about the greatness of love is shown both in the verse itself and in the verses around it.

Surely no one can argue with this: here the apostle is talking about which gifts last forever and which last only for a time—love on one side and the other gifts on the other. He is not talking about their rank or power.
When it comes to rank, not only faith but also the Word is above love. For the Word is God's power that brings salvation to everyone who believes.
Romans 1:16. Yet the Word must pass away.
But love, even though it is the fruit and result of the Word, will never be done away with.
Faith has God himself.
It has everything and can do everything. Still, it must come to an end.
Love gives to the neighbor and blesses him, as a result of faith. And love will never be done away with.
34. So when Paul says that love is greater than faith and hope, he means that love lasts—that it goes on forever.
Faith lasts only for a limited time compared with love. Because it lasts only for a while, it ranks below love.
In the same way, I could say that the kingdom of Christ on earth is greater than Christ was.

By that I do not mean that the Church in itself is better or higher in rank than Christ. I only mean that it covers more of the earth than he did. He was here only three years, and he spent them in a small area. But his kingdom has existed from the beginning and stretches across the whole earth.
In this sense, love is longer and wider than faith or hope.
Faith deals with God only in the heart and only in this life. But love's relationship both to God and to the whole world lasts forever.

Still, Christ is far better, higher and more precious than the Christian Church, even though we see him moving within smaller limits, as just one person. In the same way, faith is better, higher and more precious than love, even though it lasts only for a limited time and has only God as its object.
35. Paul praises love like this to strike a blow against false teachers. He wants to bring their bragging to nothing when they boast about faith and other gifts but have no love.
This is what he means: "If you do not have love, which lasts forever, then everything else you brag about will perish, and you will perish with it.

The Word of God and the spiritual gifts are eternal. But the outward office of preaching the Word, and the use of all the different gifts, will come to an end. And then your glory and pride will turn to ashes."
So then, faith makes us right with God through the Word, and faith produces love.

But while both the Word and faith will pass away, the righteousness and love they produce last forever. It is like a building put up with the help of scaffolding. The building still stands after the scaffolding has been taken down.
36. Look how short the word "love" is, and how easy it is to say!
Who would have thought that Paul would give this one good quality so much precious virtue and power, as the opposite of so much that is evil?
This, I think, is what it means to make love great, to paint a picture of love.
It is a better teaching about virtue and vice than anything the pagan writers wrote.
The picture the apostle gives should rightly put the false teachers to shame. They talk a lot about love, but not one of the good qualities he mentions can be found in them.
Every quality of love that he names is a punch and an attack on false teachers.
Whenever he praises love and describes her powers, he always takes a jab at the same time at those who lack any of them.
So as he describes each feature, we can well add, "But you do the very opposite."

37. It is very strange that teachers who have no love should have such gifts as Paul mentions here—speaking in tongues, prophesying, understanding mysteries. It is strange that they should have faith, give away their goods and let themselves be burned.

For we have seen what horrible things follow where there is no love. People like that are proud, jealous, puffed up, impatient, unsteady, false, poisonous, suspicious, spiteful, scornful, bitter, unwilling to serve, distrustful, selfish, power-hungry and arrogant.
How can anyone honestly claim that people like this can move mountains by faith, give their bodies to be burned, prophesy, and so on?
It is exactly as I have said.
Paul sets up an impossible idea. He is saying that because they have no love, they do not really have those gifts. They only take the name and put on the look of having them.
And to strip those gifts away from them, he admits for the sake of argument that they are what they really are not.
Text: 1 John 3:13-18.
13 Brothers, do not be amazed if the world hates you.
14 We know that we have moved out of death and into life, because we love our brothers.
Anyone who does not love is still living in death.
15 Anyone who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life living in him.
16 We know love by this: he gave his life for us. And we ought to give our lives for our brothers.
17 But suppose someone has plenty of this world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet shuts his heart and shows him no pity. How can God’s love be living in that person?
18 My little children, let us not love with words or with our tongues. Let us love with actions and in truth.
1. The Epistle and Gospel readings chosen for the Sundays of the Pentecost season all have love as their main theme.

They talk about the love we owe to Christ and God. That love is simply being thankful for the amazing gift of forgiveness of sins and salvation through Christ’s blood and death. But they also talk about the love we owe our neighbor. This is not a love that only pays back favors. It is a love that keeps on giving, forgiving, and doing every kind of good, even when nothing comes back.
2. Here John urges Christians to practice love.
Love is clearly rare among people, so this warning is needed.
He especially warns Christians not to be surprised when the world hates them and wants them dead.
That is how Cain hated his brother, as the apostle has just told us.
We have to admit that the world’s hatred pushes love away. It makes loving very hard.
3. Isn’t it very strange that someone could hate people who love him and have only been kind to him?
We say that kind of wickedness is almost impossible to imagine.
Why would anyone want to serve the world, when the world is so ungrateful that it pays back love with hatred?
But let us look at ourselves. We have been baptized and have received the Gospel. Let us admit how we repay God’s great love in giving us his Son.
What a beautiful example of happy thankfulness we show!
We should be so ashamed that we despise ourselves before God and his angels.

And what about those who cannot stand to hear the glorious message of God’s grace and blessing preached, and who call it heresy? The people who try to serve the world, help it, and save it by telling the good news are treated by them, as Paul says, “like the filth of the world, the scum of everything” (1 Corinthians 4:13).
In fact, no criminal is treated and put to death more cruelly and shamefully. The Pope and his followers are a clear example of this.

blocks.x: The World’s Hatred.

s: 4. Experience has proven this fact, even though it is hard to believe. Still, John gives his warning: “Brothers, do not be amazed if the world hates you.”
If we should not be amazed at this, is there anything in the world that should amaze us?
I would really think that hearing just one sermon about Christ’s grace would be enough. It should make the world welcome the Gospel with great joy and never forget God’s mercy and blessing.

It would be no surprise if the earth suddenly opened up and swallowed the human race because it is so ungrateful to God. God gave his Son to become a man so that he could rescue us, who were condemned to die, from sin and death, and bring us back to life and salvation.
Isn’t it horrible that anyone would avoid and fight against such a Savior and his teaching even more than he fights the devil himself?
5. But how does God feel about this kind of behavior?
He rightly says to the Jews through the prophet: “My people, what have I done to you? How have I worn you out? Testify against me!
I brought you up out of the land of Egypt. I set you free from the house of slavery. I sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam ahead of you.

My people, remember now what Balak, king of Moab, planned against you, and what Balaam, son of Beor, told him. Remember what happened between Shittim and Gilgal, so that you may know the right things Jehovah has done.”

Micah 6:3-5. And Christ rightly says to his ungrateful people: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you kill the prophets and throw stones at those who are sent to you! Again and again I longed to bring your children together, the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wings. But you refused!”
Matthew 23:37. It is as if he were saying, “I certainly did not come to bring you death and condemnation with my message.
I am about to suffer death and God’s anger for your sins.
I bring you God’s endless grace and blessing, for this life and forever.
So why do you hate me and my message so bitterly?”
6. John argues like this: “The world hates even God for being kind. So, my dear friends, do not be amazed that the same thing happens to you.
What does it matter that I show my love by risking my life and my body to defend this teaching of the Gospel and to help my neighbor?
My love is poor, small, rough, and unpleasant compared with the love that led Christ to die for me and to rescue me from eternal death.
God’s highest love is deeper than we can understand. If even that love does not make the world grateful, why be surprised if the world hates you for all your kindness?
Why pound your fist and stamp your foot in anger at such ungratefulness?
You yourselves belong to the same human race that the Son of God had to die for.
And even if you died for the Gospel, your sacrifice would be nothing compared to what God did. For the world’s sake, God did not hold back his own Son. He let the world put him to death.”
7. But where does the world’s hatred come from?
John tells us in verse twelve, where he talks about Cain. He says Cain “was of the evil one and killed his brother.
And why did he kill him?
Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s were right.”
What a fine reason for hating someone! The one who hates and murders is evil, and the one who does good is good!
In government and in the home, it is the people who do wrong and disobey who get into trouble and are punished. And that is fair.
But whenever God deals with the world, the world shows what rotten fruit it is. It hates, persecutes, and kills the very people who do it good, as if they were criminals and frauds.
John tells us the world inherits this habit from its ancestor Cain, that great “saint” who murdered his brother.
Cain is a true picture of the world in every age. The world’s spirit and ways always copy him.

8. Mother Eve was a dear, godly woman. God had promised a future seed, a descendant who would crush the serpent’s head. When she gave birth to her first son, she was full of joy and hope in that promise, and she said: “I have gotten a man with the help of Jehovah” (Genesis 4:1). She named him Cain, which means “gotten.” It was as if she were saying, “I have gotten the true treasure.”
She had never before seen a human baby born. This was the first precious fruit of the human race.
She rejoiced over Cain and called herself blessed.
This son was raised with the hope that he would be a savior for the people who would come later. He would be a comfort to his brothers and sisters and all their children.
And he knew about these proud hopes.

He proudly bossed his brother around. His brother, by contrast, had to carry the shameful name Abel, which means “nothing” or “emptiness.” It was as if the parents were saying in their hearts: “Oh no! This one has no future.
Cain is the true heir of the blessing God promised to mankind. He is lord and master over his brothers.”
9. The godly father and mother probably took comfort for many years in the hope they had in their first-born son. They longed with all their hearts to be rescued from their terrible fall.

No doubt they raised both sons very carefully. They taught them about their own sin and fall and about the promise God had given them. They did this until the sons were grown up and had begun to serve as priests.

Cain, the first-born, was especially eager in this. He wanted to be first, so he offered the first fruits of the ground. God had given them, and he had worked hard to grow them. He had no doubt seen his father make offerings like this.
But Abel, the lesser son, the poor shepherd, offered the firstborn lambs of his sheep. God had given these to him too, and they came without hard work and effort of his own.
Then God showed in an amazing way which gift on the altar he preferred.
Fire came down from heaven and burned up Abel’s offering, but Cain’s was left.
The fire was the sign that God was pleased.
The text says: “And Jehovah was pleased with Abel and his offering, but he was not pleased with Cain and his offering.”
Genesis 4:4-5.
10. Then Adam and Eve saw that the hope and comfort they had placed in their first-born son were only a false hope.
They began to learn about God’s amazing judgments. God put Abel first—Abel, the boy Cinderella. That is all he was in his own eyes when he compared himself with his brother.
Now Cain was completely sure of his position. His parents had spoiled him with the false idea that, as the first-born, he was God’s favorite. So he felt deeply insulted.
His hypocrisy had been hidden until now, but now it comes out.
He burns with secret hatred against God. He also burns with hatred and anger against his brother, and he does not even try to hide it.
His parents scold him, but it does no good.
His anger burns hotter and hotter. When he meets his brother alone in the field, he strikes him down.
He does not think about changing his ways or asking God for grace. Instead, he shows no mercy to the only brother he has on earth, who has never done him any harm at all.
He cannot forgive his brother. He cannot let him have God’s grace without being jealous.
11. That was the comfort and joy poor Adam and Eve lived to see in their first children!

From then on their life on earth was full of gloom and sorrow. This was especially hard because they could not help seeing that it all came from their own fall. They would have wasted away and died if God had not comforted them with another son.

It had become clear that their hope in Cain was false. They had also lost the son who, without a doubt, had God’s grace. Without another son, they would not have known where to look for the comfort of the promised seed.

blocks.x: Cain Pictures the World, Abel the Church.

s: 12. Notice that this man Cain shows the world in its true colors. In him we see the world’s real spirit.
There has certainly never been anyone like him.
Without question, he is a picture of the very best, the very heart of holiness on earth—the most pious servants of God.
On the other hand, Abel, that poor, miserable, lowly boy Cinderella, is a good picture of the small, unknown brotherhood, the Church of Christ.
The Church has to let Lord Cain have the honor of being everything before God. He gets to receive every gift of God and to claim all honor and every privilege.
He feels important because of his imagined greatness. He lets this attitude fill his sacrifices and his worship. He thinks God simply must favor and accept his offering instead of his brother’s.
Meanwhile, godly Abel goes on his way. He gently puts up with his brother’s contempt.
He gladly lets Cain have the honor. He thinks of himself as far below Cain. He sees no comfort for himself except the pure mercy and goodness of God.
He believes in God and hopes for the promised seed who is to come.
With this faith he offers his sacrifice as a confession, a sign that he is thankful.
13. God meant this story as a comfort for his little group. The story was not written for Abel’s sake. It was written for the sake of God’s humble children, whose situation is like Abel’s.
God has not forgotten them, even though proud Cain looks down on them and ignores them and thinks they are nothing compared to him.
God looks on them with kindness. He rejects proud Cain, along with his birthright and his offering.

14. Innocent Abel becomes the target of anger and hatred when the Word of God gets hold of Cain. God’s Word shows that God is displeased with Cain, even though Cain imagined he was worthy. It shows that God will not treat Cain’s offering and devotion as better or more deserving than his brother’s.
Cain begins to hate his brother bitterly and to persecute him.
He cannot rest until Abel is struck down and wiped off the earth.
So now you know why the world hates Christians and is angry with them. It is simply this, as John says of Cain: “Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s were right.”
15. What had godly Abel done wrong to his brother to be hated like this?
He had even treated his brother as the first-born, as far greater than himself. He had given him every honor and loved him the way a brother should.
He was easy to please. All he wanted was God’s grace.
He prayed for the promised seed. That means he prayed for the salvation and happiness of his parents, his brother, and the whole human race.
How could Cain be so cruel and inhuman in his rage that he murdered his own flesh and blood?
The answer is that the devil had filled Cain’s heart with pride and vanity about his birthright.
He thought he was an important man, with every right to God’s favor, and without sin. His brother, he thought, was nothing at all.
Cain’s heart has no true brotherly love in it. He only looks down on Abel.
He cannot stand seeing that God clearly favors his brother. And he will not listen to the command to humble himself and seek God’s grace.
Anger and jealousy take over so completely that he cannot stand to let his brother live.
He goes against God’s commandment and his own conscience and becomes a murderer. Then he goes on his way as if he had done nothing wrong.
16. This is what John means. He says Cain had no other reason for his crime than this: his own works were evil, and his brother’s were right.
In the same way, the world—that obedient daughter of “Saint” Cain—hates Christians. And it hates them for no other reason than their love and goodness of heart.
Look at the examples of the holy patriarchs, the prophets, and most of all Christ himself.
17. What sin did the dear apostles commit against the world?
They did not want to hurt anyone. They lived in deep poverty and worked hard, going around teaching people how to be saved from the devil’s kingdom and from eternal death through faith in Christ.
The world will not listen to this or put up with it. So the shouting starts: “Kill them! Kill these people!
Get them off the face of the earth!
Show them no mercy!”
Why all this hostility? Because the apostles tried to free the world from its idol worship and its damnable ways.
The world could not stand good works like these.
All it wants is praise and approval for its own evil deeds. It expects God to give an approval he could never give: “Your deeds are good, and they please me.
You are my faithful children.
Just keep on happily killing everyone who believes and preaches my Word.”
18. The world acts the same way today toward our Gospel.

We are hated and persecuted for no other reason than this: by God’s grace we have preached his Word. That Word rescued us from the blindness and idol worship we were sunk in, just as deeply as the world. And we want to rescue others too.
That is the unforgivable sin that has earned us the world’s endless anger and a hatred that can never be put out.
The world cannot let us live.
We preach no other teaching than faith in Christ. Our children pray this faith, and they themselves confess it with their words.
The only difference is what we claim: Christ was crucified for us and shed his blood to rescue us from sin and death. So our salvation does not come from our own works, holiness, or devotion.

We do not treat their faithless worship as equal to Christ himself. Instead, we teach people to trust in God’s grace, not in their own worthiness, and to thank him for his grace. The world cannot stand this.

It would be good for our opponents if they accepted this teaching. It would make them even more what they claim to be: better than us in wisdom, knowledge, and reputation. We are happy to let them have that claim.
But Cain’s works are evil, and Abel’s are right.
The world simply cannot stand the Gospel, and we should never hope for unity or peace with it.
The world will not give up its idol worship or accept the faith.
It would force us either to give up the Word of God and praise its Cain-like worship, or to be put to death by them.
19. That is why John says, “Brothers, do not be amazed if the world hates you.” The world has to act according to the nature it inherited from its father Cain.
It wants to have all the credit and give Abel none.
The world is made up of the high and mighty, the wise, the educated, and the powerful.
The Scriptures show that these people cannot help hating and persecuting the poor little group that is the Church of Christ, because of the good works the Church does.
They absolutely cannot stand being taught by this despised and humble group. They hate the teaching that salvation comes through God’s grace and mercy alone, not through people’s own merits.
They cannot bear the teaching that their offering is worth nothing before God. That offering is the Mass, which the Papists regard as a work of the highest merit and holiness.
20. The text paints a picture of the world’s nature so that we can recognize it.
It is important and valuable for a Christian to understand the world well enough to know what to expect from it.
When he is prepared like this, he will not be shocked or lose patience when he suffers. He will not let the world’s meanness and ungratefulness lead him into hatred and a wish for revenge.
He will hold on to his faith and love. If the world refuses to listen to his message, he will let it go its own way.
A Christian should expect nothing better from the world than bitter persecution in return for his good works and love.
He should remember that the Church of Christ on earth will never have an easier life.
He must not judge by what things look like on the outside, thinking: “They are the huge crowd, the wisest and smartest people on earth. How could they all be wrong and condemned?”
21. It is true that order and peace cannot exist without the most excellent, high-ranking, learned, and clever people—kings, princes, and nobles who are great in achievement and honor.
Cain is never plain and humble.
He is always very clever, wise, and holy, and far better than Abel in every way.
In fact, he has to be everything people could want, just as his name says.

And his children show the same trait. They are skilled at inventing every kind of art. How sad it is that a man with Cain’s gifts, born to godly parents and greatly honored by God, would show such hatred and cruelty toward poor Abel just because of God’s Word and Abel’s faith.

22. Knowing this is a comfort to the small, godly group of Christians. They are sure they have God’s favor, and they know that this is why they are persecuted. They have no protection or help. They face the same fate as Abel.
If things go better for them, they can thank God for it.
But they must always keep on loving God, whose love they have received and felt. And they must keep on loving people too, including their enemies.
This was Abel’s way. If he could have lived again, he would have kept loving his murderer as a brother. He would have forgiven him and even begged God to forgive him.
“We know that we have moved out of death and into life, because we love our brothers.”

blocks.x: Love Moves Christians.

s: 23. Staying in love should be what moves us Christians.
John compares this with what moves the world to hate us: its wickedness.
John’s words show that the world’s hatred of you is not strange.
You and the world are extremely different.

The world has done evil works. It does not believe. It is proud. It despises God’s Word and grace, and it persecutes godly people. Because of all this, by now the world has fallen prey to Satan and eternal death.
It rejects all the advice and help that are meant to rescue it.
It is stubborn and hard-hearted. Its own conscience clearly condemns it. Yet it has chosen to stay on the road to its doom.
But we who believe in Christ, praise God, are different people!
We have come out of death. We have passed through death and entered into life by knowing and believing in the Son of God, who loved us and gave himself for us.

24. The apostle says that God’s grace and goodness should encourage you. Do not let the world’s ungratefulness, hatred, and meanness upset you and defeat you. Do not let them make you stop your holy efforts and become evil like the world. If you do, you will lose your treasure.

This treasure is yours, not because of your own effort, but by grace alone. For there was a time when you too, just like them, were stuck in the kingdom and power of death, doing evil works, far from faith and love.
So remember to comfort yourselves with this great blessing. It is an advantage you have over others.
So what if the world, which is still in death, hates and persecutes you, who are living in life?
Who can its hatred really hurt?
The world does not have this life, but you do, and it cannot take it from you. It cannot hand you over to death either, because through Christ you have already passed out of death.

When the world does its worst, it may tell lies about you, or take away your property, or destroy your perishable body. That body will end up as a home for maggots and is going to decay anyway. So by killing your body, the world only helps you gain true life.
In this way the payback will be yours, not the world’s.
You will have the joy of being moved from death into life, while the world must stay in death.
The people of the world think they can keep you out of both the kingdom of heaven and the kingdom of earth. But they are the ones who lose body and soul.
What worse punishment could their hatred and jealousy receive?

Do not let your persecutions steal your peace and salvation. Do not let impatience and a wish for revenge make you lose your faith. Hold on, so that the devil and the world do not get that pleasure, and even more for your own good.
Instead, feel sorry for them in their misery and doom.
You lose nothing when they mistreat you. You gain, and they lose.
The world causes you a little pain in your body, for a short time. For that, it will pay dearly, both in this life and in the next.
